abstract: A network was trained by back propagation to map locative expressions of the form "noun-preposition-noun" to a semantic representation, as in Cosic and Munro (1988). The network's performance was analyzed over several simulations with training sets in both English and German. Translation of prepositions was attempted by presenting a locative expression to a network trained in one language to generate a semantic representation; the semantic representation was then presented to the network trained in the other language to generate the appropriate preposition.

paragraphs: The paper investigates translating prepositions that express spatial relationships. Its starting point is a compact expression consisting of a noun, a preposition, and another noun. A network trained by back-propagation maps this expression into a semantic representation, making the represented meaning of the relationship an intermediate step in processing.

The authors analyze network performance across several simulations using English and German training sets. To attempt translation, they first present an expression to a network trained in one language. The resulting semantic representation is then supplied to a network trained in the other language, which is used to generate the corresponding preposition.

The approach makes meaning the connection between the two language-specific networks. It frames translation as interpreting a spatial expression and then expressing that interpretation in another language. The paper’s stated contribution is the construction and analysis of this translation procedure, centered on locative prepositions and the noun contexts in which they occur.
summary.tldr: English and German networks use an intermediate semantic representation to attempt translation of spatial prepositions.

title: Translating Locative Prepositions

abstract: In the last decade the outlines of the neural structures subserving the sense of direction have begun to emerge. Several investigations have shed light on the effects of vestibular input and visual input on the head direction representation. In this paper, a model is formulated of the neural mechanisms underlying the head direction system. The model is built out of simple ingredients, depending on nothing more complicated than connectional specificity, attractor dynamics, Hebbian learning, and sigmoidal nonlinearities, but it behaves in a sophisticated way and is consistent with most of the observed properties ofreal head direction cells. In addition it makes a number of predictions that ought to be testable by reasonably straightforward experiments.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a neural model of the rat's head-direction system, which represents the direction the animal is facing. The motivating evidence concerns the neural structures involved and the effects of vestibular and visual input on that representation. The goal is to explain observed head-direction-cell behavior through an explicit set of neural mechanisms.

The model combines specific patterns of connectivity, attractor dynamics, Hebbian learning, and sigmoidal nonlinearities. These ingredients provide, respectively, structured interactions, activity patterns toward which the system tends, experience-dependent changes in connections, and nonlinear neural responses. The authors emphasize that sophisticated behavior arises from this collection of relatively simple components.

The resulting model is consistent with most observed properties of real head-direction cells and produces predictions that the authors consider testable through reasonably straightforward experiments. Its significance is the connection between a mechanistic account and empirical consequences: the same construction is used both to explain established observations and to suggest further tests. The stated agreement concerns most observed properties, preserving the scope of the authors' claim.
summary.tldr: A model built from simple neural mechanisms explains most observed head-direction-cell properties and generates testable predictions.

title: A Model of the Neural Basis of the Rat's Sense of Direction

abstract: The performance of on-line algorithms for learning dichotomies is studied. In on-line learn(cid:173) ing, the number of examples P is equivalent to the learning time, since each example is presented only once. The learning curve, or generalization error as a function of P, depends on the schedule at which the learning rate is lowered. For a target that is a perceptron rule, the learning curve of the perceptron algorithm can decrease as fast as p- 1 , if the sched(cid:173) ule is optimized. If the target is not realizable by a perceptron, the perceptron algorithm does not generally converge to the solution with lowest generalization error. For the case of unrealizability due to a simple output noise, we propose a new on-line algorithm for a perceptron yielding a learning curve that can approach the optimal generalization error as fast as p-l/2. We then generalize the perceptron algorithm to any class of thresholded smooth functions learning a target from that class. For "well-behaved" input distributions, if this algorithm converges to the optimal solution, its learning curve can decrease as fast as p-l.

paragraphs: The paper studies binary classification when each training example is presented only once. In this online setting, the number of examples also measures learning time. The authors analyze how error on unseen examples declines and show that the schedule for reducing the learning rate is central to that decline.

When the target rule can be represented by a perceptron, an optimized schedule can make error decrease as fast as the inverse of the number of examples. When the target cannot be represented, the ordinary perceptron algorithm need not reach the lowest achievable generalization error. For a particular case involving simple output noise, the authors propose an algorithm whose error can approach the optimum at an inverse-square-root rate.

They also extend the perceptron algorithm to classes of smooth functions converted into binary decisions by thresholding. For suitable input distributions, inverse-example error decay is possible if the algorithm converges to the optimal solution. That convergence condition is explicit. The results distinguish learning speed from the separate question of whether an algorithm reaches the best available predictor.
summary.tldr: Online classification rates depend on learning-rate schedules and target representability, with a modified perceptron handling a specified output-noise case.

title: On-line Learning of Dichotomies

abstract: This paper presents a rigorous characterization of how a general nonlinear learning machine generalizes during the training process when it is trained on a random sample using a gradient descent algorithm based on reduction of training error. It is shown, in particular, that best generalization performance occurs, in general, before the global minimum of the training error is achieved. The different roles played by the complexity of the machine class and the complexity of the specific machine in the class during learning are also precisely demarcated.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a rigorous characterization of how a general nonlinear learning machine generalizes during the training process when it is trained on a random sample using a gradient descent algorithm based on reduction of training error. It is shown, in particular, that best generalization performance occurs, in general, before the global minimum of the training error is achieved. The different roles played by the complexity of the machine class and the complexity of the specific machine in the class during learning are also precisely demarcated.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes how generalization changes during training for a general nonlinear learning machine. It considers training on a random sample using gradient descent to reduce training error. The question is about the course of learning: how performance beyond the training sample evolves while optimization continues to improve the training objective.

The main result is that the best generalization generally occurs before the global minimum of training error is reached. This establishes a distinction between the point favored by continued training-error reduction and the point with the best generalization. It gives a rigorous basis for treating training duration as relevant to predictive performance.

The analysis also separates the complexity of the whole machine class from the complexity of the particular machine being learned. Those are different quantities: one concerns the available family of models, and the other concerns an individual member during learning. The contribution clarifies their distinct roles while explaining why progress on the training objective need not track progress in generalization.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows that generalization generally peaks before training error reaches its global minimum.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Generalization in Neural Networks

abstract: We present two additions to the hierarchical mixture of experts (HME) architecture. By applying a likelihood splitting criteria to each expert in the HME we "grow" the tree adaptively during train(cid:173) ing. Secondly, by considering only the most probable path through the tree we may "prune" branches away, either temporarily, or per(cid:173) manently if they become redundant. We demonstrate results for the growing and path pruning algorithms which show significant speed ups and more efficient use of parameters over the standard fixed structure in discriminating between two interlocking spirals and classifying 8-bit parity patterns.

paragraphs: A hierarchical mixture of experts arranges specialized predictors in a tree. This paper asks how that tree can change during training instead of retaining a fixed structure. It introduces two complementary operations: growing the tree when additional experts are warranted and pruning branches to reduce unnecessary computation or redundant structure.

Growth uses a likelihood-based splitting criterion applied to each expert. This makes expansion depend on the learning process. The pruning procedure considers only the most probable path through the tree, allowing other branches to be omitted temporarily or removed permanently when they become redundant. The two operations address where capacity is added and where computation is spent.

The authors demonstrate the algorithms on classification involving two interlocking spirals and eight-bit parity patterns. They report substantial speed improvements and more efficient parameter use relative to the standard fixed tree. These findings support adapting the organization of the experts alongside their learned parameters, rather than treating the architecture as settled before training begins.
summary.tldr: Growing and pruning a hierarchy of experts during training improves speed and parameter efficiency on the reported classification tasks.

title: Constructive Algorithms for Hierarchical Mixtures of Experts

abstract: A neural network based approach is presented for controlling two distinct types of nonlinear systems. The first corresponds to nonlinear systems with parametric uncertainties where the parameters occur nonlinearly. The second corresponds to systems for which stabilizing control struc(cid:173) tures cannot be determined. The proposed neural controllers are shown to result in closed-loop system stability under certain conditions.
originalAbstract: A neural network based approach is presented for controlling two distinct types of nonlinear systems. The first corresponds to nonlinear systems with parametric uncertainties where the parameters occur nonlinearly. The second corresponds to systems for which stabilizing control struc(cid:173) tures cannot be determined. The proposed neural controllers are shown to result in closed-loop system stability under certain conditions.

paragraphs: This paper presents neural-network-based control for two kinds of nonlinear dynamical systems. The common challenge is selecting control actions when the relationship between the system and its controller is difficult to establish. The work centers on whether the proposed controllers can make the resulting feedback system stable.

The first kind of system has uncertain parameters that enter its dynamics nonlinearly. The uncertainty therefore concerns quantities whose influence is itself nonlinear. The second kind consists of systems for which a stabilizing control structure cannot be determined. These are distinct obstacles: uncertainty about nonlinear parameter effects and difficulty identifying a suitable form of stabilizing control.

The authors show that their neural controllers produce closed-loop stability under certain conditions. Closed-loop stability concerns the system operating together with its feedback controller, so the result addresses the behavior of the combined arrangement. The qualification matters: the claim is conditional, rather than a guarantee for every nonlinear system. The contribution establishes a stability-oriented basis for neural control across the two stated problem classes.
summary.tldr: Neural controllers provide conditional closed-loop stability for two challenging classes of nonlinear systems.

title: Neural Control for Nonlinear Dynamic Systems

abstract: The parameter space of neural networks has a Riemannian met(cid:173) ric structure. The natural Riemannian gradient should be used instead of the conventional gradient, since the former denotes the true steepest descent direction of a loss function in the Riemannian space. The behavior of the stochastic gradient learning algorithm is much more effective if the natural gradient is used. The present paper studies the information-geometrical structure of perceptrons and other networks, and prove that the on-line learning method based on the natural gradient is asymptotically as efficient as the optimal batch algorithm. Adaptive modification of the learning constant is proposed and analyzed in terms of the Riemannian mea(cid:173) sure and is shown to be efficient. The natural gradient is finally applied to blind separation of mixtured independent signal sources. 1

paragraphs: The paper argues that neural-network learning should account for the geometry of parameter space. That space has a Riemannian metric, which defines how changes in parameters are measured. Consequently, the conventional gradient need not describe the steepest decrease in loss under the geometry relevant to the model.

The natural gradient supplies that geometry-aware direction. The authors study the information-geometric structure of perceptrons and other networks and report more effective stochastic-gradient learning when this direction is used. They also propose and analyze an adaptive modification of the learning constant using the Riemannian measure.

A central theoretical result is that online natural-gradient learning is asymptotically as efficient as the optimal batch algorithm. This concerns efficiency in the asymptotic learning regime, rather than asserting identical behavior at every stage of training. The method is also applied to blind separation of mixed independent signal sources, connecting the geometric learning principle to recovering separate signals from their mixtures.
summary.tldr: Natural-gradient learning follows the geometry of parameter space and achieves a stated asymptotic efficiency match with optimal batch learning.

title: Neural Learning in Structured Parameter Spaces - Natural Riemannian Gradient

abstract: We present a method for determining the globally optimal on-line learning rule for a soft committee machine under a statistical me(cid:173) chanics framework. This work complements previous results on locally optimal rules, where only the rate of change in general(cid:173) ization error was considered. We maximize the total reduction in generalization error over the whole learning process and show how the resulting rule can significantly outperform the locally optimal rule.
originalAbstract: We present a method for determining the globally optimal on-line learning rule for a soft committee machine under a statistical me(cid:173) chanics framework. This work complements previous results on locally optimal rules, where only the rate of change in general(cid:173) ization error was considered. We maximize the total reduction in generalization error over the whole learning process and show how the resulting rule can significantly outperform the locally optimal rule.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to choose an online learning rule when the objective is improvement over the entire learning process. It studies a soft committee machine within a statistical-mechanics framework. The quantity being optimized is generalization error, which concerns the model's performance beyond the examples used to learn.

Earlier locally optimal rules considered how quickly generalization error decreases at the current stage. The authors instead maximize its total reduction across the learning process. This changes the optimization problem from choosing the best immediate improvement to choosing a rule according to the consequences of the full learning trajectory.

The resulting rule can significantly outperform the locally optimal rule in the setting studied. The finding shows why optimizing an instantaneous rate of progress need not optimize learning as a whole. The contribution is a method for deriving a globally optimal rule for the specified model and framework, together with a comparison demonstrating the value of that broader objective.
summary.tldr: Optimizing improvement across the full learning process can outperform an online rule that maximizes only immediate progress.

title: Globally Optimal On-line Learning Rules

abstract: Is there a way for an algorithm linked to an unknown body to infer by itself information about this body and the world it is in? Taking the case of space for example, is there a way for this algorithm to realize that its body is in a three dimensional world? Is it possible for this algorithm to discover how to move in a straight line? And more basically: do these questions make any sense at all given that the algorithm only has access to the very high-dimensional data consisting of its sensory inputs and motor outputs? We demonstrate in this article how these questions can be given a positive answer. We show that it is possible to make an algorithm that, by ana- lyzing the law that links its motor outputs to its sensory inputs, discovers information about the structure of the world regardless of the devices constituting the body it is linked to. We present results from simulations demonstrating a way to issue motor orders resulting in “fundamental” movements of the body as regards the structure of the physical world.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether an algorithm connected to an unfamiliar body can discover properties of that body and its environment. It considers questions such as recognizing that the world is three-dimensional and finding how to move in a straight line, despite having access only to high-dimensional sensory inputs and motor outputs.

The proposed route is to analyze the relationship between motor commands and their sensory consequences. The authors show that this relationship can reveal information about the world's structure regardless of the particular devices making up the body. This makes the connection between action and perception the basis for discovering physical organization.

Simulation results demonstrate a way to issue motor commands that produce fundamental bodily movements relative to the structure of the physical world. The contribution is a positive demonstration that meaningful spatial information and movement can be derived through sensory-motor relationships. It gives substance to the initial questions by showing how an algorithm can approach them without starting from a known description of its sensors and effectors.
summary.tldr: An algorithm can infer physical structure and generate fundamental movements by analyzing how motor outputs affect unfamiliar sensory inputs.

title: Perception of the Structure of the Physical World Using Unknown Multimodal Sensors and Effectors

abstract: We abstract out the core search problem of active learning schemes, to better understand the extent to which adaptive labeling can improve sam- ple complexity. We give various upper and lower bounds on the number of labels which need to be queried, and we prove that a popular greedy active learning rule is approximately as good as any other strategy for minimizing this number of labels.
originalAbstract: We abstract out the core search problem of active learning schemes, to better understand the extent to which adaptive labeling can improve sam- ple complexity. We give various upper and lower bounds on the number of labels which need to be queried, and we prove that a popular greedy active learning rule is approximately as good as any other strategy for minimizing this number of labels.

paragraphs: Active learning gives a learner some control over which examples receive labels. This paper isolates the search problem behind that choice to examine how much adaptive labeling can reduce the number of labels needed. The central resource is therefore access to labels, and the question is how efficiently a strategy uses that resource.

The authors derive several upper and lower bounds on label requirements. Upper bounds describe what a labeling strategy can achieve, while lower bounds identify obstacles that strategies cannot avoid within the analyzed problem. Together, these results provide a way to assess whether a method's label usage is close to what is achievable.

The main conclusion concerns a popular greedy rule for choosing queries. The authors prove that it is approximately as effective as any other strategy at minimizing the number of requested labels in their formulation. This gives theoretical support to a locally chosen sequence of queries: its simplicity can coexist with label efficiency that is close to the best available strategy.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that a popular greedy active-learning rule is approximately competitive with the best strategy for minimizing label queries.

title: Analysis of a greedy active learning strategy

This silicon cochlea includes outer hair cell (OHC) electromotility through active bidirectional coupling (ABC), a mech- anism we proposed in which OHC motile forces, through the mi- croanatomical organization of the organ of Corti, realize the cochlear ampliﬁer. Our chip measurements demonstrate that frequency responses become larger and more sharply tuned when ABC is turned on; the de- gree of the enhancement decreases with input intensity as ABC includes saturation of OHC forces. 1 Silicon Cochleae Cochlear models, mathematical and physical, with the shared goal of emulating nonlinear active cochlear behavior, shed light on how the cochlea works if based on cochlear mi- cromechanics. Among the modeling efforts, silicon cochleae have promise in meeting the need for real-time performance and low power consumption. Lyon and Mead developed the ﬁrst analog electronic cochlea [1], which employed a cascade of second-order ﬁlters with exponentially decreasing resonant frequencies. However, the cascade structure suf- fers from delay and noise accumulation and lacks fault-tolerance. paragraphs: The paper implements a model of the cochlea in an analog silicon chip. Its central concern is active hearing behavior: the cochlea does more than passively respond to sound, and outer hair cells contribute forces that can amplify its response. The chip incorporates a proposed mechanism for this amplification called active bidirectional coupling.

In this mechanism, the arrangement of structures within the organ of Corti allows outer hair cell motion to contribute to cochlear amplification. The implementation aims to reproduce this mechanical organization electronically. Its approach enhances the stimulus through active coupling, rather than obtaining amplification solely by reducing damping in individual filters.

Measurements show that switching on the coupling makes frequency responses stronger and more narrowly tuned. The enhancement becomes smaller as input intensity rises because the model includes saturation of outer hair cell forces. These results demonstrate the behavior of the proposed mechanism in hardware. The biological mechanism remains a hypothesis; the chip provides a concrete implementation with measurable, intensity-dependent amplification.
summary.tldr: An analog cochlear chip implements a proposed amplification mechanism that strengthens and sharpens frequency responses, with less enhancement at higher input intensities.

title: Active Bidirectional Coupling in a Cochlear Chip

abstract: The network topology of neurons in the brain exhibits an abundance of feedback connections, but the computational function of these feedback connections is largely unknown. We present a computational theory that characterizes the gain in computational power achieved through feedback in dynamical systems with fading memory. It implies that many such systems acquire through feedback universal computational capabilities for analog computing with a non-fading memory. In particular, we show that feedback enables such systems to process time-varying input streams in diverse ways according to rules that are implemented through internal states of the dynamical system. In contrast to previous attractor-based computational models for neural networks, these ﬂexible internal states are high-dimensional attractors of the circuit dynamics, that still allow the circuit state to absorb new information from online input streams. In this way one arrives at novel models for working memory, integration of evidence, and reward expectation in cortical circuits. We show that they are applicable to circuits of conductance-based Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) neurons with high levels of noise that reﬂect experimental data on in- vivo conditions.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theory of how feedback increases the computational power of dynamical systems whose memory otherwise fades. It is motivated by the abundance of feedback connections in the brain. The theory implies that many such systems gain universal analog computational capabilities with non-fading memory when feedback is introduced.

A key consequence is the ability to process changing input streams according to rules held in the system's internal states. These states take the form of high-dimensional attractors. They can preserve information while still allowing the circuit to incorporate new input, providing a mechanism for maintaining context during ongoing computation.

The authors use this account to develop models of working memory, evidence integration, and reward expectation in cortical circuits. They also show applicability to conductance-based Hodgkin-Huxley neuron circuits with substantial noise reflecting in-vivo experimental conditions. The contribution links an abstract result about feedback and memory to neural models that remain responsive to incoming information while retaining internal computational state.
summary.tldr: Feedback can give many fading-memory systems persistent memory and universal analog computation, supporting models of flexible cortical processing.

title: Principles of real-time computing with feedback applied to cortical microcircuit models

abstract: People perform a remarkable range of tasks that require search of the visual en- vironment for a target item among distractors. The Guided Search model (Wolfe, 1994, 2007), or GS, is perhaps the best developed psychological account of hu- man visual search. To prioritize search, GS assigns saliency to locations in the visual ﬁeld. Saliency is a linear combination of activations from retinotopic maps representing primitive visual features. GS includes heuristics for setting the gain coefﬁcient associated with each map. Variants of GS have formalized the notion of optimization as a principle of attentional control (e.g., Baldwin & Mozer, 2006; Cave, 1999; Navalpakkam & Itti, 2006; Rao et al., 2002), but every GS-like model must be ’dumbed down’ to match human data, e.g., by corrupting the saliency map with noise and by imposing arbitrary restrictions on gain modulation. We propose a principled probabilistic formulation of GS, called Experience-Guided Search (EGS), based on a generative model of the environment that makes three claims: (1) Feature detectors produce Poisson spike trains whose rates are conditioned on feature type and whether the feature belongs to a target or distractor; (2) the en- vironment and/or task is nonstationary and can change over a sequence of trials; and (3) a prior speciﬁes that features are more likely to be present for target than for distractors. Through experience, EGS infers latent environment variables that determine the gains for guiding search. Control is thus cast as probabilistic infer- ence, not optimization. We show that EGS can replicate a range of human data from visual search, including data that GS does not address.

We propose a principled probabilistic formulation of GS, called Experience-Guided Search (EGS), based on a generative model of the environment that makes three claims: (1) Feature detectors produce Poisson spike trains whose rates are conditioned on feature type and whether the feature belongs to a target or distractor; (2) the en- vironment and/or task is nonstationary and can change over a sequence of trials; and (3) a prior speciﬁes that features are more likely to be present for target than for distractors. Through experience, EGS infers latent environment variables that determine the gains for guiding search. Control is thus cast as probabilistic infer- ence, not optimization. We show that EGS can replicate a range of human data from visual search, including data that GS does not address.

paragraphs: Visual search requires directing attention toward likely targets among distractors. Guided Search models combine feature-map signals, but often need ad hoc noise or restrictions to match human behavior. Experience-Guided Search instead treats the control of those feature gains as probabilistic inference about a changing environment.

Its generative model assumes Poisson feature-detector spike trains, potentially nonstationary tasks, and a prior favoring features associated with targets. Experience updates latent variables describing the environment. Those inferred variables determine how strongly different feature maps guide attention on later trials.

The model reproduces a range of human search results, including cases outside the scope of the earlier Guided Search account. The contribution replaces arbitrary degradation of an idealized search optimizer with uncertainty and adaptation built into the model. Human-like limitations emerge from learning about the environment, making attentional control an inferential process rather than a fixed collection of gain-setting heuristics.
summary.tldr: Experience-Guided Search explains attentional gains through probabilistic learning about changing target and distractor statistics.

title: Experience-Guided Search: A Theory of Attentional Control

abstract: In the last few decades, model complexity has received a lot of press. While many methods have been proposed that jointly measure a model’s descriptive adequacy and its complexity, few measures exist that measure complexity in itself. Moreover, existing measures ignore the parameter prior, which is an inherent part of the model and affects the complexity. This paper presents a stand alone measure for model complexity, that takes the number of parameters, the functional form, the range of the parameters and the parameter prior into account. This Prior Predictive Complexity (PPC) is an intuitive and easy to compute measure. It starts from the observation that model complexity is the property of the model that enables it to fit a wide range of outcomes. The PPC then measures how wide this range exactly is.

paragraphs: The paper proposes measuring model complexity as a property in its own right. Many existing measures combine complexity with how well a model describes data. The authors instead focus on the breadth of outcomes a model can accommodate, treating that breadth as the key expression of its flexibility.

Their measure, Prior Predictive Complexity, incorporates the number of parameters, the model’s functional form, parameter ranges, and the parameter prior. Including the prior matters because it is part of the probabilistic model and affects its complexity. Counting parameters alone therefore does not capture all the ingredients that this measure is designed to consider.

PPC measures how wide the model’s range of outcomes is through its prior predictive behavior. The authors describe the measure as intuitive and easy to compute. Its conceptual contribution is a unified way to account for several sources of model flexibility while keeping the complexity question distinct from descriptive adequacy on a particular dataset.
summary.tldr: Prior Predictive Complexity measures model flexibility through the breadth of possible outcomes, accounting for parameters, functional form, ranges, and priors.

title: Measuring model complexity with the prior predictive

abstract: An accurate model of patient survival time can help in the treatment and care of cancer patients. The common practice of providing survival time estimates based only on population averages for the site and stage of cancer ignores many important individual differences among patients. In this paper, we propose a local regression method for learning patient-specific survival time distribution based on patient attributes such as blood tests and clinical assessments. When tested on a cohort of more than 2000 cancer patients, our method gives survival time predictions that are much more accurate than popular survival analysis models such as the Cox and Aalen regression models. Our results also show that using patient-specific attributes can reduce the prediction error on survival time by as much as 20% when compared to using cancer site and stage only.

It proposes a local regression method for learning an individual patient's survival-time distribution from attributes including blood tests and clinical assessments.

Estimating a patient-specific distribution makes the modeling target the range of possible survival times associated with that patient's information. The approach uses individual attributes to distinguish patients who would otherwise share a site-and-stage-based estimate. Its purpose is more accurate survival prediction, which the paper motivates as potentially useful for treatment and care.

In a cohort of more than 2,000 cancer patients, the method produces substantially more accurate predictions than Cox and Aalen regression models. The authors also report prediction-error reductions of as much as 20% when individual attributes are used instead of cancer site and stage alone. This is an observed predictive improvement in the studied cohort.
summary.tldr: Patient-specific local regression improves survival prediction in a cancer cohort, with up to 20% lower error from using individual attributes.

title: Learning Patient-Specific Cancer Survival Distributions as a Sequence of Dependent Regressors

abstract: Variability in single neuron models is typically implemented either by a stochastic Leaky-Integrate-and-Fire model or by a model of the Generalized Linear Model (GLM) family. We use analytical and numerical methods to relate state-of-the-art models from both schools of thought. First we find the analytical expressions relating the subthreshold voltage from the Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire model (AdEx) to the Spike-Response Model with escape noise (SRM as an example of a GLM). Then we calculate numerically the link-function that provides the firing probability given a deterministic membrane potential. We find a mathematical expression for this link-function and test the ability of the GLM to predict the firing probability of a neuron receiving complex stimulation. Comparing the prediction performance of various link-functions, we find that a GLM with an exponential link-function provides an excellent approximation to the Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire with colored-noise input. These results help to understand the relationship between the different approaches to stochastic neuron models.

The aim is to explain mathematically how their descriptions relate, and to test how well a GLM can reproduce firing probabilities associated with a more detailed neuronal model under complex stimulation.

The authors first derive analytical relationships between subthreshold voltage in the Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire model and a Spike-Response Model with escape noise. They then numerically calculate a link function that converts a deterministic membrane potential into a firing probability. A mathematical expression for this function makes the connection between voltage and probabilistic spiking explicit.

The study compares several link functions in firing-probability prediction. A GLM using an exponential link function provides an excellent approximation to the Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire model with colored-noise input. This is a result for the stated model and input setting. It helps explain when these different modeling approaches can give closely matching probabilistic descriptions of neuronal firing.
summary.tldr: Analytical and numerical connections show that an exponential-link GLM closely approximates AdEx firing probabilities with colored-noise input.

title: From Stochastic Nonlinear Integrate-and-Fire to Generalized Linear Models

abstract: We introduce a new convergent variant of Q-learning, called speedy Q-learning, to address the problem of slow convergence in the standard form of the Q-learning algorithm. We prove a PAC bound on the performance of SQL, which shows that for an MDP with n state-action pairs and the discount factor \gamma only T=O\big(\log(n)/(\epsilon^{2}(1-\gamma)^{4})\big) steps are required for the SQL algorithm to converge to an \epsilon-optimal action-value function with high probability. This bound has a better dependency on 1/\epsilon and 1/(1-\gamma), and thus, is tighter than the best available result for Q-learning. Our bound is also superior to the existing results for both model-free and model-based instances of batch Q-value iteration that are considered to be more efficient than the incremental methods like Q-learning.

paragraphs: The paper introduces speedy Q-learning, a convergent variant designed to address slow convergence in standard Q-learning. Its target is the action-value function, which evaluates actions in states of a Markov decision process. The main contribution is a theoretical bound on how many steps are sufficient to obtain an approximately optimal action-value function with high probability.

For n state-action pairs and discount factor gamma, the stated bound is O(log(n)/(epsilon squared times (1 minus gamma) to the fourth power)). Here epsilon determines the desired accuracy. The expression makes explicit how the sufficient step count depends on the number of state-action pairs, the accuracy target, and the discount factor.

The authors show better dependence on inverse accuracy and inverse discount gap than the best available Q-learning result they discuss. Their bound also improves on existing results for the considered model-free and model-based batch Q-value iteration methods. The finding is a stronger convergence guarantee for this variant, with the comparison expressed through theoretical performance bounds.
summary.tldr: Speedy Q-learning provides a convergent variant with a tighter high-probability step bound than the compared Q-learning and batch iteration results.

title: Speedy Q-Learning

abstract: We propose two new principal component analysis methods in this paper utilizing a semiparametric model. The according methods are named Copula Component Analysis (COCA) and Copula PCA. The semiparametric model assumes that, af- ter unspeciﬁed marginally monotone transformations, the distributions are multi- variate Gaussian. The COCA and Copula PCA accordingly estimate the leading eigenvectors of the correlation and covariance matrices of the latent Gaussian dis- tribution. The robust nonparametric rank-based correlation coefﬁcient estimator, Spearman’s rho, is exploited in estimation. We prove that, under suitable condi- tions, although the marginal distributions can be arbitrarily continuous, the COCA and Copula PCA estimators obtain fast estimation rates and are feature selection consistent in the setting where the dimension is nearly exponentially large relative to the sample size. Careful numerical experiments on the synthetic and real data are conducted to back up the theoretical results. We also discuss the relationship with the transelliptical component analysis proposed by Han and Liu (2012).

paragraphs: The paper introduces two principal component methods under a semiparametric assumption: unspecified monotone transformations of individual variables make their joint distribution multivariate Gaussian. This allows flexibility in the observed marginal distributions while retaining a structured latent distribution. The methods seek leading directions in that latent Gaussian representation.

Copula Component Analysis, or COCA, estimates leading eigenvectors of the latent correlation matrix. Copula PCA instead targets the latent covariance matrix. Both exploit Spearman's rho, a robust rank-based correlation estimator. Their distinction matters because they recover directions from different matrices, even though both use the same broad transformed-Gaussian modeling framework.

Under suitable conditions, the authors prove fast estimation rates and feature-selection consistency even when dimension is nearly exponential relative to sample size. These results allow arbitrary continuous marginal distributions within the stated model and conditions. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real data support the theory. The contribution is therefore a conditional route to high-dimensional component estimation that accommodates flexible marginal behavior.
summary.tldr: COCA and Copula PCA use rank-based estimation to recover latent Gaussian components with high-dimensional guarantees under suitable conditions.

title: Semiparametric Principal Component Analysis

abstract: A common classifier for unlabeled nodes on undirected graphs uses label propagation from the labeled nodes, equivalent to the harmonic predictor on Gaussian random fields (GRFs). For active learning on GRFs, the commonly used V-optimality criterion queries nodes that reduce the L2 (regression) loss. V-optimality satisfies a submodularity property showing that greedy reduction produces a (1 − 1/e) globally optimal solution. However, L2 loss may not characterise the true nature of 0/1 loss in classification problems and thus may not be the best choice for active learning. We consider a new criterion we call Σ-optimality, which queries the node that minimizes the sum of the elements in the predictive covariance. Σ-optimality directly optimizes the risk of the surveying problem, which is to determine the proportion of nodes belonging to one class. In this paper we extend submodularity guarantees from V-optimality to Σ-optimality using properties specific to GRFs. We further show that GRFs satisfy the suppressor-free condition in addition to the conditional independence inherited from Markov random fields. We test Σ-optimality on real-world graphs with both synthetic and real data and show that it outperforms V-optimality and other related methods on classification.

paragraphs: When labels are propagated across an undirected graph, active learning asks which node should be labeled next. A common criterion, V-optimality, selects queries to reduce squared regression loss. The paper questions whether this objective is well matched to classification, where the outcome of interest is often whether a predicted label is correct.

It directly optimizes risk for surveying: estimating the fraction of nodes belonging to one class. Using properties of Gaussian random fields, the authors extend submodularity guarantees to this objective, giving theoretical support to greedy query selection.

The analysis also establishes that these Gaussian random fields satisfy a suppressor-free condition, alongside their inherited conditional independence structure. Experiments on real graphs with synthetic and real data show better classification performance than V-optimality and related methods. The distinction between results matters: surveying provides the directly optimized risk, while the classification advantage is established empirically in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Sigma-optimality offers a theoretically supported graph-query criterion that directly targets surveying risk and improves classification in the reported experiments.

title: Σ-Optimality for Active Learning on Gaussian Random Fields

abstract: This paper presents Correlated Nystrom Views (XNV), a fast semi-supervised algorithm for regression and classification. The algorithm draws on two main ideas. First, it generates two views consisting of computationally inexpensive random features. Second, multiview regression, using Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) on unlabeled data, biases the regression towards useful features. It has been shown that CCA regression can substantially reduce variance with a minimal increase in bias if the views contains accurate estimators. Recent theoretical and empirical work shows that regression with random features closely approximates kernel regression, implying that the accuracy requirement holds for random views. We show that XNV consistently outperforms a state-of-the-art algorithm for semi-supervised learning: substantially improving predictive performance and reducing the variability of performance on a wide variety of real-world datasets, whilst also reducing runtime by orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Correlated Nystrom Views, or XNV, is a semi-supervised method for regression and classification. It combines inexpensive random features with information from unlabeled examples. The algorithm first generates two feature views, then uses canonical correlation analysis on unlabeled data to steer regression toward useful features.

The motivation comes from a conditional result about multiview regression: when the views contain accurate estimators, this procedure can substantially reduce variance while adding little bias. The paper connects that requirement to existing theoretical and empirical findings that random-feature regression closely approximates kernel regression. This provides a rationale for constructing the two views cheaply rather than requiring elaborate representations.

Across a wide variety of real-world datasets, the authors report that XNV consistently outperforms a state-of-the-art semi-supervised algorithm. They find better predictions, less variability in performance, and runtime reductions of orders of magnitude. These findings suggest that inexpensive feature construction and correlation information from unlabeled data can work together effectively in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: XNV uses correlated random-feature views and unlabeled data to improve semi-supervised prediction while greatly reducing runtime.

title: Correlated random features for fast semi-supervised learning

abstract: Stochastic Gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo (SG-MCMC) algorithms have become increasingly popular for Bayesian inference in large-scale applications. Even though these methods have proved useful in several scenarios, their performance is often limited by their bias. In this study, we propose a novel sampling algorithm that aims to reduce the bias of SG-MCMC while keeping the variance at a reasonable level. Our approach is based on a numerical sequence acceleration method, namely the Richardson-Romberg extrapolation, which simply boils down to running almost the same SG-MCMC algorithm twice in parallel with different step sizes. We illustrate our framework on the popular Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) algorithm and propose a novel SG-MCMC algorithm referred to as Stochastic Gradient Richardson-Romberg Langevin Dynamics (SGRRLD). We provide formal theoretical analysis and show that SGRRLD is asymptotically consistent, satisfies a central limit theorem, and its non-asymptotic bias and the mean squared-error can be bounded. Our results show that SGRRLD attains higher rates of convergence than SGLD in both finite-time and asymptotically, and it achieves the theoretical accuracy of the methods that are based on higher-order integrators. We support our findings using both synthetic and real data experiments.

This paper proposes reducing that bias while keeping variance at a reasonable level. Its approach uses Richardson-Romberg extrapolation, a numerical technique for improving an approximation through calculations at different resolutions.

This offers a route to improved accuracy through paired runs of a familiar sampler, with the theoretical analysis addressing the behavior of their combined estimator.

The authors establish asymptotic consistency, a central limit theorem, and finite-time bounds on bias and mean squared error. They show higher convergence rates than SGLD both at finite times and asymptotically, attaining the theoretical accuracy of methods using higher-order integrators. Synthetic and real-data experiments support the findings. The contribution ties a relatively simple sampling construction to stronger accuracy guarantees.
summary.tldr: Combining stochastic-gradient Langevin runs at different step sizes reduces bias and yields stronger convergence guarantees through Richardson-Romberg extrapolation.

title: Stochastic Gradient Richardson-Romberg Markov Chain Monte Carlo

abstract: Estimating patient's clinical state from multiple concurrent physiological streams plays an important role in determining if a therapeutic intervention is necessary and for triaging patients in the hospital. In this paper we construct a non-parametric learning algorithm to estimate the clinical state of a patient. The algorithm addresses several known challenges with clinical state estimation such as eliminating bias introduced by therapeutic intervention censoring, increasing the timeliness of state estimation while ensuring a sufficient accuracy, and the ability to detect anomalous clinical states. These benefits are obtained by combining the tools of non-parametric Bayesian inference, permutation testing, and generalizations of the empirical Bernstein inequality. The algorithm is validated using real-world data from a cancer ward in a large academic hospital.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to estimate a patient's clinical condition from several physiological measurements collected concurrently. Such estimates can inform whether an intervention is needed and how patients should be prioritized. The challenge is to turn multiple changing streams into a timely assessment whose accuracy can be supported statistically.

The authors construct a non-parametric learning algorithm that combines Bayesian inference, permutation testing, and generalizations of the empirical Bernstein inequality. The combination targets three issues together: bias caused by therapeutic intervention censoring, delays in producing sufficiently accurate estimates, and detection of anomalous clinical states. Intervention censoring matters because treatment affects which observations remain available for estimating the patient's condition.

The algorithm is validated on real patient data from a cancer ward in a large academic hospital. The stated contribution is therefore a method addressing several connected estimation problems, supported by a clinical-data evaluation. Its emphasis on timeliness alongside accuracy makes confidence in an estimate part of the learning problem, rather than treating speed and reliability as unrelated goals.
summary.tldr: A non-parametric algorithm combines statistical tools to estimate clinical state promptly, address intervention-related bias, and detect anomalies.

title: A Non-parametric Learning Method for Confidently Estimating Patient's Clinical State and Dynamics

abstract: Medical researchers are coming to appreciate that many diseases are in fact complex, heterogeneous syndromes composed of subpopulations that express different variants of a related complication. Longitudinal data extracted from individual electronic health records (EHR) offer an exciting new way to study subtle differences in the way these diseases progress over time. In this paper, we focus on answering two questions that can be asked using these databases of longitudinal EHR data. First, we want to understand whether there are individuals with similar disease trajectories and whether there are a small number of degrees of freedom that account for differences in trajectories across the population. Second, we want to understand how important clinical outcomes are associated with disease trajectories. To answer these questions, we propose the Disease Trajectory Map (DTM), a novel probabilistic model that learns low-dimensional representations of sparse and irregularly sampled longitudinal data. We propose a stochastic variational inference algorithm for learning the DTM that allows the model to scale to large modern medical datasets. To demonstrate the DTM, we analyze data collected on patients with the complex autoimmune disease, scleroderma. We find that DTM learns meaningful representations of disease trajectories and that the representations are significantly associated with important clinical outcomes.

paragraphs: Patients with the same disease label can experience different patterns of progression. This paper asks whether longitudinal health records reveal groups of similar trajectories and whether a small number of dimensions can describe differences across patients. It also asks how those trajectories relate to clinically important outcomes.

The proposed Disease Trajectory Map is a probabilistic model that learns compact representations from longitudinal observations. It explicitly addresses data that are sparse and collected at irregular times, as commonly occurs in electronic health records. A stochastic variational inference algorithm provides a way to learn the model at the scale of large medical datasets.

The authors demonstrate the approach using records from patients with scleroderma, a complex autoimmune disease. They find that the learned representations capture meaningful disease trajectories and are significantly associated with important clinical outcomes. These results support using the representation to study differences in progression and their clinical relationships. The stated finding is an association between trajectories and outcomes; it does not establish that the trajectories cause those outcomes.
summary.tldr: Disease Trajectory Maps summarize irregular patient histories into compact representations associated with meaningful clinical outcomes.

title: Disease Trajectory Maps

abstract: In unsupervised domain mapping, the learner is given two unmatched datasets $A$ and $B$. The goal is to learn a mapping $G_{AB}$ that translates a sample in $A$ to the analog sample in $B$. Recent approaches have shown that when learning simultaneously both $G_{AB}$ and the inverse mapping $G_{BA}$, convincing mappings are obtained. In this work, we present a method of learning $G_{AB}$ without learning $G_{BA}$. This is done by learning a mapping that maintains the distance between a pair of samples. Moreover, good mappings are obtained, even by maintaining the distance between different parts of the same sample before and after mapping. We present experimental results that the new method not only allows for one sided mapping learning, but also leads to preferable numerical results over the existing circularity-based constraint. Our entire code is made publicly available at~\url{https://github.com/sagiebenaim/DistanceGAN}.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain mapping starts with two datasets whose examples are not paired. The goal is to translate an example from one domain into its counterpart in the other. Previous approaches obtained convincing mappings by learning both translation directions together. This paper develops a method that learns only the desired forward mapping.

The method constrains the mapping to preserve distances between pairs of samples. This supplies a relationship that can be maintained across domains even without matched examples. The authors also show that useful mappings can be learned by preserving distances between different parts of a single sample before and after translation.

Experiments demonstrate one-sided mapping and report preferable numerical results compared with an existing circularity-based constraint. The contribution is a way to guide translation through distance relationships without requiring a separately learned reverse mapping. The results support both the between-sample and within-sample forms of this idea in the settings examined, and the authors make their implementation publicly available.
summary.tldr: Preserving distances between samples or their parts enables unsupervised domain translation without learning a reverse mapping.

title: One-Sided Unsupervised Domain Mapping

abstract: Kernel methods have recently attracted resurgent interest, showing performance competitive with deep neural networks in tasks such as speech recognition. The random Fourier features map is a technique commonly used to scale up kernel machines, but employing the randomized feature map means that $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ samples are required to achieve an approximation error of at most $\epsilon$. We investigate some alternative schemes for constructing feature maps that are deterministic, rather than random, by approximating the kernel in the frequency domain using Gaussian quadrature. We show that deterministic feature maps can be constructed, for any $\gamma > 0$, to achieve error $\epsilon$ with $O(e^{e^\gamma} + \epsilon^{-1/\gamma})$ samples as $\epsilon$ goes to 0. Our method works particularly well with sparse ANOVA kernels, which are inspired by the convolutional layer of CNNs. We validate our methods on datasets in different domains, such as MNIST and TIMIT, showing that deterministic features are faster to generate and achieve accuracy comparable to the state-of-the-art kernel methods based on random Fourier features.

This paper investigates deterministic feature maps built through Gaussian quadrature, using a numerical approximation of the kernel in the frequency domain instead of random sampling.

The authors show that, for any positive γ, deterministic maps can attain error ε with O(exp(exp(γ)) + ε⁻¹⁄γ) samples as ε approaches zero. The bound exposes a trade-off: changing γ changes both the error-dependent term and a potentially large additive term. It is an asymptotic approximation result, with the expression retaining both contributions.

The approach works particularly well with sparse ANOVA kernels, which are inspired by convolutional layers in neural networks. Evaluations on datasets including MNIST and TIMIT show that the deterministic features are faster to generate while delivering accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art kernel methods using random Fourier features. The findings support carefully designed deterministic features as a practical alternative to randomized kernel approximations.
summary.tldr: Gaussian quadrature produces deterministic kernel features with favorable asymptotic approximation bounds and competitive empirical accuracy.

title: Gaussian Quadrature for Kernel Features

abstract: In recent years, great progress has been made in a variety of application domains thanks to the development of increasingly deeper neural networks. Unfortunately, the huge number of units of these networks makes them expensive both computationally and memory-wise. To overcome this, exploiting the fact that deep networks are over-parametrized, several compression strategies have been proposed. These methods, however, typically start from a network that has been trained in a standard manner, without considering such a future compression. In this paper, we propose to explicitly account for compression in the training process. To this end, we introduce a regularizer that encourages the parameter matrix of each layer to have low rank during training. We show that accounting for compression during training allows us to learn much more compact, yet at least as effective, models than state-of-the-art compression techniques.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can require substantial memory and computation. Compression methods exploit their excess parameters, but many begin with a network trained without considering its later compression. This paper changes the training objective so that producing a compact model becomes part of learning from the outset.

The proposed regularizer encourages each layer's parameter matrix to have low rank. In plain terms, it favors matrices whose parameters can be represented through fewer independent directions. This links the structure learned during training to the structure that makes compression possible, rather than leaving all responsibility for compactness to a later processing step.

The authors report models that are substantially more compact while remaining at least as effective as those produced by the compared state-of-the-art compression techniques. The stated result supports treating training and compression as connected design decisions. Its significance is that an explicit preference for compressible parameter structure can improve the eventual size–effectiveness tradeoff, rather than requiring compactness to be pursued only after ordinary training has finished.
summary.tldr: Encouraging low-rank layer parameters during training produces more compact models while preserving effectiveness in the reported comparisons.

title: Compression-aware Training of Deep Networks

abstract: Despite advances in scalable models, the inference tools used for Gaussian processes (GPs) have yet to fully capitalize on developments in computing hardware. We present an efficient and general approach to GP inference based on Blackbox Matrix-Matrix multiplication (BBMM). BBMM inference uses a modified batched version of the conjugate gradients algorithm to derive all terms for training and inference in a single call. BBMM reduces the asymptotic complexity of exact GP inference from O(n^3) to O(n^2). Adapting this algorithm to scalable approximations and complex GP models simply requires a routine for efficient matrix-matrix multiplication with the kernel and its derivative. In addition, BBMM uses a specialized preconditioner to substantially speed up convergence. In experiments we show that BBMM effectively uses GPU hardware to dramatically accelerate both exact GP inference and scalable approximations. Additionally, we provide GPyTorch, a software platform for scalable GP inference via BBMM, built on PyTorch.

paragraphs: Gaussian process inference can be expensive even when the model itself has been designed to scale. This paper focuses on the computational machinery used for training and prediction, asking how it can better exploit modern hardware. Its proposed approach, Blackbox Matrix-Matrix multiplication, or BBMM, organizes inference around matrix-matrix operations.

BBMM uses a modified, batched conjugate-gradients algorithm to obtain all terms needed for training and inference in a single call. The paper states that this reduces the asymptotic cost of exact Gaussian process inference from cubic to quadratic in the number of observations. A specialized preconditioner further accelerates convergence of the iterative computation.

The same approach can support scalable approximations and complex Gaussian process models when efficient multiplication routines are available for their kernel matrices and derivatives. Experiments demonstrate substantial GPU acceleration for both exact inference and approximations. The authors also introduce GPyTorch, a PyTorch-based platform implementing this approach. The contribution thus joins a computational framework, a reusable interface for different models, and an accompanying software platform.
summary.tldr: BBMM reorganizes Gaussian process inference around GPU-friendly matrix operations, with quadratic stated complexity and implementation in GPyTorch.

title: GPyTorch: Blackbox Matrix-Matrix Gaussian Process Inference with GPU Acceleration

abstract: We replace the output layer of deep neural nets, typically the softmax function, by a novel interpolating function. And we propose end-to-end training and testing algorithms for this new architecture. Compared to classical neural nets with softmax function as output activation, the surrogate with interpolating function as output activation combines advantages of both deep and manifold learning. The new framework demonstrates the following major advantages: First, it is better applicable to the case with insufficient training data. Second, it significantly improves the generalization accuracy on a wide variety of networks. The algorithm is implemented in PyTorch, and the code is available at https://github.com/ BaoWangMath/DNN-DataDependentActivation.

paragraphs: The output activation is the part of a neural network that turns its learned internal representation into a final prediction. This paper changes that component by replacing the commonly used softmax function with a new interpolating function. The proposed change therefore concerns how learned features produce outputs, while remaining part of a deep-network architecture.

The authors provide training and testing algorithms for the resulting model, including end-to-end training. They describe the framework as combining advantages of deep learning and manifold learning. The motivation is to bring those two approaches together at the prediction stage, using an interpolating output function within a trainable neural system.

Compared with conventional networks using softmax, the paper reports better applicability when training data are insufficient and significant generalization improvements across a wide variety of networks. These findings suggest that output-layer design can materially affect learning from limited examples and prediction on unseen data. A PyTorch implementation accompanies the approach, making the proposed architecture and algorithms available as an implemented method.
summary.tldr: Replacing softmax with an interpolating output function improves reported generalization and suitability for limited training data.

title: Deep Neural Nets with Interpolating Function as Output Activation

abstract: We consider the setting of prediction with expert advice; a learner makes predictions by aggregating those of a group of experts. Under this setting, and for the right choice of loss function and ``mixing'' algorithm, it is possible for the learner to achieve a constant regret regardless of the number of prediction rounds. For example, a constant regret can be achieved for \emph{mixable} losses using the \emph{aggregating algorithm}. The \emph{Generalized Aggregating Algorithm} (GAA) is a name for a family of algorithms parameterized by convex functions on simplices (entropies), which reduce to the aggregating algorithm when using the \emph{Shannon entropy} $\operatorname{S}$. For a given entropy $\Phi$, losses for which a constant regret is possible using the \textsc{GAA} are called $\Phi$-mixable. Which losses are $\Phi$-mixable was previously left as an open question. We fully characterize $\Phi$-mixability and answer other open questions posed by \cite{Reid2015}. We show that the Shannon entropy $\operatorname{S}$ is fundamental in nature when it comes to mixability; any $\Phi$-mixable loss is necessarily $\operatorname{S}$-mixable, and the lowest worst-case regret of the \textsc{GAA} is achieved using the Shannon entropy. Finally, by leveraging the connection between the \emph{mirror descent algorithm} and the update step of the GAA, we suggest a new \emph{adaptive} generalized aggregating algorithm and analyze its performance in terms of the regret bound.

paragraphs: In prediction with expert advice, a learner combines forecasts from several experts. Regret measures the learner’s accumulated loss relative to an expert benchmark. For some losses and aggregation rules, this gap can remain bounded independently of how many prediction rounds occur. Mixability describes the compatibility that makes such constant regret possible.

The paper studies the Generalized Aggregating Algorithm, a family whose behavior depends on a chosen convex entropy function. It fully characterizes which losses are mixable for a given entropy, resolving an open question about when this family supports constant regret. This turns the choice of entropy into something that can be assessed through a precise characterization.

The results also establish a privileged role for Shannon entropy: every loss mixable under another entropy is also Shannon-mixable, and Shannon entropy achieves the lowest worst-case regret within the generalized algorithm family. Finally, the authors connect its update to mirror descent, propose an adaptive version, and analyze its regret bound. The claims concern this aggregation framework and its compatible losses.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes generalized mixability and shows that Shannon entropy achieves the lowest worst-case regret in the Generalized Aggregating Algorithm family.

title: Constant Regret, Generalized Mixability, and Mirror Descent

abstract: Potential based reward shaping is a powerful technique for accelerating convergence of reinforcement learning algorithms. Typically, such information includes an estimate of the optimal value function and is often provided by a human expert or other sources of domain knowledge. However, this information is often biased or inaccurate and can mislead many reinforcement learning algorithms. In this paper, we apply Bayesian Model Combination with multiple experts in a way that learns to trust a good combination of experts as training progresses. This approach is both computationally efficient and general, and is shown numerically to improve convergence across discrete and continuous domains and different reinforcement learning algorithms.

In this paper, we apply Bayesian Model Combination with multiple experts in a way that learns to trust a good combination of experts as training progresses. This approach is both computationally efficient and general, and is shown numerically to improve convergence across discrete and continuous domains and different reinforcement learning algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how reinforcement learning can benefit from several sources of expert guidance when their advice may be imperfect. It focuses on potential-based reward shaping, which uses information such as an estimate of the optimal value function to accelerate learning. Human knowledge or other domain information can supply that guidance, but bias and inaccuracies can also mislead the learner.

The proposed approach applies Bayesian Model Combination to multiple experts. As training progresses, it learns to trust a useful combination of their guidance. This makes the use of expert information adaptive: the method's treatment of the available experts develops during learning rather than assuming that a single source should be trusted throughout.

The authors describe the approach as computationally efficient and general. Numerical experiments show improved convergence across discrete and continuous domains and across different reinforcement learning algorithms. These results support combining expert guidance as a practical aid to learning in the evaluated settings, without requiring the guidance to be uniformly accurate.
summary.tldr: Bayesian combination of multiple experts adaptively guides reward shaping and improves reinforcement learning convergence in numerical evaluations.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Multiple Experts: A Bayesian Model Combination Approach

abstract: Recent milestones in equilibrium computation, such as the success of Libratus, show that it is possible to compute strong solutions to two-player zero-sum games in theory and practice. This is not the case for games with more than two players, which remain one of the main open challenges in computational game theory. This paper focuses on zero-sum games where a team of players faces an opponent, as is the case, for example, in Bridge, collusion in poker, and many non-recreational applications such as war, where the colluders do not have time or means of communicating during battle, collusion in bidding, where communication during the auction is illegal, and coordinated swindling in public. The possibility for the team members to communicate before game play—that is, coordinate their strategies ex ante—makes the use of behavioral strategies unsatisfactory. The reasons for this are closely related to the fact that the team can be represented as a single player with imperfect recall. We propose a new game representation, the realization form, that generalizes the sequence form but can also be applied to imperfect-recall games. Then, we use it to derive an auxiliary game that is equivalent to the original one. It provides a sound way to map the problem of finding an optimal ex-ante-correlated strategy for the team to the well-understood Nash equilibrium-finding problem in a (larger) two-player zero-sum perfect-recall game. By reasoning over the auxiliary game, we devise an anytime algorithm, fictitious team-play, that is guaranteed to converge to an optimal coordinated strategy for the team against an optimal opponent, and that is dramatically faster than the prior state-of-the-art algorithm for this problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies zero-sum games in which several teammates face a single opponent. Team members may coordinate their strategies before play but cannot communicate during play. This advance coordination creates dependencies between their decisions that ordinary behavioral strategies represent unsatisfactorily. Treating the team as one player introduces a related imperfect-recall difficulty.

The authors introduce the realization form, a representation that generalizes sequence form and also accommodates imperfect-recall games. They use it to construct an equivalent auxiliary game with two players and perfect recall. Although this game is larger, it translates the team's optimal advance-coordination problem into a two-player zero-sum Nash equilibrium problem, where established solution ideas apply.

Reasoning through that auxiliary game yields fictitious team-play, an anytime algorithm that can provide a strategy while computation continues. The authors guarantee convergence to an optimal coordinated team strategy against an optimal opponent. They also report that it is dramatically faster than the previous state-of-the-art algorithm for this problem. The contribution links a richer representation of coordinated behavior to both a convergence guarantee and a practical computational improvement.
summary.tldr: A new game representation turns advance team coordination into an equivalent two-player problem and enables a convergent, faster solution algorithm.

title: Ex ante coordination and collusion in zero-sum multi-player extensive-form games

abstract: Reinforcement learning is known to be sample inefficient, preventing its application to many real-world problems, especially with high dimensional observations like images. Transferring knowledge from other auxiliary tasks is a powerful tool for improving the learning efficiency. However, the usage of auxiliary tasks has been limited so far due to the difficulty in selecting and combining different auxiliary tasks. In this work, we propose a principled online learning algorithm that dynamically combines different auxiliary tasks to speed up training for reinforcement learning. Our method is based on the idea that auxiliary tasks should provide gradient directions that, in the long term, help to decrease the loss of the main task. We show in various environments that our algorithm can effectively combine a variety of different auxiliary tasks and achieves significant speedup compared to previous heuristic approches of adapting auxiliary task weights.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can require large amounts of experience, particularly when observations are high dimensional, such as images. Auxiliary tasks offer additional learning signals that can make this process more efficient. The difficulty is deciding how much influence each task should have, since selecting and combining useful tasks is itself a learning problem.

The paper proposes an online algorithm that adjusts auxiliary task weights during training. Its guiding idea is that an auxiliary task should produce parameter updates that help reduce the main task’s loss over the longer term. This gives the weighting process a criterion tied to the reinforcement learning objective, rather than relying only on a heuristic choice of weights.

Across several environments, the authors report that the algorithm successfully combines varied auxiliary tasks and speeds up training significantly compared with earlier heuristic weighting approaches. The findings support treating the balance between auxiliary tasks as something that can be learned adaptively. The contribution concerns how to use additional tasks effectively, connecting their training influence to progress on the main task.
summary.tldr: An online algorithm learns auxiliary task weights to accelerate reinforcement learning by favoring updates that help the main task over time.

title: Adaptive Auxiliary Task Weighting for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Time series with non-uniform intervals occur in many applications, and are difficult to model using standard recurrent neural networks (RNNs). We generalize RNNs to have continuous-time hidden dynamics defined by ordinary differential equations (ODEs), a model we call ODE-RNNs. Furthermore, we use ODE-RNNs to replace the recognition network of the recently-proposed Latent ODE model. Both ODE-RNNs and Latent ODEs can naturally handle arbitrary time gaps between observations, and can explicitly model the probability of observation times using Poisson processes. We show experimentally that these ODE-based models outperform their RNN-based counterparts on irregularly-sampled data.
