paragraphs: Time-series observations often arrive with unequal gaps between them, which makes them difficult to represent using standard recurrent neural networks. This paper introduces ODE-RNNs, whose hidden dynamics are defined in continuous time by ordinary differential equations. The model can therefore evolve its hidden representation over the actual interval separating successive observations.

The authors also use an ODE-RNN as the recognition network in a Latent ODE model. This applies the same continuous-time treatment when inferring a latent representation from observations. Both model families naturally accommodate arbitrary gaps, so elapsed time is directly part of the dynamics used to connect measurements across the series.

The models can additionally represent the probability of observation times through Poisson processes. This gives them a way to model when measurements occur as well as their observed values. Experiments show that the ODE-based models outperform their RNN-based counterparts on irregularly sampled data. The reported findings support continuous-time hidden dynamics as a useful modeling choice for the evaluated data, rather than establishing an advantage for every time-series problem.
summary.tldr: ODE-RNNs and Latent ODEs use continuous-time dynamics to handle irregular observations and outperform RNN counterparts in the reported experiments.

title: Latent Ordinary Differential Equations for Irregularly-Sampled Time Series

abstract: Paraphrase generation is a longstanding important problem in natural language processing. Recent progress in deep generative models has shown promising results on discrete latent variables for text generation. Inspired by variational autoencoders with discrete latent structures, in this work, we propose a latent bag of words (BOW) model for paraphrase generation. We ground the semantics of a discrete latent variable by the target BOW. We use this latent variable to build a fully differentiable content planning and surface realization pipeline. Specifically, we use source words to predict their neighbors and model the target BOW with a mixture of softmax. We use gumbel top-k reparameterization to perform differentiable subset sampling from the predicted BOW distribution. We retrieve the sampled word embeddings and use them to augment the decoder and guide its generation search space. Our latent BOW model not only enhances the decoder, but also exhibits clear interpretability. We show the model interpretability with regard to (1). unsupervised learning of word neighbors (2). the step-by-step generation procedure. Extensive experiments demonstrate the model's transparent and effective generation process.

paragraphs: Paraphrase generation requires expressing content in a different form. This paper introduces a latent bag-of-words model that gives the generator an explicit representation of intended word content. Grounding the discrete latent variable in the target bag of words makes the intermediate representation interpretable and connects content planning with the final production of text.

The model uses source words to predict neighboring words and represents the target bag-of-words distribution with a mixture of softmax components. It then applies Gumbel top-k reparameterization to sample a subset while preserving differentiability. Embeddings of the sampled words are supplied to the decoder, helping guide the space of generations it considers.

The resulting planning and surface-realization pipeline can be trained together. The paper demonstrates interpretability through the learned word neighborhoods and the step-by-step generation process, and reports extensive experiments supporting effective, transparent generation. Its contribution is to make the generator's content choices visible through a word-based latent representation while also using those choices to strengthen decoding.
summary.tldr: A differentiably sampled latent bag of words provides interpretable content plans that guide paraphrase generation.

title: Paraphrase Generation with Latent Bag of Words

abstract: Despite achieving tremendous success, existing deep learning models have exposed limitations in compositional generalization, the capability to learn compositional rules and apply them to unseen cases in a systematic manner. To tackle this issue, we propose the Neural-Symbolic Stack Machine (NeSS). It contains a neural network to generate traces, which are then executed by a symbolic stack machine enhanced with sequence manipulation operations. NeSS combines the expressive power of neural sequence models with the recursion supported by the symbolic stack machine. Without training supervision on execution traces, NeSS achieves 100% generalization performance in four domains: the SCAN benchmark of language-driven navigation tasks, the task of few-shot learning of compositional instructions, the compositional machine translation benchmark, and context-free grammar parsing tasks.

NeSS combines the expressive power of neural sequence models with the recursion supported by the symbolic stack machine. paragraphs: Compositional generalization means learning rules for combining familiar pieces and applying those rules systematically to unfamiliar combinations. The paper addresses difficulties that existing deep learning models have with this ability. Its proposed Neural-Symbolic Stack Machine, or NeSS, brings together a neural sequence model and a symbolic mechanism capable of recursive computation.

The neural component produces execution traces: sequences of instructions that the symbolic stack machine carries out. The machine also includes operations for manipulating sequences. This arrangement gives the neural model responsibility for generating the computation while supplying an explicit execution mechanism with support for recursion. The system learns without training labels that specify the correct execution traces.

The authors report 100% generalization performance in evaluations spanning four domains: SCAN navigation instructions, few-shot compositional instructions, compositional machine translation, and context-free grammar parsing. These results show that the combined architecture successfully handled the tested generalization cases across several kinds of structured sequence tasks. The finding supports pairing neural sequence generation with symbolic execution as an approach to systematic recombination.
summary.tldr: NeSS combines neural instruction generation with a symbolic stack machine and reports perfect generalization in evaluations across four compositional domains.

title: Compositional Generalization via Neural-Symbolic Stack Machines

abstract: We introduce Transductive Infomation Maximization (TIM) for few-shot learning. Our method maximizes the mutual information between the query features and their label predictions for a given few-shot task, in conjunction with a supervision loss based on the support set. Furthermore, we propose a new alternating-direction solver for our mutual-information loss, which substantially speeds up transductive inference convergence over gradient-based optimization, while yielding similar accuracy. TIM inference is modular: it can be used on top of any base-training feature extractor. Following standard transductive few-shot settings, our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that TIM outperforms state-of-the-art methods significantly across various datasets and networks, while used on top of a fixed feature extractor trained with simple cross-entropy on the base classes, without resorting to complex meta-learning schemes. It consistently brings between 2% and 5% improvement in accuracy over the best performing method, not only on all the well-established few-shot benchmarks but also on more challenging scenarios, with domain shifts and larger numbers of classes.

Furthermore, we propose a new alternating-direction solver for our mutual-information loss, which substantially speeds up transductive inference convergence over gradient-based optimization, while yielding similar accuracy. TIM inference is modular: it can be used on top of any base-training feature extractor. Following standard transductive few-shot settings, our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that TIM outperforms state-of-the-art methods significantly across various datasets and networks, while used on top of a fixed feature extractor trained with simple cross-entropy on the base classes, without resorting to complex meta-learning schemes. It consistently brings between 2% and 5% improvement in accuracy over the best performing method, not only on all the well-established few-shot benchmarks but also on more challenging scenarios, with domain shifts and larger numbers of classes.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning requires classifying new examples from only a small labeled support set. In the transductive setting studied here, the unlabeled query examples also participate in inference. Transductive Information Maximization, or TIM, uses those query features alongside the support labels to adapt predictions for the particular task.

TIM maximizes mutual information between query features and their predicted labels while also applying a supervised loss on the support set. The authors introduce an alternating-direction solver that substantially accelerates convergence compared with gradient-based optimization while achieving similar accuracy. The inference procedure is modular and can operate on top of any base-training feature extractor.

Experiments use a fixed feature extractor trained on base classes with ordinary cross-entropy, without complex meta-learning schemes. Across datasets and networks, TIM delivers reported accuracy improvements between 2% and 5% over the strongest comparison method. Improvements also extend to tested scenarios with domain shifts and more classes, supporting task-specific transductive inference as a useful component of few-shot classification.
summary.tldr: TIM combines support-label supervision with query-set information maximization to improve transductive few-shot classification.

title: Information Maximization for Few-Shot Learning

abstract: We consider the task of sampling with respect to a log concave probability distribution. The potential of the target distribution is assumed to be composite, i.e., written as the sum of a smooth convex term, and a nonsmooth convex term possibly taking infinite values. The target distribution can be seen as a minimizer of the Kullback-Leibler divergence defined on the Wasserstein space (i.e., the space of probability measures). In the first part of this paper, we establish a strong duality result for this minimization problem. In the second part of this paper, we use the duality gap arising from the first part to study the complexity of the Proximal Stochastic Gradient Langevin Algorithm (PSGLA), which can be seen as a generalization of the Projected Langevin Algorithm. Our approach relies on viewing PSGLA as a primal dual algorithm and covers many cases where the target distribution is not fully supported. In particular, we show that if the potential is strongly convex, the complexity of PSGLA is $\cO(1/\varepsilon^2)$ in terms of the 2-Wasserstein distance. In contrast, the complexity of the Projected Langevin Algorithm is $\cO(1/\varepsilon^{12})$ in terms of total variation when the potential is convex.

The abstract contrasts this with an O(1/ε¹²) result for Projected Langevin under convexity measured in total variation. Because both the assumptions and error measures differ, these are distinct theoretical guarantees. The central advance is the duality-based analysis and the stronger stated bound under strong convexity.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual view yields sampling complexity guarantees for PSGLA, including an O(1/ε²) Wasserstein bound under strong convexity.

title: Primal Dual Interpretation of the Proximal Stochastic Gradient Langevin Algorithm

abstract: We introduce the technique of adaptive discretization to design an efficient model-based episodic reinforcement learning algorithm in large (potentially continuous) state-action spaces. Our algorithm is based on optimistic one-step value iteration extended to maintain an adaptive discretization of the space. From a theoretical perspective we provide worst-case regret bounds for our algorithm which are competitive compared to the state-of-the-art model-based algorithms. Moreover, our bounds are obtained via a modular proof technique which can potentially extend to incorporate additional structure on the problem. From an implementation standpoint, our algorithm has much lower storage and computational requirements due to maintaining a more efficient partition of the state and action spaces. We illustrate this via experiments on several canonical control problems, which shows that our algorithm empirically performs significantly better than fixed discretization in terms of both faster convergence and lower memory usage. Interestingly, we observe empirically that while fixed discretization model-based algorithms vastly outperform their model-free counterparts, the two achieve comparable performance with adaptive discretization.

This paper develops a model-based episodic algorithm that represents that space using an adaptive partition. Its central idea is to change the discretization during learning, allowing a more efficient representation than a fixed division of the space.

The algorithm combines this representation with optimistic one-step value iteration. The authors establish worst-case regret bounds competitive with existing model-based approaches. Their proof is modular, which they suggest could make it possible to incorporate additional problem structure. The theoretical contribution therefore concerns both the algorithm’s guarantees and a potentially reusable way to analyze them.

On several standard control problems, the adaptive approach converges faster and uses less memory than fixed discretization. An additional empirical finding concerns the choice between model-based and model-free learning: model-based methods perform much better with fixed discretization, whereas the two approaches perform comparably with adaptive discretization. These results show that how the space is represented can substantially affect both computational demands and comparisons between learning methods.
summary.tldr: Adaptive discretization makes model-based reinforcement learning more efficient while retaining competitive regret guarantees.

title: Adaptive Discretization for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: How can we plan efficiently in real time to control an agent in a complex environment that may involve many other agents? While existing sample-based planners have enjoyed empirical success in large POMDPs, their performance heavily relies on a fast simulator. However, real-world scenarios are complex in nature and their simulators are often computationally demanding, which severely limits the performance of online planners. In this work, we propose influence-augmented online planning, a principled method to transform a factored simulator of the entire environment into a local simulator that samples only the state variables that are most relevant to the observation and reward of the planning agent and captures the incoming influence from the rest of the environment using machine learning methods. Our main experimental results show that planning on this less accurate but much faster local simulator with POMCP leads to higher real-time planning performance than planning on the simulator that models the entire environment.

paragraphs: Planning by simulation can become slow when each simulated step must account for a complex environment and many other agents. Even a successful sample-based planner depends on being able to generate those simulations quickly. This paper changes the simulator used for online planning so that computation concentrates on the planning agent's immediate needs.

Starting from a factored simulator of the full environment, the method constructs a local simulator. It samples the state variables most relevant to the agent's observations and rewards. Machine learning captures the incoming influence of the remaining environment, allowing those external effects to enter local predictions without simulating every variable in full.

Experiments using POMCP show better real-time planning performance with the local simulator, despite its lower accuracy. The result highlights a tradeoff between simulation fidelity and simulation speed: a cheaper model can support better decisions under real-time constraints. The contribution is a principled way to make that tradeoff while retaining learned information about the wider environment's effects on the agent.
summary.tldr: A faster local simulator with learned external influences improves real-time planning performance despite sacrificing some simulation accuracy.

title: Influence-Augmented Online Planning for Complex Environments

abstract: Neural network quantization methods often involve simulating the quantization process during training, making the trained model highly dependent on the target bit-width and precise way quantization is performed. Robust quantization offers an alternative approach with improved tolerance to different classes of data-types and quantization policies. It opens up new exciting applications where the quantization process is not static and can vary to meet different circumstances and implementations. To address this issue, we propose a method that provides intrinsic robustness to the model against a broad range of quantization processes. Our method is motivated by theoretical arguments and enables us to store a single generic model capable of operating at various bit-widths and quantization policies. We validate our method's effectiveness on different ImageNet Models. A reference implementation accompanies the paper.

paragraphs: Quantization changes the numerical representation used by a neural network. Methods that simulate a particular quantization process during training can make the resulting model closely dependent on that process, including its bit width and exact policy. This creates a challenge when the same model needs to operate under changing numerical requirements.

The paper proposes training for intrinsic tolerance to a broad range of quantization processes. Its method is motivated by theoretical arguments and aims to support different data types, bit widths, and quantization policies with one generic stored model. The intended flexibility is useful when the eventual quantization process varies across circumstances or implementations.

The authors validate the method on different ImageNet models and report that it is effective. The stated contribution is robustness across a broad range of quantization choices, without claiming that every possible numerical format will work equally well. By reducing dependence on one training-time quantization setup, the approach makes the same learned model usable across multiple precision and policy choices.
summary.tldr: Robust quantization trains one generic model to tolerate multiple bit widths and quantization policies, with validation on ImageNet models.

title: Robust Quantization: One Model to Rule Them All

abstract: In many game settings, the game is not explicitly given but is only accessible by playing it. While there have been impressive demonstrations in such settings, prior techniques have not offered safety guarantees, that is, guarantees on the game-theoretic exploitability of the computed strategies. In this paper we introduce an approach that shows that it is possible to provide exploitability guarantees in such settings without ever exploring the entire game. We introduce a notion of a certificatae of an extensive-form approximate Nash equilibrium. For verifying a certificate, we give an algorithm that runs in time linear in the size of the certificate rather than the size of the whole game. In zero-sum games, we further show that an optimal certificate---given the exploration so far---can be computed with any standard game-solving algorithm (e.g., using a linear program or counterfactual regret minimization). However, unlike in the cases of normal form or perfect information, we show that certain families of extensive-form games do not have small approximate certificates, even after making extremely nice assumptions on the structure of the game. Despite this difficulty, we find experimentally that very small certificates, even exact ones, often exist in large and even in infinite games. Overall, our approach enables one to try one's favorite exploration strategies while offering exploitability guarantees, thereby decoupling the exploration strategy from the equilibrium-finding process.

paragraphs: Some games can only be explored by playing them, making exhaustive analysis impractical. This paper asks whether a strategy can still carry a guarantee about how much an opponent could exploit it. It introduces certificates for approximate Nash equilibria in extensive-form games that can provide guarantees without exploring the entire game.

A certificate can be verified in time linear in its own size, rather than the size of the game. For zero-sum games, the authors show that an optimal certificate relative to the exploration completed so far can be computed using standard game-solving methods. Nevertheless, experiments find very small certificates, sometimes exact ones, in large and even infinite games. The findings establish both a useful route to exploitability guarantees and a clear theoretical boundary on when compact certification can be expected.
summary.tldr: Compact equilibrium certificates can guarantee limited exploitability without full game exploration, although some game families cannot admit small certificates.

title: Small Nash Equilibrium Certificates in Very Large Games

abstract: In this paper, we explore the limits of Microsoft Floating Point (MSFP), a new class of datatypes developed for production cloud-scale inferencing on custom hardware. Through the co-evolution of hardware design and algorithms, MSFP16 incurs 3x lower cost compared to Bfloat16 and MSFP12 has 4x lower cost compared to INT8 while delivering a comparable or better accuracy. MSFP incurs negligible impact to accuracy (<1%), requires no changes to the model topology, and is integrated with a mature cloud production pipeline. MSFP supports various classes of deep learning models including CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers without modification. Finally, we characterize the accuracy and implementation of MSFP and demonstrate its efficacy on a number of production scenarios, including models that power major online scenarios such as web search, question-answering, and image classification.

paragraphs: The numerical formats used during inference affect the cost of serving deep learning models. This paper studies Microsoft Floating Point, a family of datatypes developed for production cloud inference on custom hardware. The approach develops numerical algorithms and hardware together, making the representation of numbers part of the system design.

The authors report threefold lower cost for MSFP16 relative to Bfloat16 and fourfold lower cost for MSFP12 relative to INT8, with comparable or better accuracy. They also report an accuracy impact below one percent and no required changes to model topology. These claims concern the MSFP implementations and production settings studied in the paper.

MSFP supports convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and Transformers without modification and is integrated into an established cloud production pipeline. Evaluations include models used for web search, question answering, and image classification. The contribution is therefore both a numerical format and evidence of its deployment practicality: substantial reported cost reductions can coexist with small accuracy effects across several model classes and production applications.
summary.tldr: MSFP combines custom hardware and narrow-precision datatypes to reduce reported inference costs while preserving accuracy across production model classes.

title: Pushing the Limits of Narrow Precision Inferencing at Cloud Scale with Microsoft Floating Point

abstract: An important component of autoencoder methods is the method by which the information capacity of the latent representation is minimized or limited. In this work, the rank of the covariance matrix of the codes is implicitly minimized by relying on the fact that gradient descent learning in multi-layer linear networks leads to minimum-rank solutions. By inserting a number of extra linear layers between the encoder and the decoder, the system spontaneously learns representations with a low effective dimension. The model, dubbed Implicit Rank-Minimizing Autoencoder (IRMAE), is simple, deterministic, and learns continuous latent space. We demonstrate the validity of the method on several image generation and representation learning tasks.

paragraphs: An autoencoder maps inputs into latent codes and reconstructs them through a decoder. Controlling the information capacity of those codes is an important design choice. This paper focuses on their effective dimension: a representation can contain many coordinates while its variation across examples occupies a much smaller set of directions.

The proposed Implicit Rank-Minimizing Autoencoder inserts several additional linear layers between encoder and decoder. It relies on the tendency of gradient descent in multilayer linear networks to produce minimum-rank solutions. Through this training behavior, the model implicitly minimizes the rank of the codes' covariance matrix and learns representations with low effective dimension.

IRMAE is described as simple and deterministic, with a continuous latent space. The authors demonstrate the method on several image generation and representation learning tasks. The central contribution is a way to limit latent capacity through the interaction between architecture and optimization. Extra linear layers serve as the mechanism encouraging low-dimensional codes, rather than making latent width alone the measure of capacity.
summary.tldr: IRMAE adds linear layers between encoder and decoder so gradient-based training implicitly encourages low-dimensional latent representations.

title: Implicit Rank-Minimizing Autoencoder

abstract: Reducing the variance of the gradient estimator is known to improve the convergence rate of stochastic gradient-based optimization and sampling algorithms. One way of achieving variance reduction is to design importance sampling strategies. Recently, the problem of designing such schemes was formulated as an online learning problem with bandit feedback, and algorithms with sub-linear static regret were designed. In this work, we build on this framework and propose a simple and efficient algorithm for adaptive importance sampling for finite-sum optimization and sampling with decreasing step-sizes. Under standard technical conditions, we show that our proposed algorithm achieves O(T^{2/3}) and O(T^{5/6}) dynamic regret for SGD and SGLD respectively when run with O(1/t) step sizes. We achieve this dynamic regret bound by leveraging our knowledge of the dynamics defined by the algorithm, and combining ideas from online learning and variance-reduced stochastic optimization. We validate empirically the performance of our algorithm and identify settings in which it leads to significant improvements.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization and sampling depend on gradient estimates whose variability can slow progress. Importance sampling addresses this by changing how terms in a finite sum are selected. This paper develops an adaptive strategy for that selection, focusing on algorithms whose step sizes decrease as they run.

The method builds on a formulation of importance sampling as online learning with bandit feedback. Earlier work provided sublinear static regret; here, the authors analyze dynamic regret, addressing a comparison that can change over time. Their approach combines knowledge of the optimization or sampling dynamics with ideas from online learning and variance reduction.

Under standard technical conditions and step sizes of order 1/t, the algorithm achieves dynamic regret of order T^(2/3) for SGD and T^(5/6) for SGLD. These are guarantees for the adaptive sampling strategy under the specified conditions. Empirical results also identify settings with significant improvements, supporting the practical value of adapting sampling probabilities as the underlying algorithm evolves.
summary.tldr: An adaptive importance sampler obtains sublinear dynamic regret for SGD and SGLD with decreasing step sizes under stated technical conditions.

title: Adaptive Importance Sampling for Finite-Sum Optimization and Sampling with Decreasing Step-Sizes

abstract: High-dimensional neural recordings across multiple brain regions can be used to establish functional connectivity with good spatial and temporal resolution. We designed and implemented a novel method, Latent Dynamic Factor Analysis of High-dimensional time series (LDFA-H), which combines (a) a new approach to estimating the covariance structure among high-dimensional time series (for the observed variables) and (b) a new extension of probabilistic CCA to dynamic time series (for the latent variables). Our interest is in the cross-correlations among the latent variables which, in neural recordings, may capture the flow of information from one brain region to another. Simulations show that LDFA-H outperforms existing methods in the sense that it captures target factors even when within-region correlation due to noise dominates cross-region correlation. We applied our method to local field potential (LFP) recordings from 192 electrodes in Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) and visual area V4 during a memory-guided saccade task. The results capture time-varying lead-lag dependencies between PFC and V4, and display the associated spatial distribution of the signals.

paragraphs: Recordings from many electrodes can reveal relationships between brain regions, but strong correlations within a region may obscure the relationships of interest. LDFA-H analyzes high-dimensional time series through latent factors, aiming to extract cross-region dynamics from measurements containing substantial within-region noise correlation.

The method combines a new estimator of the covariance structure among observed time series with a dynamic extension of probabilistic canonical correlation analysis for latent variables. The focus is on cross-correlations among those latent variables. In neural data, these relationships may reflect information flowing between brain regions, although the interpretation remains a possibility rather than a direct causal conclusion.

In simulations, LDFA-H captures target factors even when noise-related within-region correlation dominates cross-region correlation, outperforming existing methods in that respect. The authors also analyze local field potentials from 192 electrodes in prefrontal cortex and visual area V4 during a memory-guided saccade task. The results reveal changing lead-lag dependencies between the regions and show where the associated signals are distributed spatially.
summary.tldr: LDFA-H extracts latent cross-region dynamics from high-dimensional neural recordings, including when within-region noise correlations dominate.

title: Latent Dynamic Factor Analysis of High-Dimensional Neural Recordings

abstract: A fundamental question in multiclass classification concerns understanding the consistency properties of surrogate risk minimization algorithms, which minimize a (often convex) surrogate to the multiclass 0-1 loss. In particular, the framework of calibrated surrogates has played an important role in analyzing the Bayes consistency properties of such algorithms, i.e. in studying convergence to a Bayes optimal classifier (Zhang, 2004; Tewari and Bartlett, 2007). However, follow-up work has suggested this framework can be of limited value when studying H-consistency; in particular, concerns have been raised that even when the data comes from an underlying linear model, minimizing certain convex calibrated surrogates over linear scoring functions fails to recover the true model (Long and Servedio, 2013). In this paper, we investigate this apparent conundrum. We find that while some calibrated surrogates can indeed fail to provide H-consistency when minimized over a natural-looking but naively chosen scoring function class F, the situation can potentially be remedied by minimizing them over a more carefully chosen class of scoring functions F. In particular, for the popular one-vs-all hinge and logistic surrogates, both of which are calibrated (and therefore provide Bayes consistency) under realizable models, but were previously shown to pose problems for realizable H-consistency, we derive a form of scoring function class F that enables H-consistency. When H is the class of linear models, the class F consists of certain piecewise linear scoring functions that are characterized by the same number of parameters as in the linear case, and minimization over which can be performed using an adaptation of the min-pooling idea from neural network training. Our experiments confirm that the one-vs-all surrogates, when trained over this class of *nonlinear* scoring functions F, yield better *linear* multiclass classifiers than when trained over standard linear scoring functions.

paragraphs: Multiclass classifiers often train with a surrogate loss because directly minimizing classification mistakes is difficult. A surrogate can have favorable Bayes-consistency properties while behaving poorly when its scoring functions are restricted. This paper examines why such guarantees may fail to deliver the best classifier within a particular model class, the concern addressed by H-consistency.

The authors show that the choice of scoring functions is central to this issue. For one-vs-all hinge and logistic losses, they derive scoring-function classes that enable H-consistency in the realizable setting considered. The implication is that a failure with one natural scoring class need not rule out the surrogate itself; a more carefully designed class can remedy the problem.

For linear classifier models, the proposed scores are certain piecewise linear functions with the same parameter count as standard linear scores. Training uses an adaptation of min-pooling. Experiments find that these nonlinear scores produce better linear multiclass classifiers than training the same surrogates with ordinary linear scores.
summary.tldr: Carefully chosen nonlinear scoring functions can restore H-consistency for particular surrogates and improve the linear multiclass classifiers they produce.

title: Bayes Consistency vs. H-Consistency: The Interplay between Surrogate Loss Functions and the Scoring Function Class

abstract: Recent research has seen several advances relevant to black-box VI, but the current state of automatic posterior inference is unclear. One such advance is the use of normalizing flows to define flexible posterior densities for deep latent variable models. Another direction is the integration of Monte-Carlo methods to serve two purposes; first, to obtain tighter variational objectives for optimization, and second, to define enriched variational families through sampling. However, both flows and variational Monte-Carlo methods remain relatively unexplored for black-box VI. Moreover, on a pragmatic front, there are several optimization considerations like step-size scheme, parameter initialization, and choice of gradient estimators, for which there are no clear guidance in the existing literature. In this paper, we postulate that black-box VI is best addressed through a careful combination of numerous algorithmic components. We evaluate components relating to optimization, flows, and Monte-Carlo methods on a benchmark of 30 models from the Stan model library. The combination of these algorithmic components significantly advances the state-of-the-art "out of the box" variational inference.
originalAbstract: Recent research has seen several advances relevant to black-box VI, but the current state of automatic posterior inference is unclear. One such advance is the use of normalizing flows to define flexible posterior densities for deep latent variable models. Another direction is the integration of Monte-Carlo methods to serve two purposes; first, to obtain tighter variational objectives for optimization, and second, to define enriched variational families through sampling. However, both flows and variational Monte-Carlo methods remain relatively unexplored for black-box VI. Moreover, on a pragmatic front, there are several optimization considerations like step-size scheme, parameter initialization, and choice of gradient estimators, for which there are no clear guidance in the existing literature. In this paper, we postulate that black-box VI is best addressed through a careful combination of numerous algorithmic components. We evaluate components relating to optimization, flows, and Monte-Carlo methods on a benchmark of 30 models from the Stan model library. The combination of these algorithmic components significantly advances the state-of-the-art "out of the box" variational inference.

paragraphs: Black-box variational inference aims to approximate posterior distributions with little model-specific intervention. This paper asks how several recent methodological advances should fit together to make that process work reliably out of the box. Its central proposal is that progress depends on carefully combining components, rather than treating any single advance as a complete solution.

The authors investigate three connected areas. Normalizing flows provide more flexible probability distributions for approximating a posterior. Monte Carlo methods can supply tighter optimization objectives and enrich the distributions available through sampling. Optimization choices, including step sizes, initialization, and gradient estimators, determine how effectively these ingredients can actually be trained.

The study evaluates these components on 30 models from the Stan model library. Their combination substantially improves the reported state of automatic variational inference. The finding gives practical significance to the interaction between representation and optimization: having a richer approximation is only part of the design problem, alongside choosing an objective and a training procedure that make it useful.
summary.tldr: Combining flexible posterior approximations, Monte Carlo methods, and careful optimization substantially improves out-of-the-box variational inference on a 30-model benchmark.

title: Advances in Black-Box VI: Normalizing Flows, Importance Weighting, and Optimization

abstract: Components of machine learning systems are not (yet) perceived as security hotspots. Secure coding practices, such as ensuring that no execution paths depend on confidential inputs, have not yet been adopted by ML developers. We initiate the study of code security of ML systems by investigating how nucleus sampling---a popular approach for generating text, used for applications such as auto-completion---unwittingly leaks texts typed by users. Our main result is that the series of nucleus sizes for many natural English word sequences is a unique fingerprint. We then show how an attacker can infer typed text by measuring these fingerprints via a suitable side channel (e.g., cache access times), explain how this attack could help de-anonymize anonymous texts, and discuss defenses.

paragraphs: The paper examines a privacy risk in the implementation of machine-learning text generation. Nucleus sampling changes the set of eligible next tokens depending on the preceding text. The authors ask whether those input-dependent operations can reveal information even when the text itself is not directly exposed.

Their main finding is that the sequence of nucleus sizes forms a unique fingerprint for many natural English word sequences. They show how an attacker could infer typed text by observing such fingerprints through a suitable side channel, with cache-access timing given as an example.

The paper discusses how this could help link anonymous text to a user and considers defenses. The abstract does not claim that every deployment exposes the necessary side channel or that every possible sentence has a unique fingerprint. Its contribution is identifying an implementation-level leakage mechanism and showing why generation procedures deserve security scrutiny alongside their model outputs.
summary.tldr: Input-dependent nucleus-sampling behavior can expose text through implementation side channels.

title: De-Anonymizing Text by Fingerprinting Language Generation

abstract: Motivated by the prevailing paradigm of using unsupervised learning for efficient exploration in reinforcement learning (RL) problems [tang2017exploration,bellemare2016unifying], we investigate when this paradigm is provably efficient. We study episodic Markov decision processes with rich observations generated from a small number of latent states. We present a general algorithmic framework that is built upon two components: an unsupervised learning algorithm and a no-regret tabular RL algorithm. Theoretically, we prove that as long as the unsupervised learning algorithm enjoys a polynomial sample complexity guarantee, we can find a near-optimal policy with sample complexity polynomial in the number of latent states, which is significantly smaller than the number of observations. Empirically, we instantiate our framework on a class of hard exploration problems to demonstrate the practicality of our theory.

paragraphs: An agent can receive many different observations even when the environment has only a small number of underlying states. This makes exploration difficult if learning depends on the size of the observation space. The paper asks when unsupervised learning can exploit that hidden structure to make reinforcement learning provably more sample-efficient.

The setting is an episodic Markov decision process whose rich observations are generated from a small latent state space. The proposed framework combines an unsupervised learning algorithm with a no-regret tabular reinforcement-learning algorithm. The guarantee is conditional: if the unsupervised component has polynomial sample complexity, the combined approach can find a near-optimal policy with sample complexity polynomial in the number of latent states.

This matters because the latent-state count can be much smaller than the number of possible observations. The guarantee connects the quality of the unsupervised learning component to efficient decision making, rather than assuming that any learned representation will suffice. The authors also instantiate the framework on a class of difficult exploration problems, providing empirical evidence that the theoretical construction can be useful in practice.
summary.tldr: Under a sample-complexity guarantee for unsupervised learning, the framework learns near-optimal policies with complexity polynomial in the latent-state count.

title: Provably Efficient Exploration for Reinforcement Learning Using Unsupervised Learning

abstract: In comparison to the interpretation of classification models, the explanation of sequence generation models is also an important problem, however it has seen little attention. In this work, we study model-agnostic explanations of a representative text generation task -- dialogue response generation. Dialog response generation is challenging with its open-ended sentences and multiple acceptable responses. To gain insights into the reasoning process of a generation model, we propose a new method, local explanation of response generation (LERG) that regards the explanations as the mutual interaction of segments in input and output sentences. LERG views the sequence prediction as uncertainty estimation of a human response and then creates explanations by perturbing the input and calculating the certainty change over the human response. We show that LERG adheres to desired properties of explanations for text generation including unbiased approximation, consistency and cause identification. Empirically, our results show that our method consistently improves other widely used methods on proposed automatic- and human- evaluation metrics for this new task by $4.4$-$12.8$\%. Our analysis demonstrates that LERG can extract both explicit and implicit relations between input and output segments.

paragraphs: Explaining a dialogue response is more complicated than explaining a single predicted class: sentences are open-ended, and several responses may be acceptable. This paper introduces Local Explanation of Response Generation, or LERG, a model-agnostic method that treats an explanation as a set of interactions between segments of the input and output.

LERG frames sequence prediction in terms of uncertainty about a human response. It perturbs the input and measures how the model's certainty about that response changes. This provides a way to connect particular input segments with particular parts of the response. The explanation can therefore describe relationships within a generated sequence rather than assigning importance only to the response as a whole.

The authors show that LERG satisfies desired properties including unbiased approximation, consistency, and cause identification. On the proposed automatic and human evaluation metrics, it improves over widely used methods by 4.4–12.8%. Further analysis finds that it captures both explicit and implicit input-output relationships, supporting its usefulness for examining dialogue models at the segment level.
summary.tldr: LERG explains dialogue responses through input-output segment relationships measured by changes in response certainty after input perturbations.

title: Local Explanation of Dialogue Response Generation

abstract: When compared to the image classification models, black-box adversarial attacks against video classification models have been largely understudied. This could be possible because, with video, the temporal dimension poses significant additional challenges in gradient estimation. Query-efficient black-box attacks rely on effectively estimated gradients towards maximizing the probability of misclassifying the target video. In this work, we demonstrate that such effective gradients can be searched for by parameterizing the temporal structure of the search space with geometric transformations. Specifically, we design a novel iterative algorithm GEOmetric TRAnsformed Perturbations (GEO-TRAP), for attacking video classification models. GEO-TRAP employs standard geometric transformation operations to reduce the search space for effective gradients into searching for a small group of parameters that define these operations. This group of parameters describes the geometric progression of gradients, resulting in a reduced and structured search space. Our algorithm inherently leads to successful perturbations with surprisingly few queries. For example, adversarial examples generated from GEO-TRAP have better attack success rates with ~73.55% fewer queries compared to the state-of-the-art method for video adversarial attacks on the widely used Jester dataset. Overall, our algorithm exposes vulnerabilities of diverse video classification models and achieves new state-of-the-art results under black-box settings on two large datasets.

The paper investigates whether structure across time can reduce the number of queries needed to find effective perturbations.

These findings show that geometric structure can make query-based video attacks substantially more efficient in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: GEO-TRAP uses geometric transformations to structure video attack searches, achieving stronger attacks with substantially fewer queries in the reported experiments.

title: Adversarial Attacks on Black Box Video Classifiers: Leveraging the Power of Geometric Transformations

abstract: While causal models are becoming one of the mainstays of machine learning, the problem of uncertainty quantification in causal inference remains challenging. In this paper, we study the causal data fusion problem, where data arising from multiple causal graphs are combined to estimate the average treatment effect of a target variable. As data arises from multiple sources and can vary in quality and sample size, principled uncertainty quantification becomes essential. To that end, we introduce \emph{Bayesian Causal Mean Processes}, the framework which combines ideas from probabilistic integration and kernel mean embeddings to represent interventional distributions in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space, while taking into account the uncertainty within each causal graph. To demonstrate the informativeness of our uncertainty estimation, we apply our method to the Causal Bayesian Optimisation task and show improvements over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Combining causal evidence from multiple sources requires more than producing a single treatment-effect estimate. Sources can differ in sample size and quality, and their data may arise from different causal graphs. The paper studies how to combine this evidence while accounting for uncertainty in the estimated average effect on a target variable.

Its framework, Bayesian Causal Mean Processes, combines probabilistic integration with kernel mean embeddings. These tools represent distributions associated with interventions in a mathematical feature space while incorporating uncertainty within each causal graph. The central idea is to make uncertainty part of the data-fusion calculation, rather than treating every source’s contribution as equally well established.

The authors evaluate the usefulness of these uncertainty estimates through causal Bayesian optimisation, where estimates inform the search for interventions. They report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in that task. This connects uncertainty quantification to a practical decision process: the framework is intended to support better intervention choices as well as estimates of causal effects.
summary.tldr: BayesIMP combines causal evidence across sources while tracking uncertainty, improving the reported causal Bayesian optimisation results.

title: BayesIMP: Uncertainty Quantification for Causal Data Fusion

abstract: Visual question answering (VQA) is designed to examine the visual-textual reasoning ability of an intelligent agent. However, recent observations show that many VQA models may only capture the biases between questions and answers in a dataset rather than showing real reasoning abilities. For example, given a question, some VQA models tend to output the answer that occurs frequently in the dataset and ignore the images. To reduce this tendency, existing methods focus on weakening the language bias. Meanwhile, only a few works also consider vision bias implicitly. However, these methods introduce additional annotations or show unsatisfactory performance. Moreover, not all biases are harmful to the models. Some “biases” learnt from datasets represent natural rules of the world and can help limit the range of answers. Thus, how to filter and remove the true negative biases in language and vision modalities remain a major challenge. In this paper, we propose a method named D-VQA to alleviate the above challenges from the feature and sample perspectives. Specifically, from the feature perspective, we build a question-to-answer and vision-to-answer branch to capture the language and vision biases, respectively. Next, we apply two unimodal bias detection modules to explicitly recognise and remove the negative biases. From the sample perspective, we construct two types of negative samples to assist the training of the models, without introducing additional annotations. Extensive experiments on the VQA-CP v2 and VQA v2 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our D-VQA method.

These examples support the model’s training alongside the feature-based bias handling. Experiments on VQA-CP v2 and VQA v2 demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a combined treatment of language and visual shortcuts that also acknowledges the potential usefulness of legitimate patterns in the data.
summary.tldr: D-VQA targets harmful language and visual biases using dedicated detection modules and negative training examples without additional annotations.

title: Debiased Visual Question Answering from Feature and Sample Perspectives

abstract: We consider the problem of learning multivariate Gaussians under the constraint of approximate differential privacy. We prove that $\widetilde{O}(k^2 d \log^{3/2}(1/\delta) / \alpha^2 \varepsilon)$ samples are sufficient to learn a mixture of $k$ axis-aligned Gaussians in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to within total variation distance $\alpha$ while satisfying $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy. This is the first result for privately learning mixtures of unbounded axis-aligned (or even unbounded univariate) Gaussians. If the covariance matrices of each of the Gaussians is the identity matrix, we show that $\widetilde{O}(kd/\alpha^2 + kd \log(1/\delta) / \alpha \varepsilon)$ samples are sufficient.To prove our results, we design a new technique for privately learning mixture distributions. A class of distributions $\mathcal{F}$ is said to be list-decodable if there is an algorithm that, given "heavily corrupted" samples from $f \in \mathcal{F}$, outputs a list of distributions one of which approximates $f$. We show that if $\mathcal{F}$ is privately list-decodable then we can learn mixtures of distributions in $\mathcal{F}$. Finally, we show axis-aligned Gaussian distributions are privately list-decodable, thereby proving mixtures of such distributions are privately learnable.

It focuses on axis-aligned Gaussian components and establishes the first private learning result for their unbounded mixtures, including the univariate case. The guarantee measures how closely the learned distribution approximates the target in total variation distance.

The authors provide sufficient sample bounds in terms of the number of mixture components, dimension, desired accuracy, and privacy parameters. They also obtain a stronger sufficient bound when every component has identity covariance. These are learning guarantees under specified distributional structure, with a separate improvement for the more restricted covariance setting.

The authors show that private list decodability of a distribution family is sufficient for privately learning its mixtures. They then establish this property for axis-aligned Gaussians. This turns a method for finding a useful candidate among several possibilities into a general route to private mixture learning.
summary.tldr: Private list decoding provides a new route to learning unbounded mixtures of axis-aligned Gaussians with sufficient sample guarantees.

title: Privately Learning Mixtures of Axis-Aligned Gaussians

abstract: Multi-agent control is a central theme in the Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). However, current control methods either receive non-Markovian states due to insufficient sensing and decentralized design, or suffer from poor convergence. This paper presents the Delayed Propagation Transformer (DePT), a new transformer-based model that specializes in the global modeling of CPS while taking into account the immutable constraints from the physical world. DePT induces a cone-shaped spatial-temporal attention prior, which injects the information propagation and aggregation principles and enables a global view. With physical constraint inductive bias baked into its design, our DePT is ready to plug and play for a broad class of multi-agent systems. The experimental results on one of the most challenging CPS -- network-scale traffic signal control system in the open world -- show that our model outperformed the state-of-the-art expert methods on synthetic and real-world datasets. Our codes are released at: https://github.com/VITA-Group/DePT.

paragraphs: Multi-agent control in cyber-physical systems must account for both interactions among agents and constraints imposed by the physical world. Limited sensing and decentralized decisions can leave controllers with states that do not contain enough information about what happens next. The paper also identifies poor convergence as a difficulty for existing control methods.

The Delayed Propagation Transformer, or DePT, addresses these issues through global modeling with a physically informed attention structure. It introduces a cone-shaped pattern over space and time that encodes principles of information propagation and aggregation. This gives the model a global view while building physical constraints directly into how it attends to information.

The authors present DePT as applicable to a broad class of multi-agent systems and evaluate it on network-scale traffic signal control. On synthetic and real-world datasets, it outperforms the compared state-of-the-art expert methods. Those findings support the approach in the tested traffic-control setting. The central design idea is that transformer attention can incorporate knowledge about physical information flow, providing a structured basis for coordinating multiple controllers.
summary.tldr: DePT builds physical information-propagation constraints into transformer attention and improves reported network-scale traffic signal control results.

title: Delayed Propagation Transformer: A Universal Computation Engine towards Practical Control in Cyber-Physical Systems

abstract: The (partial) ranking loss is a commonly used evaluation measure for multi-label classification, which is usually optimized with convex surrogates for computational efficiency. Prior theoretical efforts on multi-label ranking mainly focus on (Fisher) consistency analyses. However, there is a gap between existing theory and practice --- some inconsistent pairwise losses can lead to promising performance, while some consistent univariate losses usually have no clear superiority in practice. To take a step towards filling up this gap, this paper presents a systematic study from two complementary perspectives of consistency and generalization error bounds of learning algorithms. We theoretically find two key factors of the distribution (or dataset) that affect the learning guarantees of algorithms: the instance-wise class imbalance and the label size $c$. Specifically, in an extremely imbalanced case, the algorithm with the consistent univariate loss has an error bound of $O(c)$, while the one with the inconsistent pairwise loss depends on $O(\sqrt{c})$ as shown in prior work. This may shed light on the superior performance of pairwise methods in practice, where real datasets are usually highly imbalanced. Moreover, we present an inconsistent reweighted univariate loss-based algorithm that enjoys an error bound of $O(\sqrt{c})$ for promising performance as well as the computational efficiency of univariate losses. Finally, experimental results confirm our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Multi-label ranking seeks to order relevant labels ahead of irrelevant ones. Efficient training often substitutes a convex loss for the ranking measure itself. Yet theoretical consistency has not reliably predicted which substitutes perform best: some inconsistent pairwise losses work well, while consistent losses that treat labels individually show no clear practical advantage.

The paper examines consistency alongside generalization bounds and identifies two influential factors: imbalance within each example and the number of labels, c. In an extremely imbalanced setting, a consistent univariate method has an O(c) error bound, compared with the O(square root of c) dependence established for an inconsistent pairwise method. This may help explain the observed advantage of pairwise approaches.

The authors then introduce a reweighted univariate algorithm that is inconsistent but achieves an O(square root of c) bound while retaining computational efficiency. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution shows why consistency and finite-data guarantees should be considered together, rather than treating consistency alone as a sufficient guide to practical loss selection.
summary.tldr: Analyzing imbalance and generalization explains why inconsistent ranking losses can work well and motivates an efficient reweighted univariate alternative.

title: Rethinking and Reweighting the Univariate Losses for Multi-Label Ranking: Consistency and Generalization

abstract: Blame attribution is one of the key aspects of accountable decision making, as it provides means to quantify the responsibility of an agent for a decision making outcome. In this paper, we study blame attribution in the context of cooperative multi-agent sequential decision making. As a particular setting of interest, we focus on cooperative decision making formalized by Multi-Agent Markov Decision Processes (MMDPs), and we analyze different blame attribution methods derived from or inspired by existing concepts in cooperative game theory. We formalize desirable properties of blame attribution in the setting of interest, and we analyze the relationship between these properties and the studied blame attribution methods. Interestingly, we show that some of the well known blame attribution methods, such as Shapley value, are not performance-incentivizing, while others, such as Banzhaf index, may over-blame agents. To mitigate these value misalignment and fairness issues, we introduce a novel blame attribution method, unique in the set of properties it satisfies, which trade-offs explanatory power (by under-blaming agents) for the aforementioned properties. We further show how to account for uncertainty about agents' decision making policies, and we experimentally: a) validate the qualitative properties of the studied blame attribution methods, and b) analyze their robustness to uncertainty.

This paper formalizes blame attribution in cooperative multi-agent Markov decision processes. It examines methods drawn from cooperative game theory and defines properties that a desirable attribution rule should satisfy.

The analysis shows that familiar methods can conflict with those properties. Shapley-value attribution does not provide the studied performance incentive, while the Banzhaf index can assign excessive blame. These findings show why importing a recognized attribution method does not automatically produce the desired combination of fairness and incentives in sequential decision making.

The authors introduce a method with a distinctive combination of satisfied properties. It gains those properties by allowing under-blaming, which sacrifices some explanatory power. They also extend attribution to account for uncertainty about agents’ policies. Experiments validate qualitative properties and investigate robustness to that uncertainty, making the tradeoffs between explanation, fairness, and behavioral incentives explicit.
summary.tldr: A formal study of multi-agent blame identifies incentive and fairness failures in familiar methods and proposes an alternative that deliberately permits under-blaming.

title: On Blame Attribution for Accountable Multi-Agent Sequential Decision Making

abstract: We study the online problem of minimizing power consumption in systems with multiple power-saving states. During idle periods of unknown lengths, an algorithm has to choose between power-saving states of different energy consumption and wake-up costs. We develop a learning-augmented online algorithm that makes decisions based on (potentially inaccurate) predicted lengths of the idle periods. The algorithm's performance is near-optimal when predictions are accurate and degrades gracefully with increasing prediction error, with a worst-case guarantee almost identical to the optimal classical online algorithm for the problem. A key ingredient in our approach is a new algorithm for the online ski-rental problem in the learning augmented setting with tight dependence on the prediction error. We support our theoretical findings with experiments.

paragraphs: A system with several power-saving states must decide how deeply to sleep during an idle period whose duration is unknown. Different states consume different amounts of energy and impose different wake-up costs. The best decision therefore depends on future inactivity, making predictions potentially useful but also creating a need to handle prediction errors.

The paper develops an online algorithm that incorporates predicted idle durations without assuming they are accurate. Its performance is near optimal when predictions are accurate and worsens gracefully as prediction error grows. It also retains a worst-case guarantee almost matching that of the optimal classical online algorithm, connecting predictive benefits with protection against poor forecasts.

A key technical ingredient is a new learning-augmented algorithm for the ski-rental problem, with tight dependence on prediction error. The authors use this ingredient to address the multiple-state power-management setting and support the theoretical findings with experiments. The contribution is thus a quantified relationship between forecast quality and energy-management performance, rather than a requirement that forecasts always be dependable.
summary.tldr: The proposed power-management algorithm benefits from accurate idle-time predictions while retaining strong worst-case protection when predictions are wrong.

title: Learning-Augmented Dynamic Power Management with Multiple States via New Ski Rental Bounds

abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have recently received explosive popularity, but their enormous model sizes and training costs remain daunting. Conventional post-training pruning often incurs higher training budgets. In contrast, this paper aims to trim down both the training memory overhead and the inference complexity, without sacrificing the achievable accuracy. We carry out the first-of-its-kind comprehensive exploration, on taking a unified approach of integrating sparsity in ViTs "from end to end''. Specifically, instead of training full ViTs, we dynamically extract and train sparse subnetworks, while sticking to a fixed small parameter budget. Our approach jointly optimizes model parameters and explores connectivity throughout training, ending up with one sparse network as the final output. The approach is seamlessly extended from unstructured to structured sparsity, the latter by considering to guide the prune-and-grow of self-attention heads inside ViTs. We further co-explore data and architecture sparsity for additional efficiency gains by plugging in a novel learnable token selector to adaptively determine the currently most vital patches. Extensive results on ImageNet with diverse ViT backbones validate the effectiveness of our proposals which obtain significantly reduced computational cost and almost unimpaired generalization. Perhaps most surprisingly, we find that the proposed sparse (co-)training can sometimes \textit{improve the ViT accuracy} rather than compromising it, making sparsity a tantalizing "free lunch''. For example, our sparsified DeiT-Small at ($5\%$, $50\%$) sparsity for (data, architecture), improves $\mathbf{0.28\%}$ top-1 accuracy, and meanwhile enjoys $\mathbf{49.32\%}$ FLOPs and $\mathbf{4.40\%}$ running time savings. Our codes are available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/SViTE.

The approach also supports structured sparsity by pruning and growing self-attention heads.

Those separate savings show that reduced operation counts and actual speed improvements are distinct reported outcomes.
summary.tldr: Dynamically training sparse vision transformers and selecting useful image patches reduces computation while largely preserving, and sometimes improving, accuracy.

title: Chasing Sparsity in Vision Transformers: An End-to-End Exploration

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are ubiquitous in today's computer vision landscape, despite involving considerable computational costs. The mainstream approaches for runtime acceleration consist in pruning connections (unstructured pruning) or, better, filters (structured pruning), both often requiring data to retrain the model. In this paper, we present RED, a data-free, unified approach to tackle structured pruning. First, we propose a novel adaptive hashing of the scalar DNN weight distribution densities to increase the number of identical neurons represented by their weight vectors. Second, we prune the network by merging redundant neurons based on their relative similarities, as defined by their distance. Third, we propose a novel uneven depthwise separation technique to further prune convolutional layers. We demonstrate through a large variety of benchmarks that RED largely outperforms other data-free pruning methods, often reaching performance similar to unconstrained, data-driven methods.

paragraphs: Compressing a neural network often involves removing connections or entire filters, followed by retraining with data. RED addresses structured compression without requiring data. Its central strategy is to look for redundancy within the network's weights and use that redundancy to reduce the network's structure.

The method begins with adaptive hashing based on the density distribution of scalar weights, increasing the number of neurons whose weight vectors are identical. It then merges redundant neurons according to their relative similarities, measured through distances. A further technique, called uneven depthwise separation, provides additional pruning of convolutional layers. These components form a unified procedure for finding and reducing repeated or similar structure.

Across a broad collection of benchmarks, the authors report that RED substantially outperforms other data-free pruning methods. They also find that it often reaches performance similar to methods allowed to use data. The qualification matters: comparable performance is reported frequently, not universally. The contribution shows how inspecting a model's own weights can support substantial structured compression when training data are unavailable.
summary.tldr: RED compresses neural networks without data by creating and merging redundant neurons and further pruning convolutional layers.

title: RED : Looking for Redundancies for Data-FreeStructured Compression of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Meta learning with multiple objectives has been attracted much attention recently since many applications need to consider multiple factors when designing learning models. Existing gradient-based works on meta learning with multiple objectives mainly combine multiple objectives into a single objective in a weighted sum manner. This simple strategy usually works but it requires to tune the weights associated with all the objectives, which could be time consuming. Different from those works, in this paper, we propose a gradient-based Multi-Objective Meta Learning (MOML) framework without manually tuning weights. Specifically, MOML formulates the objective function of meta learning with multiple objectives as a Multi-Objective Bi-Level optimization Problem (MOBLP) where the upper-level subproblem is to solve several possibly conflicting objectives for the meta learner. To solve the MOBLP, we devise the first gradient-based optimization algorithm by alternatively solving the lower-level and upper-level subproblems via the gradient descent method and the gradient-based multi-objective optimization method, respectively. Theoretically, we prove the convergence properties of the proposed gradient-based optimization algorithm. Empirically, we show the effectiveness of the proposed MOML framework in several meta learning problems, including few-shot learning, domain adaptation, multi-task learning, and neural architecture search. The source code of MOML is available at https://github.com/Baijiong-Lin/MOML.

paragraphs: Meta-learning applications may need to optimize several objectives that can conflict. A common approach combines them into a weighted sum, but choosing those weights can require substantial tuning. This paper introduces Multi-Objective Meta Learning, or MOML, to handle multiple objectives without manually selecting a weight for each one.

MOML expresses the task as a multi-objective bilevel optimization problem. The upper level handles several objectives for the meta-learner, while the lower level supplies the other part of the nested learning problem. The proposed algorithm alternates between the levels, using gradient descent for the lower subproblem and a gradient-based multi-objective optimization method for the upper one.

The authors prove convergence properties of this optimization algorithm and evaluate the framework on few-shot learning, domain adaptation, multi-task learning, and neural architecture search. The experiments support its effectiveness across these settings. Its central contribution is a way to optimize competing meta-learning objectives directly within the bilevel structure, reducing dependence on manually tuned weighted combinations.
summary.tldr: MOML uses multi-objective bilevel optimization to train meta-learners without manually tuning objective weights.

title: Multi-Objective Meta Learning

abstract: The state-of-the-art deep neural networks are vulnerable to common corruptions (e.g., input data degradations, distortions, and disturbances caused by weather changes, system error, and processing). While much progress has been made in analyzing and improving the robustness of models in image understanding, the robustness in video understanding is largely unexplored. In this paper, we establish a corruption robustness benchmark, Mini Kinetics-C and Mini SSV2-C, which considers temporal corruptions beyond spatial corruptions in images. We make the first attempt to conduct an exhaustive study on the corruption robustness of established CNN-based and Transformer-based spatial-temporal models. The study provides some guidance on robust model design and training: Transformer-based model performs better than CNN-based models on corruption robustness; the generalization ability of spatial-temporal models implies robustness against temporal corruptions; model corruption robustness (especially robustness in the temporal domain) enhances with computational cost and model capacity, which may contradict the current trend of improving the computational efficiency of models. Moreover, we find the robustness intervention for image-related tasks (e.g., training models with noise) may not work for spatial-temporal models. Our codes are available on https://github.com/Newbeeyoung/Video-Corruption-Robustness.

paragraphs: Video models must handle changes in image content and disruptions in how that content unfolds over time. This paper introduces Mini Kinetics-C and Mini SSV2-C to evaluate both kinds of corruption. The benchmarks address a gap left by robustness research focused mainly on still images.

The study compares established convolutional and Transformer-based models that process spatial and temporal information. In the reported experiments, Transformer-based modeling provides better corruption robustness than the convolutional alternatives. The authors also connect generalization ability with resistance to temporal corruptions and find that greater model capacity and computational cost accompany improved robustness, especially for temporal disturbances.

These findings suggest a potential tension between computational efficiency and robustness in the evaluated video models. The authors further find that interventions used for image tasks, including training with noise, may not work for spatial-temporal models. The benchmark therefore offers a way to evaluate video-specific robustness and examine whether design and training choices withstand both spatial and temporal degradation.
summary.tldr: Two video benchmarks reveal how model architecture, capacity, and training choices relate to robustness against spatial and temporal corruptions.

title: Benchmarking the Robustness of Spatial-Temporal Models Against Corruptions

abstract: We consider dynamic multi-product pricing and assortment problems under an unknown demand over T periods, where in each period, the seller decides on the price for each product or the assortment of products to offer to a customer who chooses according to an unknown Multinomial Logit Model (MNL). Such problems arise in many applications, including online retail and advertising. We propose a randomized dynamic pricing policy based on a variant of the Online Newton Step algorithm (ONS) that achieves a $O(d\sqrt{T}\log(T))$ regret guarantee under an adversarial arrival model. We also present a new optimistic algorithm for the adversarial MNL contextual bandits problem, which achieves a better dependency than the state-of-the-art algorithms in a problem-dependent constant $\kappa$ (potentially exponentially small). Our regret upper bound scales as $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{\kappa T}+ \log(T)/\kappa)$, which gives a stronger bound than the existing $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{T}/\kappa)$ guarantees.

Such problems arise in many applications, including online retail and advertising. We propose a randomized dynamic pricing policy based on a variant of the Online Newton Step algorithm (ONS) that achieves a $O(d\sqrt{T}\log(T))$ regret guarantee under an adversarial arrival model. We also present a new optimistic algorithm for the adversarial MNL contextual bandits problem, which achieves a better dependency than the state-of-the-art algorithms in a problem-dependent constant $\kappa$ (potentially exponentially small).
