paragraphs: Learning a useful robot policy involves both achieving goals and respecting safety constraints. This paper considers offline reinforcement learning, where training uses a fixed dataset instead of gathering experience through new interactions. That setting is valuable when exploratory actions could be unsafe, but the learner still has to reconcile reward maximization with limits on costly behavior.

The proposed method, DRCORL, first trains a diffusion model to capture the behavior represented in the dataset. It then extracts a simpler policy for efficient inference. A further gradient manipulation step adapts learning to safety requirements, balancing the reward objective against constraint satisfaction. The approach therefore combines a rich model of recorded behavior with a policy intended to be practical to execute.

Across the reported robot learning tasks, DRCORL achieves strong rewards, fast inference, and reliable safety performance. It consistently meets cost limits in comparisons with existing safe offline methods and works well with the same hyperparameters. These empirical results support its practical promise within the tested settings, while the approach explicitly draws on high-quality offline data.
summary.tldr: DRCORL combines diffusion-based behavior modeling, policy simplification, and safety adaptation to achieve strong rewards while meeting cost limits in robot learning experiments.

title: Don’t Trade Off Safety: Diffusion Regularization for Constrained Offline RL

abstract: Test-time scaling enhances large language model performance by allocating additional compute resources during decoding. Best-of-$N$ (BoN) sampling serves as a common sampling-based scaling technique, broadening the search space in parallel to find better solutions from the model distribution. However, its cost–performance trade-off is still underexplored. Two main challenges limit the efficiency of BoN sampling: (1) Generating $N$ full samples consumes substantial GPU memory, reducing inference capacity under limited resources. (2) Reward models add extra memory and latency overhead, and training strong reward models introduces potential training data costs. Although some studies have explored efficiency improvements, none have addressed both challenges at once. To address this gap, we propose **Self-Truncation Best-of-$N$ (ST-BoN)**, a decoding method that avoids fully generating all $N$ samples and eliminates the need for reward models. It leverages early sampling consistency in the model’s internal states to identify the most promising path and truncate suboptimal ones. In terms of cost, ST-BoN reduces dynamic GPU memory usage by over 80% and inference latency by 50%. In terms of cost–performance trade-off, ST-BoN achieves the same performance as Full-BoN while saving computational cost by 70%–80%, and under the same cost, it can improve accuracy by 3–4 points.

In terms of cost–performance trade-off, ST-BoN achieves the same performance as Full-BoN while saving computational cost by 70%–80%, and under the same cost, it can improve accuracy by 3–4 points.

paragraphs: Best-of-N sampling improves language-model outputs by generating several candidates and selecting a promising result. Its expense comes from completing all candidates and, often, using a separate reward model to judge them. This paper introduces Self-Truncation Best-of-N, a decoding procedure designed to reduce both sources of overhead while retaining the benefit of searching multiple possibilities.

The method examines early sampling consistency in the language model's internal states. It uses this signal to identify a promising continuation and stop less promising candidates before they finish. Because this selection comes from the model's own internal information, the procedure also avoids a separate reward model and its associated memory, latency, and training demands.

The authors report over 80% lower dynamic GPU memory usage and 50% lower inference latency. They also report matching full Best-of-N performance with 70–80% less computational cost, or improving accuracy by three to four points at equal cost. These results indicate that early candidate selection can make additional decoding-time search substantially more economical in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: ST-BoN uses early internal-state signals to stop weaker candidates and avoid reward models, reducing the cost of Best-of-N decoding.

title: Sampling-Efficient Test-Time Scaling: Self-Estimating the Best-of-N Sampling in Early Decoding

abstract: Suppose Alice trains an open-weight language model and Bob uses a blackbox derivative of Alice’s model to produce text. Can Alice prove that Bob is using her model, either by querying Bob’s derivative model (query setting) or from the text alone ( observational setting)? We formulate this question as an independence testing problem—in which the null hypothesis is that Bob’s model or text is independent of Alice’s randomized training run—and investigate it through the lens of palimpsestic memorization in language models: models are more likely to memorize data seen later in training, so we can test whether Bob is using Alice’s model using test statistics that capture correlation between Bob’s model or text and the ordering of training examples in Alice’s training run. If Alice has randomly shuffled her training data, then any significant correlation amounts to exactly quantifiable statistical evidence against the null hypothesis, regardless of the composition of Alice’s training data. In the query setting, we directly estimate (via prompting) the likelihood Bob’s model gives to Alice’s training examples and their training order; we correlate the likelihoods of over 40 fine-tunes of various Pythia and OLMo base models ranging from 1B to 12B parameters with the base model’s training data order, achieving a p-value on the order of at most $1 \times 10^{-8}$ in all but six cases. In the observational setting, we try two approaches based on estimating 1) the likelihood of Bob’s text overlapping with spans of Alice’s training examples and 2) the likelihood of Bob’s text with respect to different versions of Alice’s model we obtain by repeating the last phase (e.g., 1%) of her training run on reshuffled data. The second approach can reliably distinguish Bob’s text from as little as a few hundred tokens; the first does not involve any retraining but requires many more tokens (several hundred thousand) to achieve high power.

title: Blackbox Model Provenance via Palimpsestic Membership Inference

abstract: While LLM/VLM-powered AI agents have advanced rapidly in math, coding, and computer use, their applications in complex physical and social environments remain challenging. Building agents that can survive and thrive in the real world (e.g., by autonomously earning income) requires massive-scale interaction, reasoning, training, and evaluation across diverse scenarios. However, existing world simulators for such development fall short: they often rely on limited hand-crafted environments, simulate simplified game-like physics and social rules, and lack native support for LLM/VLM agents. We introduce SimWorld, a new simulator built on Unreal Engine 5, designed for developing and evaluating LLM/VLM agents in rich, real-world-like settings. SimWorld offers three core capabilities: (1) realistic, open-ended world simulation, including accurate physical and social dynamics and language-driven procedural environment generation; (2) rich interface for LLM/VLM agents, with multi-modal world inputs/feedback and open-vocabulary action outputs at varying levels of abstraction; and (3) diverse physical and social reasoning scenarios that are easily customizable by users. We demonstrate SimWorld by deploying frontier LLM agents (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-Prover-V2) on both short-horizon navigation tasks requiring grounded re-planning, and long-horizon multi-agent food delivery tasks involving strategic cooperation and competition. The results reveal distinct reasoning patterns and limitations across models. We open-source SimWorld and hope it becomes a foundational platform for advancing real-world agent intelligence across disciplines. Please refer to the project website for the most up-to-date information: http://simworld.org/.

paragraphs: SimWorld is a simulator for developing language- and vision-language-model agents in physical and social environments. The motivation is that success in coding or mathematics does not resolve the challenges of acting over time in a changing world. Agents need environments that support interaction, training, and evaluation across varied situations.

Built on Unreal Engine 5, SimWorld combines physical and social simulation with language-driven procedural environment generation. Agents receive multimodal observations and feedback and can express open-vocabulary actions at different levels of abstraction. Users can customize scenarios involving physical or social reasoning, making the platform adaptable to different agent-development questions.

The authors demonstrate several frontier models on short navigation tasks that require replanning and longer multi-agent food-delivery tasks involving cooperation and competition. These evaluations reveal different reasoning patterns and limitations across the models. The contribution is an open-source environment and an initial demonstration of its use, providing a setting for studying how agents connect observations, decisions, and interactions over different time horizons.
summary.tldr: SimWorld provides customizable physical and social simulations for evaluating language-model agents on navigation and multi-agent tasks.

title: SimWorld: An Open-ended Simulator for Agents in Physical and Social Worlds

abstract: We study how to fine-tune LLMs using user-edit deployment data consisting of a set of context, an agent's response, and user edits. This deployment data is naturally generated by users in applications such as LLMs-based writing assistants and coding agents. The _natural_ origin of user edits makes it a desired source for adapting and personalizing of LLMs. In this setup, there emerges a unification of various feedback types namely preferences, supervised labels, and cost that are typically studied separately in the literature. In this paper, we initiate the theoretical investigation of learning from user edits. We first derive bounds for learning algorithms that learn from each of these feedback types. We prove that these algorithms have different trade-offs depending upon the user, data distribution, and model class. We then propose a simple ensembling procedure to jointly learn from these feedback types. On two domains from Gao et al. 2024, we show our ensembling procedure outperforms these methods that learn from individual feedback. Further, we show that our proposed procedure can robustly adapt to different user-edit distributions at test time.

paragraphs: Users of writing assistants and coding agents naturally produce edits to model responses. This paper studies how to learn from records containing the original context, the agent's response, and the user's revision. Such records offer several kinds of feedback together: preferences, supervised targets, and cost information that are often considered separately.

The authors first derive learning bounds for methods using each feedback type on its own. Their analysis shows that the trade-offs depend on the user, the data distribution, and the model class. This means the usefulness of a particular feedback interpretation depends on the learning setting. They then propose a simple ensemble procedure that learns jointly from the different signals.

Evaluations on two domains show that the ensemble outperforms methods trained from individual feedback types. The procedure also adapts robustly to different user-edit distributions at test time in the reported experiments. The work provides a theoretical and practical basis for treating ordinary user corrections as a combined source of information for model adaptation and personalization.
summary.tldr: A simple ensemble combines preference, supervision, and cost signals from user edits to improve language-model adaptation.

title: Principled Fine-tuning of LLMs from User-Edits: A Medley of Preference, Supervision, and Reward

abstract: In this paper, we study the finite-sample statistical rates of distributional temporal difference (TD) learning with linear function approximation. The aim of distributional TD learning is to estimate the return distribution of a discounted Markov decision process for a given policy $\pi$. Previous works on statistical analysis of distributional TD learning mainly focus on the tabular case. In contrast, we first consider the linear function approximation setting and derive sharp finite-sample rates. Our theoretical results demonstrate that the sample complexity of linear distributional TD learning matches that of classic linear TD learning. This implies that, with linear function approximation, learning the full distribution of the return from streaming data is no more difficult than learning its expectation (value function). To derive tight sample complexity bounds, we conduct a fine-grained analysis of the linear-categorical Bellman equation and employ the exponential stability arguments for products of random matrices. Our results provide new insights into the statistical efficiency of distributional reinforcement learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Distributional temporal difference learning estimates the distribution of future discounted returns for a fixed policy. That is a richer target than the usual value function, which captures only the expected return. This paper asks how much streaming data is needed to learn that richer target when predictions use linear function approximation.

Earlier statistical analyses mainly addressed tabular settings. The authors derive sharp finite-sample rates for the linear approximation setting, making the amount of available data an explicit part of the guarantee. Their central finding is that the sample complexity matches that of conventional linear temporal difference learning.

The proof combines a detailed analysis of the linear-categorical Bellman equation with exponential stability arguments for products of random matrices. The significance is statistical: within the analyzed setting, estimating a full return distribution does not require a worse sample-complexity rate than estimating its mean. This provides a theoretical reason to view richer return predictions as compatible with sample-efficient learning, rather than automatically assuming that a richer prediction target demands more observations.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that linear distributional TD learning matches the sample-complexity rates of learning expected returns in its analyzed setting.

title: A Finite Sample Analysis of Distributional TD Learning with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: In this paper, we study optimization methods consisting of iteratively minimizing surrogates of an objective function. By proposing several algorithmic variants and simple convergence analyses, we make two main contributions. First, we provide a unified viewpoint for several first-order optimization techniques such as accelerated proximal gradient, block coordinate descent, or Frank-Wolfe algorithms. Second, we introduce a new incremental scheme that experimentally matches or outperforms state-of-the-art solvers for large-scale optimization problems typically arising in machine learning.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study optimization methods consisting of iteratively minimizing surrogates of an objective function. By proposing several algorithmic variants and simple convergence analyses, we make two main contributions. First, we provide a unified viewpoint for several first-order optimization techniques such as accelerated proximal gradient, block coordinate descent, or Frank-Wolfe algorithms. Second, we introduce a new incremental scheme that experimentally matches or outperforms state-of-the-art solvers for large-scale optimization problems typically arising in machine learning.

paragraphs: Many optimization procedures can be understood as repeatedly replacing an objective with a surrogate and minimizing that surrogate. This paper studies that shared pattern through first-order surrogate functions. The aim is to explain several established techniques within one framework while also using the framework to construct additional algorithms for machine learning optimization.

The authors propose several algorithmic variants and provide simple convergence analyses. Their unified viewpoint encompasses accelerated proximal gradient, block coordinate descent, and Frank–Wolfe methods. Bringing these techniques into the same account makes their surrogate-minimization structure explicit, connecting algorithms that are often presented separately through a common way of organizing successive optimization steps.

The paper also introduces a new incremental scheme. In experiments on large-scale optimization problems typical of machine learning, it matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art solvers. That is an empirical finding about the evaluated problems. Together, the conceptual framework and the new scheme show how studying existing optimization methods through surrogates can produce both explanatory and practical contributions.
summary.tldr: First-order surrogate functions unify several optimization methods and lead to an incremental scheme that matches or outperforms leading solvers experimentally.

title: Optimization with First-Order Surrogate Functions

abstract: Latent Gaussian models (LGMs) are widely used in statistics and machine learning. Bayesian inference in non-conjugate LGM is difficult due to intractable integrals involving the Gaussian prior and non-conjugate likelihoods. Algorithms based on Variational Gaussian (VG) approximations are widely employed since they strike a favorable balance between accuracy, generality, speed, and ease of use. However, the structure of optimization problems associated with them remains poorly understood, and standard solvers take too long to converge. In this paper, we derive a novel dual variational inference approach, which exploits the convexity property of the VG approximations. The implications of our approach is that we obtain an algorithm that solves a convex optimization problem, reduces the number of variational parameters, and converges much faster than previous methods. Using real world data, we demonstrate these advantages on a variety of LGMs including Gaussian process classification and latent Gaussian Markov random fields.

paragraphs: Latent Gaussian models combine unobserved Gaussian quantities with a model of the observations. When the observation likelihood is non-conjugate, Bayesian inference involves integrals that are difficult to compute. Variational Gaussian approximations offer a practical compromise, but the optimization problems behind them can converge slowly with standard solvers.

The paper introduces a dual variational inference formulation that exploits convexity in these approximations. This leads to an algorithm that solves a convex optimization problem while using fewer variational parameters. The contribution concerns how the approximation is optimized: exposing useful mathematical structure reduces the burden of finding the approximate posterior.

The authors report substantially faster convergence than previous methods and demonstrate the advantages using real-world data across several latent Gaussian models. The examples include Gaussian process classification and latent Gaussian Markov random fields. Together, the formulation and evaluation show how understanding the optimization structure can improve computation across multiple applications of the same broad inference approach.
summary.tldr: A dual formulation exploits convexity to reduce variational parameters and accelerate Gaussian approximate inference in non-conjugate latent Gaussian models.

title: Fast Dual Variational Inference for Non-Conjugate Latent Gaussian Models

abstract: There has been much interest recently in the problem of rank aggregation from pairwise data. A natural question that arises is: under what sorts of statistical assumptions do various rank aggregation algorithms converge to an ‘optimal’ ranking? In this paper, we consider this question in a natural setting where pairwise comparisons are drawn randomly and independently from some underlying probability distribution. We first show that, under a ‘time-reversibility’ or Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) condition on the distribution generating the outcomes of the pairwise comparisons, the rank centrality (PageRank) and least squares (HodgeRank) algorithms both converge to an optimal ranking. Next, we show that a matrix version of the Borda count algorithm, and more surprisingly, an algorithm which performs maximal likelihood estimation under a BTL assumption, both converge to an optimal ranking under a ‘low-noise’ condition that is strictly more general than BTL. Finally, we propose a new SVM-based algorithm for rank aggregation from pairwise data, and show that this converges to an optimal ranking under an even more general condition that we term ‘generalized low-noise’. In all cases, we provide explicit sample complexity bounds for exact recovery of an optimal ranking. Our experiments confirm our theoretical findings and help to shed light on the statistical behavior of various rank aggregation algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper asks when combining pairwise comparisons will recover an optimal overall ranking. It assumes that comparisons are drawn randomly and independently from an underlying probability distribution. Within that setting, it compares algorithms by the statistical conditions sufficient for their convergence, making the data-generating assumptions central to the analysis.

Rank centrality and least squares ranking converge under a time-reversibility, or Bradley–Terry–Luce, condition. A matrix form of Borda count works under a strictly more general low-noise condition. Interestingly, maximum likelihood estimation based on the Bradley–Terry–Luce model also succeeds under that broader condition. Its convergence therefore does not require the data distribution to satisfy the narrower assumption used to construct the estimator.

The authors introduce an SVM-based ranking method with a guarantee under an even more general condition, called generalized low-noise. They provide explicit sample complexity bounds for exact recovery in every case. Experiments support the theoretical findings, helping explain how different ranking procedures behave under different statistical assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies progressively broader statistical conditions under which pairwise ranking algorithms recover an optimal ranking.

title: A Statistical Convergence Perspective of Algorithms for Rank Aggregation from Pairwise Data

abstract: Learning a statistical model for high-dimensional data is an important topic in machine learning. Although this problem has been well studied in the supervised setting, little is known about its unsupervised counterpart. In this work, we focus on the problem of clustering high-dimensional data with sparse centers. In particular, we address the following open question in unsupervised learning: “is it possible to reliably cluster high-dimensional data when the number of samples is smaller than the data dimensionality?" We develop an efficient clustering algorithm that is able to estimate sparse cluster centers with a single pass over the data. Our theoretical analysis shows that the proposed algorithm is able to accurately recover cluster centers with only O(s\log d) number of samples (data points), provided all the cluster centers are s-sparse vectors in a d dimensional space. Experimental results verify both the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed clustering algorithm compared to the state-of-the-art algorithms on several benchmark datasets.

In particular, we address the following open question in unsupervised learning: “is it possible to reliably cluster high-dimensional data when the number of samples is smaller than the data dimensionality?" paragraphs: Clustering high-dimensional data means finding groups when each observation has many coordinates. This paper asks whether useful recovery is possible even when there are fewer observations than coordinates. Its focus is on sparse cluster centers: the representative vector for each group has only a limited number of nonzero entries.

The authors develop an algorithm that estimates these centers while making just one pass through the data. Their theoretical analysis gives a sample requirement of O(s log d), provided every center is s-sparse in a space with d dimensions. Here, s measures the number of nonzero coordinates in a center, so the stated dependence reflects sparsity rather than the full dimension alone.

This result supports the possibility of accurate center recovery with fewer samples than dimensions when sparsity makes that bound sufficiently small. The single-pass design also addresses computational efficiency. Experiments on several benchmark datasets support both the effectiveness and efficiency of the method compared with the algorithms considered.
summary.tldr: A single-pass clustering algorithm can accurately recover sparse high-dimensional cluster centers with a sample requirement of O(s log d).

title: A Single-Pass Algorithm for Efficiently Recovering Sparse Cluster Centers of High-dimensional Data

abstract: We derive ensembles of decision trees through a nonparametric Bayesian model, allowing us to view such ensembles as samples from a posterior distribution. This insight motivates a class of Bayesian Forest (BF) algorithms that provide small gains in performance and large gains in interpretability. Based on the BF framework, we are able to show that high-level tree hierarchy is stable in large samples. This motivates an empirical Bayesian Forest (EBF) algorithm for building approximate BFs on massive distributed datasets and we show that EBFs outperform sub-sampling based alternatives by a large margin.

This insight motivates a class of Bayesian Forest (BF) algorithms that provide small gains in performance and large gains in interpretability. Based on the BF framework, we are able to show that high-level tree hierarchy is stable in large samples. This motivates an empirical Bayesian Forest (EBF) algorithm for building approximate BFs on massive distributed datasets and we show that EBFs outperform sub-sampling based alternatives by a large margin.

paragraphs: An ensemble of decision trees combines multiple trees into a predictive model. This paper derives such ensembles from a nonparametric Bayesian model, allowing the trees to be interpreted as samples from a posterior distribution. That interpretation gives the ensemble a probabilistic basis and motivates a class of algorithms called Bayesian Forests.

The authors report small predictive performance gains and large improvements in interpretability for these algorithms. Within the same framework, they show that the high-level tree hierarchy becomes stable in large samples. This result concerns the broad organization of the trees and provides a reason to exploit that organization when constructing forests at larger scales.

The stability finding motivates Empirical Bayesian Forests, an approximate approach intended for massive datasets distributed across machines. The paper reports that these forests outperform alternatives based on subsampling by a large margin. The contributions therefore connect an interpretable Bayesian account of tree ensembles with a computational strategy for building approximate versions on distributed data.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian interpretation of tree ensembles motivates more interpretable forests and a scalable approximation for massive distributed datasets.

title: Bayesian and Empirical Bayesian Forests

abstract: In reinforcement learning, the notions of experience replay, and of planning as learning from replayed experience, have long been used to find good policies with minimal training data. Replay can be seen either as model-based reinforcement learning, where the store of past experiences serves as the model, or as a way to avoid a conventional model of the environment altogether. In this paper, we look more deeply at how replay blurs the line between model-based and model-free methods. First, we show for the first time an exact equivalence between the sequence of value functions found by a model-based policy-evaluation method and by a model-free method with replay. Second, we present a general replay method that can mimic a spectrum of methods ranging from the explicitly model-free (TD(0)) to the explicitly model-based (linear Dyna). Finally, we use insights gained from these relationships to design a new model-based reinforcement learning algorithm for linear function approximation. This method, which we call forgetful LSTD(lambda), improves upon regular LSTD(lambda) because it extends more naturally to online control, and improves upon linear Dyna because it is a multi-step method, enabling it to perform well even in non-Markov problems or, equivalently, in problems with significant function approximation.

In this paper, we look more deeply at how replay blurs the line between model-based and model-free methods. paragraphs: Experience replay lets a reinforcement learning agent reuse past interactions to improve its decisions. It also complicates the distinction between model-based learning and model-free learning: stored experiences can act as an environment model, even when no conventional model is explicitly fitted. This paper investigates that connection at the level of the learning updates.

The authors establish an exact equivalence between the sequence of value functions produced by a particular model-based policy-evaluation method and a model-free method using replay. They also introduce a general replay procedure capable of reproducing methods across a range from TD(0) to linear Dyna. Thus, seemingly different approaches can share the same underlying progression of value estimates.

These relationships motivate forgetful LSTD(lambda), a new model-based algorithm using linear function approximation. The paper reports that it extends more naturally to online control than regular LSTD(lambda). Its multi-step structure also offers an advantage over linear Dyna, enabling good performance in non-Markov settings or problems with substantial function approximation. The contribution connects a theoretical equivalence to a concrete algorithmic design.
summary.tldr: Exact connections between replay and model-based evaluation motivate a multi-step algorithm better suited to online control.

title: A Deeper Look at Planning as Learning from Replay

abstract: We propose a method for learning expressive energy-based policies for continuous states and actions, which has been feasible only in tabular domains before. We apply our method to learning maximum entropy policies, resulting into a new algorithm, called soft Q-learning, that expresses the optimal policy via a Boltzmann distribution. We use the recently proposed amortized Stein variational gradient descent to learn a stochastic sampling network that approximates samples from this distribution. The benefits of the proposed algorithm include improved exploration and compositionality that allows transferring skills between tasks, which we confirm in simulated experiments with swimming and walking robots. We also draw a connection to actor-critic methods, which can be viewed performing approximate inference on the corresponding energy-based model.

abstract: This paper describes an expectation propagation (EP) method for multi-class classification with Gaussian processes that scales well to very large datasets. In such a method the estimate of the log-marginal-likelihood involves a sum across the data instances. This enables efficient training using stochastic gradients and mini-batches. When this type of training is used, the computational cost does not depend on the number of data instances N. Furthermore, extra assumptions in the approximate inference process make the memory cost independent of N. The consequence is that the proposed EP method can be used on datasets with millions of instances. We compare empirically this method with alternative approaches that approximate the required computations using variational inference. The results show that it performs similar or even better than these techniques, which sometimes give significantly worse predictive distributions in terms of the test log-likelihood. Besides this, the training process of the proposed approach also seems to converge in a smaller number of iterations.

summary.tldr: Mini-batch expectation propagation enables multiclass Gaussian process classification on millions of observations with competitive predictive distributions.

title: Scalable Multi-Class Gaussian Process Classification using Expectation Propagation

abstract: Training large neural networks requires distributing learning across multiple workers, where the cost of communicating gradients can be a significant bottleneck. signSGD alleviates this problem by transmitting just the sign of each minibatch stochastic gradient. We prove that it can get the best of both worlds: compressed gradients and SGD-level convergence rate. The relative $\ell_1/\ell_2$ geometry of gradients, noise and curvature informs whether signSGD or SGD is theoretically better suited to a particular problem. On the practical side we find that the momentum counterpart of signSGD is able to match the accuracy and convergence speed of Adam on deep Imagenet models. We extend our theory to the distributed setting, where the parameter server uses majority vote to aggregate gradient signs from each worker enabling 1-bit compression of worker-server communication in both directions. Using a theorem by Gauss we prove that majority vote can achieve the same reduction in variance as full precision distributed SGD. Thus, there is great promise for sign-based optimisation schemes to achieve fast communication and fast convergence. Code to reproduce experiments is to be found at https://github.com/jxbz/signSGD.

paragraphs: Distributed neural-network training can spend substantial effort communicating gradients between workers and a server. signSGD reduces this communication by sending only the sign of each minibatch gradient component. Each transmitted component says which direction the gradient points, discarding its magnitude and allowing a one-bit representation.

The authors prove that this compression can retain an SGD-level convergence rate. Their analysis relates the suitability of signSGD versus SGD to the relative l1 and l2 geometry of gradients, noise, and curvature. In distributed training, the server aggregates signs by majority vote. The paper proves that this voting scheme can achieve the same variance reduction as full-precision distributed SGD while supporting one-bit communication in both directions.

Empirically, the momentum version of signSGD matches Adam’s accuracy and convergence speed on the studied deep ImageNet models. Together, the theory and experiments support sign-based updates as a promising way to reduce communication without necessarily sacrificing optimization performance. The geometric analysis also makes clear that theoretical suitability depends on the problem.
summary.tldr: signSGD communicates gradient signs and can retain strong convergence while sharply compressing distributed training messages.

title: signSGD: Compressed Optimisation for Non-Convex Problems

abstract: We present a stochastic algorithm to compute the barycenter of a set of probability distributions under the Wasserstein metric from optimal transport. Unlike previous approaches, our method extends to continuous input distributions and allows the support of the barycenter to be adjusted in each iteration. We tackle the problem without regularization, allowing us to recover a sharp output whose support is contained within the support of the true barycenter. We give examples where our algorithm recovers a more meaningful barycenter than previous work. Our method is versatile and can be extended to applications such as generating super samples from a given distribution and recovering blue noise approximations.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter summarizes a collection of probability distributions using the geometry of optimal transport. Computing that representative distribution requires deciding both how to place its probability mass and where that mass can be located. This paper introduces a stochastic algorithm that can work with continuous input distributions.

A central feature is that the barycenter’s support—the locations where it places mass—can change at every iteration. The method also solves the problem without regularization. The authors state that this allows recovery of a sharp output whose support is contained in that of the true barycenter, tying the output’s locations to the target distribution’s support.

Examples show cases where the algorithm produces a more meaningful barycenter than previous approaches. The paper also describes extensions for generating super samples from a distribution and recovering blue-noise approximations. These applications illustrate the method’s versatility, while the main contribution is a barycenter computation procedure that accommodates continuous inputs and an adjustable support.
summary.tldr: A stochastic, unregularized algorithm computes Wasserstein barycenters with continuous inputs and support that can adapt during optimization.

title: Stochastic Wasserstein Barycenters

abstract: Non-convex optimization problems arise frequently in machine learning, including feature selection, structured matrix learning, mixture modeling, and neural network training. We consider the problem of finding critical points of a broad class of non-convex problems with non-smooth components. We analyze the behavior of two gradient-based methods—namely a sub-gradient method, and a proximal method. Our main results are to establish rates of convergence for general problems, and also exhibit faster rates for sub-analytic functions. As an application of our theory, we obtain a simplification of the popular CCCP algorithm, which retains all the desirable convergence properties of the original method, along with a significantly lower cost per iteration. We illustrate our methods and theory via application to the problems of best subset selection, robust estimation, and shape from shading reconstruction.

Its target is finding critical points, so the convergence results concern that objective rather than a claim that the methods always find the best possible solution.

The authors analyze two approaches: a sub-gradient method and a proximal method. They establish convergence rates for the general problem class and obtain faster rates for functions with an additional property called sub-analyticity. This distinction matters because the stronger conclusions rely on extra mathematical structure in the objective.

The theory also leads to a simpler version of the popular CCCP algorithm. According to the paper, the simplified method preserves the original algorithm’s desirable convergence properties while substantially reducing the cost of each iteration. Applications to best subset selection, robust estimation, and shape-from-shading reconstruction illustrate the methods and theory across different optimization tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes critical-point convergence rates for non-convex, non-smooth optimization and derives a cheaper CCCP variant.

title: Convergence guarantees for a class of non-convex and non-smooth optimization problems

abstract: We consider the scenario of online learning with sleeping experts, where not all experts are available at each round, and analyze the general framework of learning with feedback graphs, where the loss observations associated with each expert are characterized by a graph. A critical assumption in this framework is that the loss observations and the set of sleeping experts at each round are independent. We first extend the classical sleeping experts algorithm of Kleinberg et al. 2008 to the feedback graphs scenario, and prove matching upper and lower bounds for the sleeping regret of the resulting algorithm under the independence assumption. Our main contribution is then to relax this assumption, present a more general notion of sleeping regret, and derive a general algorithm with strong theoretical guarantees. We apply this new framework to the important scenario of online learning with abstention, where a learner can elect to abstain from making a prediction at the price of a certain cost. We empirically validate our algorithm against multiple online abstention algorithms on several real-world datasets, showing substantial performance improvements.

paragraphs: Online learning with sleeping experts allows some candidate predictors to be unavailable on a given round. Feedback graphs add another complication: the learner's choice determines which experts' losses it can observe. This paper studies the combination, initially assuming that loss observations and the set of unavailable experts are independent.

Under that assumption, the authors extend a classical sleeping-experts algorithm and prove matching upper and lower bounds on sleeping regret. Their main contribution then relaxes independence. They introduce a more general regret notion and an algorithm with theoretical guarantees, broadening the framework to accommodate dependencies excluded by the initial analysis.

The authors apply the framework to online prediction with abstention, where the learner may decline to predict while paying a specified cost. This creates a concrete setting in which prediction choices and available feedback must be handled together. Experiments on several real-world datasets show substantial improvements over multiple online abstention algorithms, providing empirical support for this application of the more general framework.
summary.tldr: A generalized sleeping-experts framework relaxes independence assumptions about feedback and availability, with theoretical guarantees and improved online abstention results.

title: Online Learning with Sleeping Experts and Feedback Graphs

abstract: Clustering large-scale networks is a central topic in unsupervised learning with many applications in machine learning and data mining. A classic approach to cluster a network is to identify regions of high edge density, which in the literature is captured by two fundamental problems: the densest subgraph and the $k$-core decomposition problems. We design massively parallel computation (MPC) algorithms for these problems that are considerably faster than prior work. In the case of $k$-core decomposition, our work improves exponentially on the algorithm provided by Esfandiari et al. (ICML’18). Compared to the prior work on densest subgraph presented by Bahmani et al. (VLDB’12, ’14), our result requires quadratically fewer MPC rounds. We complement our analysis with an experimental scalability analysis of our techniques.

paragraphs: One way to find structure in a large network is to identify regions with many edges. This paper targets two fundamental problems used in that approach: finding a densest subgraph and computing a k-core decomposition. Both support density-based analysis, but processing very large networks makes algorithmic scalability a central concern.

The authors design algorithms for the massively parallel computation model. Their improvements concern how efficiently these network problems can be solved across parallel computation rounds. For k-core decomposition, they report an exponential improvement over the referenced prior algorithm. For densest subgraph, their result uses quadratically fewer rounds than the cited earlier work.

These are improvements relative to specific previous methods within the stated computation model, rather than a universal claim about every network clustering procedure. The authors complement the algorithmic analysis with experiments examining scalability. Together, the results address the computational machinery behind density-based network analysis: faster parallel solutions to these foundational problems can make the corresponding structural analysis more practical at large scales.
summary.tldr: New massively parallel algorithms improve the round complexity of densest subgraph and k-core decomposition over the cited prior methods.

title: Improved Parallel Algorithms for Density-Based Network Clustering

abstract: We introduce a novel approach to perform first-order optimization with orthogonal and unitary constraints. This approach is based on a parametrization stemming from Lie group theory through the exponential map. The parametrization transforms the constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one over a Euclidean space, for which common first-order optimization methods can be used. The theoretical results presented are general enough to cover the special orthogonal group, the unitary group and, in general, any connected compact Lie group. We discuss how this and other parametrizations can be computed efficiently through an implementation trick, making numerically complex parametrizations usable at a negligible runtime cost in neural networks. In particular, we apply our results to RNNs with orthogonal recurrent weights, yielding a new architecture called expRNN. We demonstrate how our method constitutes a more robust approach to optimization with orthogonal constraints, showing faster, accurate, and more stable convergence in several tasks designed to test RNNs.

Such constraints restrict the allowable matrices, making optimization different from freely adjusting ordinary numerical parameters. The authors use a parametrization derived from Lie group theory, specifically the exponential map, to express the problem through unconstrained variables in Euclidean space.

They apply the method to recurrent networks whose recurrent weights are orthogonal, producing an architecture called expRNN. On several tasks designed to test recurrent networks, they report faster, accurate, and more stable convergence. The contribution therefore connects a general mathematical parametrization with a practical implementation and an experimentally supported approach to optimization under orthogonal constraints.
summary.tldr: An exponential-map parametrization makes orthogonal and unitary optimization unconstrained and supports efficient, stable training of expRNN.

title: Cheap Orthogonal Constraints in Neural Networks: A Simple Parametrization of the Orthogonal and Unitary Group

abstract: In order to learn quickly with few samples, meta-learning utilizes prior knowledge learned from previous tasks. However, a critical challenge in meta-learning is task uncertainty and heterogeneity, which can not be handled via globally sharing knowledge among tasks. In this paper, based on gradient-based meta-learning, we propose a hierarchically structured meta-learning (HSML) algorithm that explicitly tailors the transferable knowledge to different clusters of tasks. Inspired by the way human beings organize knowledge, we resort to a hierarchical task clustering structure to cluster tasks. As a result, the proposed approach not only addresses the challenge via the knowledge customization to different clusters of tasks, but also preserves knowledge generalization among a cluster of similar tasks. To tackle the changing of task relationship, in addition, we extend the hierarchical structure to a continual learning environment. The experimental results show that our approach can achieve state-of-the-art performance in both toy-regression and few-shot image classification problems.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience from previous tasks to help a model learn new tasks from few examples. A difficulty arises when those tasks differ substantially or their relationships are uncertain. Sharing the same knowledge globally cannot adequately handle this heterogeneity, motivating a way to customize what transfers between tasks.

Hierarchically Structured Meta-learning builds on gradient-based meta-learning and organizes tasks into a hierarchy of clusters. Transferable knowledge is tailored to different clusters, while similar tasks within a cluster still benefit from shared knowledge. The hierarchy therefore gives the method a structure for deciding which prior experience is relevant to which group of tasks.

The authors also extend the hierarchy to continual learning, where task relationships can change over time. Experiments on toy regression and few-shot image classification show that the approach can achieve state-of-the-art performance. These findings support organizing transfer around task relationships: customization can address differences between groups while preserving generalization among related tasks, instead of requiring a single globally shared source of knowledge.
summary.tldr: HSML organizes tasks hierarchically so that transferable knowledge can be customized to task clusters while remaining shared among similar tasks.

title: Hierarchically Structured Meta-learning

abstract: We investigate the use of a non-parametric independence measure, the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), as a loss-function for learning robust regression and classification models. This loss-function encourages learning models where the distribution of the residuals between the label and the model prediction is statistically independent of the distribution of the instances themselves. This loss-function was first proposed by \citet{mooij2009regression} in the context of learning causal graphs. We adapt it to the task of learning for unsupervised covariate shift: learning on a source domain without access to any instances or labels from the unknown target domain, but with the assumption that $p(y|x)$ (the conditional probability of labels given instances) remains the same in the target domain. We show that the proposed loss is expected to give rise to models that generalize well on a class of target domains characterised by the complexity of their description within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Experiments on unsupervised covariate shift tasks demonstrate that models learned with the proposed loss-function outperform models learned with standard loss functions, achieving state-of-the-art results on a challenging cell-microscopy unsupervised covariate shift task.

paragraphs: This paper studies a learning objective based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, or HSIC. The objective encourages prediction residuals—the differences between labels and predictions—to be statistically independent of the input instances. The authors adapt this independence-based loss, previously proposed for causal graph learning, to robust regression and classification under covariate shift.

The setting is demanding: training uses a source domain without access to examples or labels from the unknown target domain. It assumes that the conditional distribution of labels given inputs remains unchanged. Under this setup, the analysis identifies a class of target domains on which the loss is expected to support good generalization, characterized through complexity in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

Experiments on unsupervised covariate shift tasks show improvements over standard losses, including state-of-the-art results on a challenging cell-microscopy task. The findings support residual independence as a useful training objective for the studied shifts. The theoretical expectation is tied to the specified target-domain class and unchanged label-given-input relationship.
summary.tldr: An HSIC-based loss encourages input-independent prediction residuals and improves robustness to evaluated covariate shifts without target-domain training data.

title: Robust Learning with the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion

abstract: To simultaneously capture syntax and global semantics from a text corpus, we propose a new larger-context recurrent neural network (RNN) based language model, which extracts recurrent hierarchical semantic structure via a dynamic deep topic model to guide natural language generation. Moving beyond a conventional RNN-based language model that ignores long-range word dependencies and sentence order, the proposed model captures not only intra-sentence word dependencies, but also temporal transitions between sentences and inter-sentence topic dependencies. For inference, we develop a hybrid of stochastic-gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo and recurrent autoencoding variational Bayes. Experimental results on a variety of real-world text corpora demonstrate that the proposed model not only outperforms larger-context RNN-based language models, but also learns interpretable recurrent multilayer topics and generates diverse sentences and paragraphs that are syntactically correct and semantically coherent.

paragraphs: Generating coherent text requires modeling both nearby word relationships and meaning that persists across sentences. This paper combines a recurrent neural language model with a dynamic deep topic model. The topic model extracts hierarchical semantic structure that changes through a text and uses that structure to guide language generation over a larger context.

The combined model represents word dependencies within sentences, transitions between sentences, and topic dependencies across sentences. These components give sentence order and broader semantic context an explicit role in generation. For inference, the authors develop a hybrid procedure combining stochastic-gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo with recurrent autoencoding variational Bayes.

Experiments on several real-world text collections show improvements over larger-context recurrent language models. The learned multilayer topics are interpretable, and the generated sentences and paragraphs are reported to be diverse, grammatically correct, and semantically coherent. These findings support using recurrent topic structure to connect local language modeling with the broader organization of a passage.
summary.tldr: A dynamic hierarchical topic model guides a recurrent language model to capture cross-sentence meaning and generate more coherent text.

title: Recurrent Hierarchical Topic-Guided RNN for Language Generation

abstract: Gaussian Process Factor Analysis (GPFA) has been broadly applied to the problem of identifying smooth, low-dimensional temporal structure underlying large-scale neural recordings. However, spike trains are non-Gaussian, which motivates combining GPFA with discrete observation models for binned spike count data. The drawback to this approach is that GPFA priors are not conjugate to count model likelihoods, which makes inference challenging. Here we address this obstacle by introducing a fast, approximate inference method for non-conjugate GPFA models. Our approach uses orthogonal second-order polynomials to approximate the nonlinear terms in the non-conjugate log-likelihood, resulting in a method we refer to as polynomial approximate log-likelihood (PAL) estimators. This approximation allows for accurate closed-form evaluation of marginal likelihoods and fast numerical optimization for parameters and hyperparameters. We derive PAL estimators for GPFA models with binomial, Poisson, and negative binomial observations and find the PAL estimation is highly accurate, and achieves faster convergence times compared to existing state-of-the-art inference methods. We also find that PAL hyperparameters can provide sensible initialization for black box variational inference (BBVI), which improves BBVI accuracy. We demonstrate that PAL estimators achieve fast and accurate extraction of latent structure from multi-neuron spike train data.

paragraphs: Gaussian process factor analysis extracts smooth, low-dimensional patterns from recordings of many neurons. Neural spike counts, however, are not Gaussian. Using count-based observation models better accommodates this data type, but creates a mismatch between the prior and likelihood that makes inference difficult.

The paper addresses that difficulty with polynomial approximate log-likelihood estimators, called PAL. These replace nonlinear likelihood terms with orthogonal second-order polynomial approximations. The resulting structure permits accurate approximate marginal-likelihood evaluation in closed form and fast numerical optimization of model parameters and hyperparameters. summary.tldr: Quadratic likelihood approximations enable fast, accurate inference of latent neural activity in Gaussian process models with spike-count observations.

title: Efficient Non-conjugate Gaussian Process Factor Models for Spike Count Data using Polynomial Approximations

abstract: This paper studies the sample complexity (aka number of comparisons) bounds for the active best-$k$ items selection from pairwise comparisons. From a given set of items, the learner can make pairwise comparisons on every pair of items, and each comparison returns an independent noisy result about the preferred item. At any time, the learner can adaptively choose a pair of items to compare according to past observations (i.e., active learning). The learner’s goal is to find the (approximately) best-$k$ items with a given confidence, while trying to use as few comparisons as possible. In this paper, we study two problems: (i) finding the probably approximately correct (PAC) best-$k$ items and (ii) finding the exact best-$k$ items, both under strong stochastic transitivity and stochastic triangle inequality. For PAC best-$k$ items selection, we first show a lower bound and then propose an algorithm whose sample complexity upper bound matches the lower bound up to a constant factor. For the exact best-$k$ items selection, we first prove a worst-instance lower bound. We then propose two algorithms based on our PAC best items selection algorithms: one works for $k=1$ and is sample complexity optimal up to a loglog factor, and the other works for all values of $k$ and is sample complexity optimal up to a log factor.

paragraphs: Selecting the best k items from noisy comparisons requires deciding which pairs to compare and when enough evidence has been collected. This paper studies an active learner that can compare any pair, receives independent noisy outcomes, and chooses subsequent comparisons using previous results. The goal is reliable selection with as few comparisons as possible.

The analysis covers approximate and exact selection under strong stochastic transitivity and a stochastic triangle inequality. For probably approximately correct selection, the authors establish a lower bound on required comparisons and provide an algorithm matching it up to a constant factor. This identifies the achievable sample complexity within the stated assumptions.

For exact selection, they prove a worst-instance lower bound and construct two algorithms using their approximate-selection methods. The single-best-item algorithm is optimal up to a loglog factor, while the algorithm for arbitrary k is optimal up to a log factor. These results separate the costs of approximate and exact answers while giving near-optimal procedures for both.
summary.tldr: The paper gives optimal or nearly optimal comparison bounds for approximate and exact top-k selection under specified stochastic ordering assumptions.

title: The Sample Complexity of Best-$k$ Items Selection from Pairwise Comparisons

abstract: The standard normalization method for neural network (NN) models used in Natural Language Processing (NLP) is layer normalization (LN).This is different than batch normalization (BN), which is widely-adopted in Computer Vision. The preferred use of LN in NLP is principally due to the empirical observation that a (naive/vanilla) use of BN leads to significant performance degradation for NLP tasks; however, a thorough understanding of the underlying reasons for this is not always evident. In this paper, we perform a systematic study of NLP transformer models to understand why BN has a poor performance, as compared to LN. We find that the statistics of NLP data across the batch dimension exhibit large fluctuations throughout training. This results in instability, if BN is naively implemented. To address this, we propose Power Normalization (PN), a novel normalization scheme that resolves this issue by (i) relaxing zero-mean normalization in BN, (ii) incorporating a running quadratic mean instead of per batch statistics to stabilize fluctuations, and (iii) using an approximate backpropagation for incorporating the running statistics in the forward pass. We show theoretically, under mild assumptions, that PN leads to a smaller Lipschitz constant for the loss, compared with BN. Furthermore, we prove that the approximate backpropagation scheme leads to bounded gradients. We extensively test PN for transformers on a range of NLP tasks, and we show that it significantly outperforms both LN and BN. In particular, PN outperforms LN by 0.4/0.6 BLEU on IWSLT14/WMT14 and 5.6/3.0 PPL on PTB/WikiText-103. We make our code publicly available at https://github.com/sIncerass/powernorm.

paragraphs: Transformers for language typically use layer normalization, whereas batch normalization is common in computer vision. This paper investigates why applying ordinary batch normalization to language transformers often degrades performance. Its systematic study finds large fluctuations in statistics across the batch dimension throughout training, which create instability when batch normalization is used naively.

Power Normalization addresses this in three linked ways. It relaxes the requirement to normalize activations to zero mean, replaces individual-batch statistics with a running quadratic mean, and uses approximate backpropagation to accommodate running statistics in the forward computation. These changes target the fluctuating quantities identified by the study rather than simply transplanting the standard batch-normalization procedure.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that Power Normalization gives the loss a smaller Lipschitz constant than batch normalization. They also prove bounded gradients for the approximate backpropagation scheme. Experiments across transformer language tasks report significant improvements over both layer and batch normalization, including gains in translation BLEU and language-model perplexity. The theoretical and empirical results jointly support the revised normalization design.
summary.tldr: PowerNorm stabilizes batch-based normalization in language transformers using running quadratic statistics and approximate backpropagation, improving evaluated NLP performance.

title: PowerNorm: Rethinking Batch Normalization in Transformers

abstract: Randomized smoothing is the current state-of-the-art defense with provable robustness against $\ell_2$ adversarial attacks. Many works have devised new randomized smoothing schemes for other metrics, such as $\ell_1$ or $\ell_\infty$; however, substantial effort was needed to derive such new guarantees. This begs the question: can we find a general theory for randomized smoothing? We propose a novel framework for devising and analyzing randomized smoothing schemes, and validate its effectiveness in practice. Our theoretical contributions are: (1) we show that for an appropriate notion of "optimal", the optimal smoothing distributions for any "nice" norms have level sets given by the norm’s *Wulff Crystal*; (2) we propose two novel and complementary methods for deriving provably robust radii for any smoothing distribution; and, (3) we show fundamental limits to current randomized smoothing techniques via the theory of *Banach space cotypes*. By combining (1) and (2), we significantly improve the state-of-the-art certified accuracy in $\ell_1$ on standard datasets. Meanwhile, we show using (3) that with only label statistics under random input perturbations, randomized smoothing cannot achieve nontrivial certified accuracy against perturbations of $\ell_p$-norm $\Omega(\min(1, d^{\frac{1}{p} - \frac{1}{2}}))$, when the input dimension $d$ is large. We provide code in github.com/tonyduan/rs4a.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing certifies robustness by studying predictions under random input perturbations. Extending it to different measures of perturbation size has often required separate derivations. This paper proposes a general framework for choosing smoothing distributions and analyzing their guarantees, with both constructive results and limits on what current techniques can certify.

For an appropriate definition of optimality and a class of suitably well-behaved norms, the authors identify optimal distributions whose equal-density surfaces follow the norm’s Wulff crystal. They also introduce two complementary methods for deriving certified radii for any smoothing distribution. Combining these results substantially improves reported certified accuracy against perturbations measured by the l1 norm on standard datasets.

The limits use Banach-space cotype theory. When certification relies only on label statistics from randomly perturbed inputs, the authors rule out nontrivial certified accuracy against lp perturbations at the stated scale Ω(min(1, d^(1/p − 1/2))) in high dimension d. This qualification matters: the impossibility result concerns that information setting, while the constructive results explain how distribution geometry can improve achievable certificates.
summary.tldr: A general theory of randomized smoothing improves l1 robustness certificates and establishes high-dimensional limits for methods using only perturbed-label statistics.

title: Randomized Smoothing of All Shapes and Sizes

abstract: Many transfer problems require re-using previously optimal decisions for solving new tasks, which suggests the need for learning algorithms that can modify the mechanisms for choosing certain actions independently of those for choosing others. However, there is currently no formalism nor theory for how to achieve this kind of modular credit assignment. To answer this question, we define modular credit assignment as a constraint on minimizing the algorithmic mutual information among feedback signals for different decisions. We introduce what we call the modularity criterion for testing whether a learning algorithm satisfies this constraint by performing causal analysis on the algorithm itself. We generalize the recently proposed societal decision-making framework as a more granular formalism than the Markov decision process to prove that for decision sequences that do not contain cycles, certain single-step temporal difference action-value methods meet this criterion while all policy-gradient methods do not. Empirical evidence suggests that such action-value methods are more sample efficient than policy-gradient methods on transfer problems that require only sparse changes to a sequence of previously optimal decisions.

paragraphs: Transferring behavior to a new task may require changing only a few previously successful decisions. This motivates learning procedures that can update one decision mechanism independently of others. The paper gives this notion of modular credit assignment a formal definition, focusing on how much algorithmic information different decisions' feedback signals share.

The authors introduce a modularity criterion based on causal analysis of the learning algorithm itself. They also generalize a societal decision-making framework to describe decisions more finely than a Markov decision process. For decision sequences without cycles, they prove that certain single-step temporal-difference action-value methods satisfy the criterion, whereas all policy-gradient methods fail it.

The absence of cycles is an explicit condition on that theoretical comparison. Empirical evidence further suggests that the qualifying action-value methods use samples more efficiently on transfer problems requiring sparse changes to previously optimal decision sequences. The contribution links a formal property of feedback signals to a specific kind of transfer, rather than asserting general superiority across reinforcement-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: A formal modularity criterion distinguishes how reinforcement-learning methods assign credit and helps explain performance on sparse-change transfer tasks.

title: Modularity in Reinforcement Learning via Algorithmic Independence in Credit Assignment

abstract: We analyze the properties of gradient descent on convex surrogates for the zero-one loss for the agnostic learning of halfspaces. We show that when a quantity we refer to as the \textit{soft margin} is well-behaved—a condition satisfied by log-concave isotropic distributions among others—minimizers of convex surrogates for the zero-one loss are approximate minimizers for the zero-one loss itself. As standard convex optimization arguments lead to efficient guarantees for minimizing convex surrogates of the zero-one loss, our methods allow for the first positive guarantees for the classification error of halfspaces learned by gradient descent using the binary cross-entropy or hinge loss in the presence of agnostic label noise.

paragraphs: A halfspace classifier separates inputs using a linear decision boundary. Its classification error counts incorrect predictions, but directly optimizing that count is difficult. Training therefore often uses a more manageable convex loss, such as binary cross-entropy or hinge loss. This paper asks when minimizing those substitutes also gives meaningful guarantees about classification error when labels contain agnostic noise.

The analysis introduces a quantity called the soft margin. When this quantity behaves suitably, minimizers of the convex substitute loss approximately minimize classification error itself. The required condition holds for isotropic log-concave distributions, among others. This condition is central: the paper establishes a connection under suitable distributional behavior rather than claiming it for every possible dataset.

Standard convex-optimization guarantees then connect the analysis to efficient training by gradient descent. The authors describe the resulting classification-error guarantees for cross-entropy and hinge-loss training under agnostic label noise as the first positive results of their kind. The contribution explains when progress on a tractable training objective translates into progress on the actual prediction objective.
summary.tldr: Under a suitable soft-margin condition, gradient descent on convex classification losses has provable error guarantees despite agnostic label noise.

title: Agnostic Learning of Halfspaces with Gradient Descent via Soft Margins

abstract: We consider the adversarial multi-armed bandit problem under delayed feedback. We analyze variants of the Exp3 algorithm that tune their step size using only information (about the losses and delays) available at the time of the decisions, and obtain regret guarantees that adapt to the observed (rather than the worst-case) sequences of delays and/or losses. First, through a remarkably simple proof technique, we show that with proper tuning of the step size, the algorithm achieves an optimal (up to logarithmic factors) regret of order $\sqrt{\log(K)(TK + D)}$ both in expectation and in high probability, where $K$ is the number of arms, $T$ is the time horizon, and $D$ is the cumulative delay. The high-probability version of the bound, which is the first high-probability delay-adaptive bound in the literature, crucially depends on the use of implicit exploration in estimating the losses. Then, following Zimmert and Seldin (2019), we extend these results so that the algorithm can “skip” rounds with large delays, resulting in regret bounds of order $\sqrt{TK\log(K)} + |R| + \sqrt{D_{\bar{R}}\log(K)}$, where $R$ is an arbitrary set of rounds (which are skipped) and $D_{\bar{R}}$ is the cumulative delay of the feedback for other rounds. Finally, we present another, data-adaptive (AdaGrad-style) version of the algorithm for which the regret adapts to the observed (delayed) losses instead of only adapting to the cumulative delay (this algorithm requires an a priori upper bound on the maximum delay, or the advance knowledge of the delay for each decision when it is made). The resulting bound can be orders of magnitude smaller on benign problems, and it can be shown that the delay only affects the regret through the loss of the best arm.

paragraphs: A bandit learner repeatedly chooses an option while receiving only limited feedback, which may arrive late. This paper studies adversarial losses and modifies Exp3 so that its step size uses information available when each decision is made. Its guarantees adapt to observed delays or losses rather than only their worst possible values.

With suitable tuning, regret scales as the square root of log(K) times (TK + D), where K counts options, T counts rounds, and D totals delays. This is optimal up to logarithmic factors, both in expectation and with high probability. The latter guarantee depends on implicit exploration in loss estimation. A further extension allows unusually delayed rounds to be skipped, trading their count against the remaining delay burden.

An additional AdaGrad-style variant adapts to observed losses and can give much smaller bounds on benign problems. It requires either an advance upper bound on the maximum delay or knowledge of each decision’s delay when choosing. In its bound, delays affect regret only through the best option’s loss.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Exp3 variants obtain regret guarantees that respond to actual feedback delays and losses, with additional delay information required for the loss-adaptive version.

title: Adapting to Delays and Data in Adversarial Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: Group equivariant neural networks are used as building blocks of group invariant neural networks, which have been shown to improve generalisation performance and data efficiency through principled parameter sharing. Such works have mostly focused on group equivariant convolutions, building on the result that group equivariant linear maps are necessarily convolutions. In this work, we extend the scope of the literature to self-attention, that is emerging as a prominent building block of deep learning models. We propose the LieTransformer, an architecture composed of LieSelfAttention layers that are equivariant to arbitrary Lie groups and their discrete subgroups. We demonstrate the generality of our approach by showing experimental results that are competitive to baseline methods on a wide range of tasks: shape counting on point clouds, molecular property regression and modelling particle trajectories under Hamiltonian dynamics.

paragraphs: Symmetry-aware neural networks share parameters in ways that respect transformations of their inputs. An equivariant layer changes its output consistently when the input is transformed, and such layers can form networks whose final predictions are invariant. This principled sharing has been shown to help generalization and data efficiency.

Much of this work has focused on convolutions, partly because equivariant linear maps must take convolutional form. The paper extends the architectural possibilities to self-attention. Its LieTransformer consists of LieSelfAttention layers designed to be equivariant to arbitrary Lie groups and their discrete subgroups, bringing a broad class of transformation symmetries into attention-based models.

The authors demonstrate the approach on shape counting in point clouds, molecular property regression, and particle trajectories governed by Hamiltonian dynamics. Results are competitive with the evaluated baselines across these tasks. The significance is the breadth of the construction: one attention framework accommodates group symmetry across several different modeling problems, with experiments supporting that generality.
summary.tldr: LieTransformer extends group-equivariant neural-network design to self-attention and shows competitive results across geometric and physical modeling tasks.

title: LieTransformer: Equivariant Self-Attention for Lie Groups

abstract: Deep Metric Learning (DML) provides a crucial tool for visual similarity and zero-shot retrieval applications by learning generalizing embedding spaces, although recent work in DML has shown strong performance saturation across training objectives. However, generalization capacity is known to scale with the embedding space dimensionality. Unfortunately, high dimensional embeddings also create higher retrieval cost for downstream applications. To remedy this, we propose S2SD - Simultaneous Similarity-based Self-distillation. S2SD extends DML with knowledge distillation from auxiliary, high-dimensional embedding and feature spaces to leverage complementary context during training while retaining test-time cost and with negligible changes to the training time. Experiments and ablations across different objectives and standard benchmarks show S2SD offering highly significant improvements of up to 7% in Recall@1, while also setting a new state-of-the-art.
