paragraphs: Deep metric learning builds embedding spaces in which similarity supports tasks such as visual retrieval. Higher-dimensional embeddings can improve generalization, but they also make retrieval more costly. This paper addresses that tradeoff by using richer representations during training while retaining the test-time cost of the deployed embedding.

The proposed method, S2SD, transfers knowledge from auxiliary high-dimensional embeddings and feature spaces through simultaneous similarity-based self-distillation. Those auxiliary spaces provide complementary context to the representation being trained. The purpose is to capture some of the benefit of higher dimensionality without carrying its retrieval cost into downstream use. The authors report negligible changes to training time as well.

Experiments and ablations span different training objectives and standard benchmarks. The abstract reports highly significant improvements reaching up to 7% in Recall@1 and a new state of the art. The maximum improvement describes the reported evaluations rather than a uniform gain across all settings. Overall, the findings support enriching training representations as a way to improve retrieval embeddings at unchanged test-time cost.
summary.tldr: S2SD distills richer auxiliary representations into retrieval embeddings, improving reported accuracy without increasing test-time cost.

title: Simultaneous Similarity-based Self-Distillation for Deep Metric Learning

abstract: It is well-known that stochastic gradient noise (SGN) acts as implicit regularization for deep learning and is essentially important for both optimization and generalization of deep networks. Some works attempted to artificially simulate SGN by injecting random noise to improve deep learning. However, it turned out that the injected simple random noise cannot work as well as SGN, which is anisotropic and parameter-dependent. For simulating SGN at low computational costs and without changing the learning rate or batch size, we propose the Positive-Negative Momentum (PNM) approach that is a powerful alternative to conventional Momentum in classic optimizers. The introduced PNM method maintains two approximate independent momentum terms. Then, we can control the magnitude of SGN explicitly by adjusting the momentum difference. We theoretically prove the convergence guarantee and the generalization advantage of PNM over Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). By incorporating PNM into the two conventional optimizers, SGD with Momentum and Adam, our extensive experiments empirically verified the significant advantage of the PNM-based variants over the corresponding conventional Momentum-based optimizers. Code: \url{https://github.com/zeke-xie/Positive-Negative-Momentum}.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient noise influences both optimization and generalization in deep learning. The paper emphasizes that this noise varies by direction and depends on model parameters, so injecting simple random noise does not reproduce its behavior well. The authors seek a low-cost way to manipulate stochastic gradient noise without changing the learning rate or batch size.

Positive-Negative Momentum, or PNM, maintains two approximately independent momentum terms. Adjusting their difference provides explicit control over the noise magnitude. The mechanism serves as an alternative to conventional momentum and can be incorporated into familiar optimizers, connecting noise control to the optimizer’s existing treatment of gradient information.

The paper provides a convergence guarantee and a theoretical generalization advantage over stochastic gradient descent. It also incorporates PNM into momentum SGD and Adam. Extensive experiments report significant advantages over the corresponding conventional-momentum versions. These findings support momentum design as a means of shaping the noise involved in learning, with both theoretical analysis and empirical comparisons motivating the proposed replacement.
summary.tldr: Positive-Negative Momentum controls stochastic gradient noise through two momentum terms, with theoretical and empirical evidence of improved generalization.

title: Positive-Negative Momentum: Manipulating Stochastic Gradient Noise to Improve Generalization

abstract: While Backpropagation (BP) has been applied to spiking neural networks (SNNs) achieving encouraging results, a key challenge involved is to backpropagate a differentiable continuous-valued loss over layers of spiking neurons exhibiting discontinuous all-or-none firing activities. Existing methods deal with this difficulty by introducing compromises that come with their own limitations, leading to potential performance degradation. We propose a novel BP-like method, called neighborhood aggregation (NA), which computes accurate error gradients guiding weight updates that may lead to discontinuous modifications of firing activities. NA achieves this goal by aggregating the error gradient over multiple spike trains in the neighborhood of the present spike train of each neuron. The employed aggregation is based on a generalized finite difference approximation with a proposed distance metric quantifying the similarity between a given pair of spike trains. Our experiments show that the proposed NA algorithm delivers state-of-the-art performance for SNN training on several datasets including CIFAR10.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks create a difficulty for ordinary backpropagation: their neurons fire in discrete, all-or-none events, while the training loss can vary continuously. Weight changes can therefore alter firing activity discontinuously. The paper addresses how to calculate useful error gradients across this mismatch without relying on the same compromises as existing training approaches.

The proposed neighborhood aggregation method looks beyond each neuron’s current spike train. It aggregates error-gradient information over several nearby spike trains, using a newly proposed distance measure to quantify how similar two trains are. A generalized finite-difference approximation provides the basis for this calculation. The resulting gradient guides weight updates that may change the firing pattern discontinuously.

The central idea is to make neighboring firing patterns part of the gradient calculation, so the update reflects possible changes in discrete activity. Experiments report state-of-the-art spiking-network training performance on several datasets, including CIFAR10. These results support neighborhood aggregation as an effective training method for the evaluated networks and tasks, alongside its proposed way of handling discontinuous firing.
summary.tldr: Neighborhood aggregation trains spiking networks by combining gradient information from nearby spike trains to handle discontinuous firing changes.

title: Backpropagated Neighborhood Aggregation for Accurate Training of Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: While adversarial training becomes one of the most promising defending approaches against adversarial attacks for deep neural networks, the conventional wisdom through robust optimization may usually not guarantee good generalization for robustness. Concerning with robust generalization over unseen adversarial data, this paper investigates adversarial training from a novel perspective of shift consistency in latent space. We argue that the poor robust generalization of adversarial training is owing to the significantly dispersed latent representations generated by training and test adversarial data, as the adversarial perturbations push the latent features of natural examples in the same class towards diverse directions. This is underpinned by the theoretical analysis of the robust generalization gap, which is upper-bounded by the standard one over the natural data and a term of feature inconsistent shift caused by adversarial perturbation {–} a measure of latent dispersion. Towards better robust generalization, we propose a new regularization method {–} shift consistency regularization (SCR) {–} to steer the same-class latent features of both natural and adversarial data into a common direction during adversarial training. The effectiveness of SCR in adversarial training is evaluated through extensive experiments over different datasets, such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, against several competitive methods.

abstract: We consider the experimental design problem in an online environment, an important practical task for reducing the variance of estimates in randomized experiments which allows for greater precision, and in turn, improved decision making. In this work, we present algorithms that build on recent advances in online discrepancy minimization which accommodate both arbitrary treatment probabilities and multiple treatments. The proposed algorithms are computational efficient, minimize covariate imbalance, and include randomization which enables robustness to misspecification. We provide worst case bounds on the expected mean squared error of the causal estimate and show that the proposed estimator is no worse than an implicit ridge regression, which are within a logarithmic factor of the best known results for offline experimental design. We conclude with a detailed simulation study showing favorable results relative to complete randomization as well as to offline methods for experimental design with time complexities exceeding our algorithm, which has a linear dependence on the number of observations, by polynomial factors.

paragraphs: Randomized experiments can estimate treatment effects more precisely when treatment groups are balanced on observed covariates. This paper studies how to achieve that balance online, as observations arrive, rather than requiring all observations in advance. The proposed algorithms support multiple treatments and arbitrary treatment probabilities.

The approach builds on online discrepancy minimization to control covariate imbalance while retaining randomization. That randomization supplies robustness to model misspecification. Computational efficiency is also central: the algorithm’s runtime grows linearly with the number of observations, making sequential assignment compatible with a low computational cost.

The authors provide worst-case bounds on the expected mean squared error of the causal estimate. They show that the estimator performs no worse than an implicit ridge regression, with guarantees within a logarithmic factor of the best known offline experimental-design results. Simulations report favorable comparisons with complete randomization and with offline methods whose runtimes grow by larger polynomial factors. The results connect fast sequential balancing to both theoretical precision guarantees and observed improvements in experimental estimation.
summary.tldr: Fast online treatment-assignment algorithms balance covariates while retaining randomization and strong causal-estimation error guarantees.

title: Online Balanced Experimental Design

abstract: We study human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (RL) with trajectory preferences, where instead of receiving a numeric reward at each step, the RL agent only receives preferences over trajectory pairs from a human overseer. The goal of the RL agent is to learn the optimal policy which is most preferred by the human overseer. Despite the empirical success in various real-world applications, the theoretical understanding of preference-based RL (PbRL) is only limited to the tabular case. In this paper, we propose the first optimistic model-based algorithm for PbRL with general function approximation, which estimates the model using value-targeted regression and calculates the exploratory policies by solving an optimistic planning problem. We prove that our algorithm achieves the regret bound of $\tilde{O} (\operatorname{poly}(d H) \sqrt{K} )$, where $d$ is the complexity measure of the transition and preference model depending on the Eluder dimension and log-covering numbers, $H$ is the planning horizon, $K$ is the number of episodes, and $\tilde O(\cdot)$ omits logarithmic terms. Our lower bound indicates that our algorithm is near-optimal when specialized to the linear setting. Furthermore, we extend the PbRL problem by formulating a novel problem called RL with $n$-wise comparisons, and provide the first sample-efficient algorithm for this new setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretical result for PbRL with (general) function approximation.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in which a human compares pairs of trajectories instead of supplying a numerical reward at every step. The theoretical challenge is to support general function approximation, extending analysis beyond settings represented by tables of states and actions.

The proposed algorithm learns an environment model through value-targeted regression and selects exploratory policies through optimistic planning. The authors prove a regret bound that grows with the square root of the number of episodes, apart from logarithmic factors, multiplied by a polynomial in model complexity and planning horizon. The complexity term depends on properties of both transition and preference models.

A lower bound indicates that the algorithm is near-optimal when specialized to the linear setting. The paper also introduces comparisons involving n alternatives and provides a sample-efficient algorithm for that setting. Its contribution is a theoretical account of learning from trajectory preferences with rich function classes, together with an extension beyond pairwise feedback. The near-optimality claim specifically concerns the linear specialization.
summary.tldr: The paper gives regret guarantees for preference-based reinforcement learning with general function approximation and extends learning to n-wise comparisons.

title: Human-in-the-loop: Provably Efficient Preference-based Reinforcement Learning with General Function Approximation

abstract: In pure-exploration problems, information is gathered sequentially to answer a question on the stochastic environment. While best-arm identification for linear bandits has been extensively studied in recent years, few works have been dedicated to identifying one arm that is $\varepsilon$-close to the best one (and not exactly the best one). In this problem with several correct answers, an identification algorithm should focus on one candidate among those answers and verify that it is correct. We demonstrate that picking the answer with highest mean does not allow an algorithm to reach asymptotic optimality in terms of expected sample complexity. Instead, a furthest answer should be identified. Using that insight to choose the candidate answer carefully, we develop a simple procedure to adapt best-arm identification algorithms to tackle $\varepsilon$-best-answer identification in transductive linear stochastic bandits. Finally, we propose an asymptotically optimal algorithm for this setting, which is shown to achieve competitive empirical performance against existing modified best-arm identification algorithms.

paragraphs: Sequential exploration gathers information to answer a question about an uncertain environment. This paper studies a version in which an algorithm only needs to identify an option whose expected reward is within a specified tolerance, epsilon, of the best. Several answers can therefore be correct, making the choice of which answer to verify part of the problem.

The authors show that always targeting the option with the highest mean prevents an algorithm from attaining asymptotically optimal expected sample complexity. They instead identify a preferred target called a furthest answer. The important distinction is between finding the highest reward and choosing an acceptable answer that supports the most efficient verification strategy.

Using this insight, the paper gives a simple procedure for adapting best-arm identification algorithms to epsilon-best-answer identification in transductive linear stochastic bandits. It also proposes an asymptotically optimal algorithm and reports competitive empirical performance against modified existing methods. Thus, allowing approximate answers changes both the stopping goal and how an efficient algorithm should choose its candidate.
summary.tldr: Choosing which acceptable answer to verify enables asymptotically optimal identification of approximately best options in linear bandits.

title: Choosing Answers in Epsilon-Best-Answer Identification for Linear Bandits

abstract: Conventional domain adaptation (DA) techniques aim to improve domain transferability by learning domain-invariant representations; while concurrently preserving the task-discriminability knowledge gathered from the labeled source data. However, the requirement of simultaneous access to labeled source and unlabeled target renders them unsuitable for the challenging source-free DA setting. The trivial solution of realizing an effective original to generic domain mapping improves transferability but degrades task discriminability. Upon analyzing the hurdles from both theoretical and empirical standpoints, we derive novel insights to show that a mixup between original and corresponding translated generic samples enhances the discriminability-transferability trade-off while duly respecting the privacy-oriented source-free setting. A simple but effective realization of the proposed insights on top of the existing source-free DA approaches yields state-of-the-art performance with faster convergence. Beyond single-source, we also outperform multi-source prior-arts across both classification and semantic segmentation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation aims to preserve useful task knowledge while adapting to a different data domain. Conventional methods often access labeled source data and unlabeled target data together. This paper addresses the source-free setting, where that simultaneous access is unavailable. The challenge is to improve transfer without losing the distinctions needed to perform the task.

The authors analyze a tension in mapping original samples into a more generic domain: the mapping can improve transferability while weakening task discriminability. Their proposed response is mixup between an original sample and its corresponding translated generic sample. Theoretical and empirical analyses support this mixing strategy as a way to improve the balance between the two objectives.

The approach is implemented on top of existing source-free adaptation methods while respecting the setting’s restriction on source access. The authors report leading performance and faster convergence, with results extending beyond single-source adaptation. They also report improvements over earlier multi-source methods on classification and semantic segmentation benchmarks, supporting the usefulness of the proposed trade-off across these tasks.
summary.tldr: Mixing original samples with their generic-domain translations improves the reported balance between task discrimination and source-free transfer.

title: Balancing Discriminability and Transferability for Source-Free Domain Adaptation

abstract: Diffusion models have recently been shown to generate high-quality synthetic images, especially when paired with a guidance technique to trade off diversity for fidelity. We explore diffusion models for the problem of text-conditional image synthesis and compare two different guidance strategies: CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance. We find that the latter is preferred by human evaluators for both photorealism and caption similarity, and often produces photorealistic samples. Samples from a 3.5 billion parameter text-conditional diffusion model using classifier-free guidance are favored by human evaluators to those from DALL-E, even when the latter uses expensive CLIP reranking. Additionally, we find that our models can be fine-tuned to perform image inpainting, enabling powerful text-driven image editing. We train a smaller model on a filtered dataset and release the code and weights at https://github.com/openai/glide-text2im.

paragraphs: This paper investigates diffusion models that generate images from text descriptions. Guidance is a central design choice because it can trade image diversity for fidelity. The authors compare CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance, asking which produces images that people judge as more photorealistic and better matched to their captions.

Evaluators also favor samples from the authors’ 3.5-billion-parameter text-conditioned model over samples from DALL-E, even when DALL-E uses expensive CLIP reranking. These are comparative human judgments from the reported evaluation, supporting the particular guidance choice and model studied.

The work also shows that the models can be fine-tuned for image inpainting, enabling text-directed editing of images. This extends the approach from producing an image to modifying image content through textual instructions. The authors additionally train and release a smaller model on filtered data, so the released model is distinguished from the larger model used in the highlighted comparison.
summary.tldr: GLIDE finds strong human preference for classifier-free text-guided diffusion and extends the approach to text-driven image editing.

title: GLIDE: Towards Photorealistic Image Generation and Editing with Text-Guided Diffusion Models

abstract: Representing visual signals by coordinate-based deep fully-connected networks has been shown advantageous in fitting complex details and solving inverse problems than discrete grid-based representation. However, acquiring such a continuous Implicit Neural Representation (INR) requires tedious per-scene training on tons of signal measurements, which limits its practicality. In this paper, we present a generic INR framework that achieves both data and training efficiency by learning a Neural Implicit Dictionary (NID) from a data collection and representing INR as a functional combination of wavelets sampled from the dictionary. Our NID assembles a group of coordinate-based subnetworks which are tuned to span the desired function space. After training, one can instantly and robustly acquire an unseen scene representation by solving the coding coefficients. To parallelly optimize a large group of networks, we borrow the idea from Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) to design and train our network with a sparse gating mechanism. Our experiments show that, NID can improve reconstruction of 2D images or 3D scenes by 2 orders of magnitude faster with up to 98% less input data. We further demonstrate various applications of NID in image inpainting and occlusion removal, which are considered to be challenging with vanilla INR. Our codes are available in https://github.com/VITA-Group/Neural-Implicit-Dict.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations describe visual signals through networks that map coordinates to signal values. They can capture detailed images or scenes, but fitting a separate network for each scene can require extensive training and many measurements. This paper seeks to reduce both costs by learning reusable components from a collection of data.

Its Neural Implicit Dictionary consists of coordinate-based subnetworks trained to cover the desired space of functions. A new scene is represented by combining wavelets sampled from that dictionary and solving for their coding coefficients. To train a large group of subnetworks in parallel, the framework uses a mixture-of-experts design with sparse gating.

Experiments report reconstruction of 2D images and 3D scenes two orders of magnitude faster, using up to 98% less input data. The authors also demonstrate image inpainting and occlusion removal. These results show the practical value of moving substantial representation learning into a reusable dictionary, leaving a smaller coefficient-solving problem for unseen scenes.
summary.tldr: A learned dictionary of implicit neural functions enables faster scene reconstruction with substantially fewer measurements in the reported experiments.

title: Neural Implicit Dictionary Learning via Mixture-of-Expert Training

abstract: Data valuation is a powerful framework for providing statistical insights into which data are beneficial or detrimental to model training. Many Shapley-based data valuation methods have shown promising results in various downstream tasks, however, they are well known to be computationally challenging as it requires training a large number of models. As a result, it has been recognized as infeasible to apply to large datasets. To address this issue, we propose Data-OOB, a new data valuation method for a bagging model that utilizes the out-of-bag estimate. The proposed method is computationally efficient and can scale to millions of data by reusing trained weak learners. Specifically, Data-OOB takes less than $2.25$ hours on a single CPU processor when there are $10^6$ samples to evaluate and the input dimension is $100$. Furthermore, Data-OOB has solid theoretical interpretations in that it identifies the same important data point as the infinitesimal jackknife influence function when two different points are compared. We conduct comprehensive experiments using 12 classification datasets, each with thousands of sample sizes. We demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art data valuation methods in identifying mislabeled data and finding a set of helpful (or harmful) data points, highlighting the potential for applying data values in real-world applications.

paragraphs: Data valuation asks which training examples help or harm a model. Shapley-based approaches can provide useful answers, but training many models makes them computationally demanding. Data-OOB offers an alternative for bagging models by using out-of-bag estimates and reusing weak learners that have already been trained.

The reuse is central to its scalability. The authors report evaluating one million examples with 100 input dimensions in less than 2.25 hours on a single CPU processor. They also provide a theoretical interpretation: when comparing two data points, Data-OOB identifies the same important point as the infinitesimal jackknife influence function. Data-OOB significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art valuation methods at detecting mislabeled examples and selecting helpful or harmful subsets. The contribution therefore combines lower computational demands with evidence that its values support practical data-quality decisions, within its stated bagging-model setting.
summary.tldr: Data-OOB reuses bagging models to value training examples efficiently, with strong results for detecting mislabeled and helpful or harmful data.

title: Data-OOB: Out-of-bag Estimate as a Simple and Efficient Data Value

abstract: We consider the problem of global optimization with noisy zeroth order oracles — a well-motivated problem useful for various applications ranging from hyper-parameter tuning for deep learning to new material design. Existing work relies on Gaussian processes or other non-parametric family, which suffers from the curse of dimensionality. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm GO-UCB that leverages a parametric family of functions (e.g., neural networks) instead. Under a realizable assumption and a few other mild geometric conditions, we show that GO-UCB achieves a cumulative regret of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ where $T$ is the time horizon. At the core of GO-UCB is a carefully designed uncertainty set over parameters based on gradients that allows optimistic exploration. Synthetic and real-world experiments illustrate GO-UCB works better than popular Bayesian optimization approaches, even if the model is misspecified.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find a function’s global optimum when evaluations are noisy and provide values without derivatives. Such problems arise in hyperparameter tuning and materials design. The authors identify dimensionality as a challenge for existing approaches based on Gaussian processes or other nonparametric function families, motivating an alternative built around a parametric approximation.

Their algorithm, GO-UCB, can use a function family such as neural networks. It constructs an uncertainty set over model parameters using gradients, then uses that uncertainty to guide optimistic exploration. The distinction between observations and internal calculations matters: the oracle supplies noisy function values, while gradients of the approximation help organize the search.

Under a realizability assumption and additional geometric conditions, GO-UCB achieves cumulative regret of order √T, up to logarithmic factors. Realizability means the chosen function family can represent the objective. Synthetic and real-world experiments report advantages over popular Bayesian optimization approaches even with model misspecification, extending the empirical evidence beyond the assumptions of the stated guarantee.
summary.tldr: GO-UCB uses parametric function models and gradient-based parameter uncertainty to guide global optimization from noisy function evaluations.

title: Global Optimization with Parametric Function Approximation

abstract: We provide a full characterisation of all of the possible group equivariant neural networks whose layers are some tensor power of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ for three symmetry groups that are missing from the machine learning literature: $O(n)$, the orthogonal group; $SO(n)$, the special orthogonal group; and $Sp(n)$, the symplectic group. In particular, we find a spanning set of matrices for the learnable, linear, equivariant layer functions between such tensor power spaces in the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ when the group is $O(n)$ or $SO(n)$, and in the symplectic basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ when the group is $Sp(n)$.

In particular, we find a spanning set of matrices for the learnable, linear, equivariant layer functions between such tensor power spaces in the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ when the group is $O(n)$ or $SO(n)$, and in the symplectic basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ when the group is $Sp(n)$.

paragraphs: This paper characterizes neural networks that respect three specified families of symmetry: the orthogonal, special orthogonal, and symplectic groups. Respecting a symmetry means that transforming a layer's input produces the corresponding transformation of its output. The networks considered have layers built from tensor powers of an n-dimensional real vector space, giving the characterization a precise architectural scope.

The central result identifies spanning sets of matrices for the learnable linear maps between these layers. A spanning set provides building blocks whose linear combinations cover every permitted linear equivariant map. This turns an abstract requirement about respecting group transformations into an explicit description of the linear functions a layer can learn.

For the orthogonal and special orthogonal cases, the matrices are expressed in the standard basis; the symplectic case uses a symplectic basis. The contribution is a complete mathematical characterization within the stated layer setting. Its significance lies in describing the full space of allowable linear layers, rather than supplying only selected examples of symmetry-respecting constructions.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes tensor-based equivariant networks for three symmetry groups through explicit spanning sets of linear layer maps.

title: Brauer’s Group Equivariant Neural Networks

abstract: The mechanisms behind the success of multi-view self-supervised learning (MVSSL) are not yet fully understood. Contrastive MVSSL methods have been studied through the lens of InfoNCE, a lower bound of the Mutual Information (MI). However, the relation between other MVSSL methods and MI remains unclear. We consider a different lower bound on the MI consisting of an entropy and a reconstruction term (ER), and analyze the main MVSSL families through its lens. Through this ER bound, we show that clustering-based methods such as DeepCluster and SwAV maximize the MI. We also re-interpret the mechanisms of distillation-based approaches such as BYOL and DINO, showing that they explicitly maximize the reconstruction term and implicitly encourage a stable entropy, and we confirm this empirically. We show that replacing the objectives of common MVSSL methods with this ER bound achieves competitive performance, while making them stable when training with smaller batch sizes or smaller exponential moving average (EMA) coefficients.

paragraphs: Multi-view self-supervised learning learns representations from related views of data, but its different method families are not equally well understood. Contrastive approaches have a familiar connection to mutual information through the InfoNCE bound. This paper develops another perspective using a lower bound composed of entropy and reconstruction terms.

Through this entropy-reconstruction bound, the authors show that clustering-based methods such as DeepCluster and SwAV maximize mutual information. For distillation-based methods such as BYOL and DINO, they identify a more specific division of roles: the methods explicitly maximize reconstruction while implicitly encouraging stable entropy. Empirical results support that interpretation, connecting these methods through a shared analytical framework without assigning them identical mechanisms.

The authors also replace objectives in common multi-view methods with the proposed bound. The resulting training achieves competitive performance and is more stable with smaller batches or smaller exponential-moving-average coefficients. The contribution therefore goes beyond explaining existing objectives: it supplies an alternative objective whose separated terms help account for behavior and whose reported experiments show practical stability benefits.
summary.tldr: An entropy-reconstruction bound connects several self-supervised learning families and provides competitive objectives with improved stability in the evaluated settings.

title: The Role of Entropy and Reconstruction in Multi-View Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Multi-player online games depict the interaction of multiple players with each other over time. Strongly monotone games are of particular interest since they have benign properties and also relate to many classic games that have applications in real life. Existing works mainly focus on the time-invariant case with provable guarantees established. However, the research of the more general time-varying games in changing environments is underexplored and the best-known result cannot match the guarantees in the time-invariant case. In this work, we present a new decentralized online algorithm for time-varying strongly monotone games, which greatly improves existing results and obtains fast rates, matching the best time-invariant guarantee without knowing the environmental non-stationarity. Furthermore, to achieve faster rates, we generalize the RVU property with smoothness and establish a series of problem-dependent bounds that also match the best time-invariant one. To realize all those results, we make a comprehensive use of the techniques in non-stationary and universal online learning.

abstract: The self-attention mechanism prevails in modern machine learning. It has an interesting functionality of adaptively selecting tokens from an input sequence by modulating the degree of attention localization, which many researchers speculate is the basis of the powerful model performance but complicates the underlying mechanism of the learning dynamics. In recent years, mainly two arguments have connected attention localization to the model performances. One is the rank collapse, where the embedded tokens by a self-attention block become very similar across different tokens, leading to a less expressive network. The other is the entropy collapse, where the attention probability approaches non-uniform and entails low entropy, making the learning dynamics more likely to be trapped in plateaus. These two failure modes may apparently contradict each other because the rank and entropy collapses are relevant to uniform and non-uniform attention, respectively. To this end, we characterize the notion of attention localization by the eigenspectrum of query-key parameter matrices and reveal that a small eigenspectrum variance leads attention to be localized. Interestingly, the small eigenspectrum variance prevents both rank and entropy collapse, leading to better model expressivity and trainability.

paragraphs: Self-attention adjusts which tokens receive emphasis, but the relationship between that localization and model behavior is difficult to explain. Two failure modes seem to point in different directions: rank collapse makes token representations too similar, while entropy collapse produces strongly nonuniform attention and can make learning more prone to plateaus.

The paper studies localization through the eigenspectrum of query-key parameter matrices. Rather than describing attention only by the probabilities it assigns to tokens, the authors connect its behavior to a spectral property of the parameters that generate those probabilities. They find that small variance in this eigenspectrum leads to localized attention.

The analysis further shows that small eigenspectrum variance prevents both rank collapse and entropy collapse, improving expressivity and trainability. This connects apparently conflicting accounts through a common parameter-level characterization. The finding matters because localization and the two kinds of collapse need not be treated as interchangeable: the spectral view identifies a setting in which attention localizes while avoiding both problematic behaviors.
summary.tldr: Small query-key eigenspectrum variance leads to localized attention while preventing both rank and entropy collapse.

title: Self-attention Networks Localize When QK-eigenspectrum Concentrates

abstract: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) has emerged as a highly effective self-supervised approach in graph representation learning. However, prevailing GCL methods confront two primary challenges: 1) They predominantly operate under homophily assumptions, focusing on low-frequency signals in node features while neglecting heterophilic edges that connect nodes with dissimilar features. 2) Their reliance on neighborhood aggregation for inference leads to scalability challenges and hinders deployment in real-time applications. In this paper, we introduce S3GCL, an innovative framework designed to tackle these challenges. Inspired by spectral GNNs, we initially demonstrate the correlation between frequency and homophily levels. Then, we propose a novel cosine-parameterized Chebyshev polynomial as low/high-pass filters to generate biased graph views. To resolve the inference dilemma, we incorporate an MLP encoder and enhance its awareness of graph context by introducing structurally and semantically neighboring nodes as positive pairs in the spatial domain. Finally, we formulate a cross-pass GCL objective between full-pass MLP and biased-pass GNN filtered features, eliminating the need for augmentation. Extensive experiments on real-world tasks validate S3GCL proficiency in generalization to diverse homophily levels and its superior inference efficiency.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning often emphasizes connections between nodes with similar features, an assumption called homophily. That can neglect useful connections between dissimilar nodes. Many methods also aggregate neighborhood information during inference, creating a deployment cost. S3GCL addresses both the diversity of graph relationships and the expense of using them at prediction time.

These filters produce views emphasizing different frequency content. An MLP encoder gains graph context through positive pairs formed from structurally and semantically neighboring nodes.

A contrastive objective connects the MLP's full-pass features with the graph network's filtered features. This cross-pass training removes the need for augmentation while supporting an inference approach based on the MLP. Experiments on real-world tasks show generalization across different homophily levels and improved inference efficiency. The method therefore uses graph structure during learning to support representations that are less costly to deploy.
summary.tldr: S3GCL combines spectral graph filtering with contrastive MLP training to handle varied homophily levels and improve inference efficiency.

title: S3GCL: Spectral, Swift, Spatial Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: Two-stage Stochastic Programming (2SP) is a standard framework for modeling decision-making problems under uncertainty. While numerous methods exist, solving such problems with many scenarios remains challenging. Selecting representative scenarios is a practical method for accelerating solutions. However, current approaches typically rely on clustering or Monte Carlo sampling, failing to integrate scenario information deeply and overlooking the significant impact of the scenario order on solving time. To address these issues, we develop HGCN2SP, a novel model with a hierarchical graph designed for 2SP problems, encoding each scenario and modeling their relationships hierarchically. The model is trained in a reinforcement learning paradigm to utilize the feedback of the solver. The policy network is equipped with a hierarchical graph convolutional network for feature encoding and an attention-based decoder for scenario selection in proper order. Evaluation of two classic 2SP problems demonstrates that HGCN2SP provides high-quality decisions in a short computational time. Furthermore, HGCN2SP exhibits remarkable generalization capabilities in handling large-scale instances, even with a substantial number of variables or scenarios that were unseen during the training phase.

paragraphs: Two-stage stochastic programming models decisions under uncertainty by considering possible scenarios. Solving a problem can become expensive when there are many scenarios, so selecting representative ones is a practical shortcut. This paper argues that selection should account for relationships among scenarios and for the order in which selected scenarios reach the solver.

HGCN2SP represents the problem using a hierarchical graph that encodes individual scenarios and their relationships. A hierarchical graph convolutional network extracts features, and an attention-based decoder chooses scenarios in an appropriate order. Reinforcement learning trains this selection policy using feedback from the solver, connecting the learned choices to the behavior of the solution process.

Evaluation on two classic stochastic-programming problems reports high-quality decisions within short computational times. The model also generalizes to larger instances with numbers of variables or scenarios not seen during training. These findings suggest that learning both scenario representation and selection order can make representative-scenario methods useful beyond the instance sizes used to train the policy.
summary.tldr: HGCN2SP uses hierarchical graph representations and solver feedback to learn which uncertainty scenarios to select and in what order.

title: HGCN2SP: Hierarchical Graph Convolutional Network for Two-Stage Stochastic Programming

abstract: Pre-trained 3D vision models have gained significant attention for their promising performance on point cloud data. However, fully fine-tuning these models for downstream tasks is computationally expensive and storage-intensive. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approaches, which focus primarily on input token prompting, struggle to achieve competitive performance due to their limited ability to capture the geometric information inherent in point clouds. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Geometry-Aware Point Cloud Prompt (GAPrompt) that leverages geometric cues to enhance the adaptability of 3D vision models. First, we introduce a Point Prompt that serves as an auxiliary input alongside the original point cloud, explicitly guiding the model to capture fine-grained geometric details. Additionally, we present a Point Shift Prompter designed to extract global shape information from the point cloud, enabling instance-specific geometric adjustments at the input level. Moreover, our proposed Prompt Propagation mechanism incorporates the shape information into the model’s feature extraction process, further strengthening its ability to capture essential geometric characteristics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GAPrompt significantly outperforms state-of-the-art PEFT methods and achieves competitive results compared to full fine-tuning on various benchmarks, while utilizing only 2.19% of trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained 3D vision model by updating all its parameters can require substantial computation and storage. Parameter-efficient methods reduce that burden, but prompting based mainly on input tokens can struggle to capture point-cloud geometry. GAPrompt makes geometric information an explicit part of adaptation, aiming to retain strong performance while training a small fraction of parameters.

The method combines three components. A Point Prompt accompanies the original point cloud and guides attention to fine geometric details. A Point Shift Prompter extracts information about overall shape and enables geometric adjustments tailored to each input. Prompt Propagation then brings that shape information into the model's feature extraction process. Together, these components connect local detail, global shape, and internal representation.

Across the reported benchmarks, GAPrompt significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods and achieves results competitive with full fine-tuning. It does so using only 2.19% trainable parameters. The finding supports geometry-aware adaptation as a way to improve the performance-efficiency trade-off for pretrained 3D models, with both input-level adjustments and propagated shape information contributing to the proposed design.
summary.tldr: GAPrompt incorporates local and global point-cloud geometry into efficient adaptation, achieving competitive results with only 2.19% trainable parameters.

title: GAPrompt: Geometry-Aware Point Cloud Prompt for 3D Vision Model

abstract: Nearest neighbor search is a fundamental data structure problem with many applications. Although the main objective of the data structure is to quickly report data points that are closest to a given query, it has long been noted that without additional constraints the reported answers can be redundant and/or duplicative. This issue is typically addressed in two stages: in the first stage, the algorithm retrieves a (large) number $r$ of points closest to the query, while in the second stage, the $r$ points are post-processed and a small subset is selected to maximize the desired diversity objective. Although popular, this method suffers from a fundamental efficiency bottleneck, as the set of points retrieved in the first stage often needs to be much larger than the final output. In this paper we present provably efficient algorithms for approximate nearest neighbor search with diversity constraints that bypass this two stage process. Our algorithms are based on popular graph-based methods, which allows us to “piggy-back” on the existing efficient implementations. These are the first graph-based algorithms for nearest neighbor search with diversity constraints. For data sets with low intrinsic dimension, our data structures report a diverse set of $k$ points approximately closest to the query, in time that only depends on $k$ and $\log \Delta$, where $\Delta$ is the ratio of the diameter to the closest pair distance in the data set. This bound is qualitatively similar to the best known bounds for standard (non-diverse) graph-based algorithms. Our experiments show that the search time of our algorithms is substantially lower than that using the standard two-stage approach.

A common solution retrieves a large candidate pool and then selects a smaller, more diverse subset. This paper targets the resulting inefficiency: finding a small final answer may require retrieving far more candidates first.

The authors develop graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor algorithms that incorporate diversity constraints directly into search. Their design builds on popular graph-search methods, allowing it to use existing efficient implementations. The approach combines the goals of closeness and diversity within the retrieval procedure, bypassing the usual retrieve-then-filter process.

For datasets with low intrinsic dimension, the authors prove a search-time bound depending only on the requested result count k and log Δ, where Δ compares the dataset's diameter with its closest-pair distance. They describe this as qualitatively similar to bounds for standard graph search without diversity constraints. Experiments also show substantially lower search time than the two-stage approach, supporting the practical value of enforcing diversity during retrieval.
summary.tldr: Graph-based search algorithms retrieve diverse approximate neighbors directly, reducing search time and providing efficiency guarantees for low-intrinsic-dimensional data.

title: Graph-Based Algorithms for Diverse Similarity Search

abstract: In this paper, we empirically demonstrate that natural images can be reconstructed with high fidelity from compressed representations using a simple first-order norm-plus-linear autoregressive (FINOLA) process—without relying on explicit positional information. Through systematic analysis, we observe that the learned coefficient matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) in FINOLA are typically invertible, and their product, $\mathbf{AB}^{-1}$, is diagonalizable across training runs. This structure enables a striking interpretation: FINOLA’s latent dynamics resemble a system of one-way wave equations evolving in a compressed latent space. Under this framework, each image corresponds to a unique solution of these equations. This offers a new perspective on image invariance, suggesting that the underlying structure of images may be governed by simple, invariant dynamic laws. Our findings shed light on a novel avenue for understanding and modeling visual data through the lens of latent-space dynamics and wave propagation.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a simple process operating on compressed representations can capture useful structure in natural images. The process, called FINOLA, combines normalization with linear autoregressive updates. Experiments show that it can reconstruct images with high fidelity without being supplied explicit positional information, motivating a closer look at what its learned dynamics represent.

The analysis focuses on two learned coefficient matrices. Across training runs, the authors observe that these matrices are typically invertible and that the product of one with the other's inverse is diagonalizable. This observed structure permits an interpretation of the latent dynamics as a system resembling one-way wave equations.

Within that interpretation, each image corresponds to a unique solution of the equations in compressed latent space. The result suggests that simple shared dynamic laws may help describe image structure and invariance. This is an empirical observation and a mathematical interpretation of the learned process, rather than a claim that all natural images must obey universal wave laws. It opens a route for modeling images through the evolution of their latent representations.
summary.tldr: FINOLA reconstructs images from compressed representations, and observed matrix structure lets its latent dynamics be interpreted as one-way wave equations.

title: Exploring Invariance in Images through One-way Wave Equations

abstract: How can we verify whether copyrighted content was used to train a large vision-language model (VLM) without direct access to its training data? Motivated by the hypothesis that a VLM is able to recognize images from its training corpus, we propose DIS-CO, a novel approach to infer the inclusion of copyrighted content during the model’s development. By repeatedly querying a VLM with specific frames from targeted copyrighted material, DIS-CO extracts the content’s identity through free-form text completions. To assess its effectiveness, we introduce MovieTection, a benchmark comprising 14,000 frames paired with detailed captions, drawn from films released both before and after a model’s training cutoff. Our results show that DIS-CO significantly improves detection performance, nearly doubling the average AUC of the best prior method on models with logits available. Our findings also highlight a broader concern: all tested models appear to have been exposed to some extent to copyrighted content. We provide the code in the supplementary materials.

paragraphs: DIS-CO investigates whether a vision-language model's responses can reveal that copyrighted material appeared in its training data. The motivating hypothesis is that a model can recognize images from its training corpus. This turns recognition behavior into a possible signal of training exposure when the underlying dataset cannot be inspected directly.

The method repeatedly presents selected frames from targeted material and examines free-form text responses for the content's identity. Its films were released both before and after a model's training cutoff, providing a benchmark organized around the question of possible training exposure.

The reported detection performance nearly doubles the best prior method's average AUC on models whose logits are available. The authors also find that every tested model appears to have encountered some copyrighted content. That conclusion remains an inference from model behavior, consistent with the method's recognition hypothesis; the stated finding is apparent exposure rather than direct inspection of training records.
summary.tldr: DIS-CO uses repeated frame-recognition queries to infer possible copyrighted training content and reports stronger detection on a new film benchmark.

title: DIS-CO: Discovering Copyrighted Content in VLMs Training Data

abstract: AI models make mistakes when recognizing images—whether in-domain, out-of-domain, or adversarial. Predicting these errors is critical for improving system reliability, reducing costly mistakes, and enabling proactive corrections in real-world applications such as healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems. However, understanding what mistakes AI models make, why they occur, and how to predict them remains an open challenge. Here, we conduct comprehensive empirical evaluations using a "mentor" model—a deep neural network designed to predict another "mentee" model’s errors. Our findings show that the mentor excels at learning from a mentee’s mistakes on adversarial images with small perturbations and generalizes effectively to predict in-domain and out-of-domain errors of the mentee. Additionally, transformer-based mentor models excel at predicting errors across various mentee architectures. Subsequently, we draw insights from these observations and develop an "oracle" mentor model, dubbed SuperMentor, that can outperform baseline mentors in predicting errors across different error types from the ImageNet-1K dataset. Our framework paves the way for future research on anticipating and correcting AI model behaviors, ultimately increasing trust in AI systems. Our data and code are available at here.

paragraphs: Image-recognition models can fail on familiar data, unfamiliar distributions, and adversarially modified images. This paper studies whether a separate neural network can anticipate those failures. The authors call the predictor a mentor and the model whose errors it studies a mentee, making error prediction itself the learning task.

Their empirical evaluations find that mentors learn effectively from a mentee's mistakes on images with small adversarial perturbations. That learning transfers to predicting errors on both in-domain and out-of-domain images. They also find that transformer-based mentors perform well across different mentee architectures, suggesting that the approach can apply beyond a single pairing of model designs.

Using these observations, the authors develop SuperMentor, which can outperform baseline mentors across different error types from ImageNet-1K. Although described as an oracle mentor, its reported contribution is improved empirical error prediction, not infallible knowledge of every failure. The findings support anticipating model mistakes as a separate capability and provide a foundation for future work on using those predictions to correct behavior.
summary.tldr: Mentor networks learn to predict another model's errors, with adversarial-error training transferring to other error types and informing SuperMentor.

title: Unveiling AI’s Blind Spots: An Oracle for In-Domain, Out-of-Domain, and Adversarial Errors

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have exhibited remarkable emergent capabilities through extensive pre-training, they still face critical limitations in generalizing to specialized domains and handling diverse linguistic variations, known as distribution shifts. In this paper, we propose a Test-Time Learning (TTL) paradigm for LLMs, namely TLM, which dynamically adapts LLMs to target domains using only unlabeled test data during testing. Specifically, we first provide empirical evidence and theoretical insights to reveal that more accurate predictions from LLMs can be achieved by minimizing the input perplexity of the unlabeled test data. Based on this insight, we formulate the Test-Time Learning process of LLMs as input perplexity minimization, enabling self-supervised enhancement of LLM performance. Furthermore, we observe that high-perplexity samples tend to be more informative for model optimization. Accordingly, we introduce a Sample Efficient Learning Strategy that actively selects and emphasizes these high-perplexity samples for test-time updates. Lastly, to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and ensure adaptation stability, we adopt Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) instead of full-parameter optimization, which allows lightweight model updates while preserving more original knowledge from the model. We introduce the AdaptEval benchmark for TTL and demonstrate through experiments that TLM improves performance by at least 20% compared to original LLMs on domain knowledge adaptation.

paragraphs: A pretrained language model may struggle when its inputs shift to specialized domains or unfamiliar linguistic patterns. TLM addresses this through test-time learning: it adapts the model during testing using only unlabeled data from the target domain. The approach makes the incoming text itself a source of self-supervised learning.

The paper provides empirical evidence and theoretical insights connecting lower input perplexity with more accurate predictions. It therefore formulates adaptation as minimizing perplexity on test inputs. Because high-perplexity examples tend to provide more useful information for optimization, a sample-selection strategy emphasizes those examples. Updates use Low-Rank Adaptation to keep adaptation lightweight, improve stability, and mitigate forgetting of the model’s original knowledge.

The authors introduce AdaptEval to evaluate this setting and report at least a 20% improvement over the original language models on domain-knowledge adaptation. The findings support perplexity reduction as an adaptation signal when labeled target-domain examples are unavailable. The sample-selection and low-rank update components address how to make that adaptation efficient while retaining more of the pretrained model’s capabilities.
summary.tldr: TLM adapts language models on unlabeled test inputs by minimizing perplexity, emphasizing informative samples, and applying lightweight low-rank updates.

title: Test-Time Learning for Large Language Models

abstract: In this work, we propose a new architecture-agnostic method for training idempotent neural networks. An idempotent operator satisfies $f(x) = f(f(x))$, meaning it can be applied iteratively with no effect beyond the first application. Some neural networks used in data transformation tasks, such as image generation and augmentation, can represent non-linear idempotent projections. Using methods from perturbation theory we derive the recurrence relation ${\mathbf{K}’ \leftarrow 3\mathbf{K}^2 - 2\mathbf{K}^3}$ for iteratively projecting a real-valued matrix $\mathbf{K}$ onto the manifold of idempotent matrices. Our analysis shows that for linear, single-layer MLP networks this projection 1) has idempotent fixed points, and 2) is attracting only around idempotent points. We give an extension to non-linear networks by considering our approach as a substitution of the gradient for the canonical loss function, achieving an architecture-agnostic training scheme. We provide experimental results for MLP- and CNN-based architectures with significant improvement in idempotent error over the canonical gradient-based approach. Finally, we demonstrate practical applications of the method as we train a generative network successfully using only a simple reconstruction loss paired with our method.

paragraphs: An idempotent transformation produces no further change when applied again to its own output. The aim is for a network’s first output to already be stable under another application.

For linear, single-layer networks, they show that idempotent matrices are fixed points and that attraction occurs only around idempotent points. Experiments with multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks report substantially lower idempotency error than the canonical gradient approach. The authors also successfully train a generative network using the method with only a simple reconstruction loss.
summary.tldr: A matrix-derived training update helps neural networks become idempotent, reducing repeated-application error across tested architectures.

title: Enforcing Idempotency in Neural Networks

abstract: To improve the training efficiency of federated learning (FL), previous research has employed low-rank decomposition techniques to reduce communication overhead. In this paper, we seek to enhance the performance of these low-rank decomposition methods. Specifically, we focus on three key issues related to decomposition in FL: what to decompose, how to decompose, and how to aggregate. Subsequently, we introduce three novel techniques: Model Update Decomposition (MUD), Block-wise Kronecker Decomposition (BKD), and Aggregation-Aware Decomposition (AAD), each targeting a specific issue. These techniques are complementary and can be applied simultaneously to achieve optimal performance. Additionally, we provide a rigorous theoretical analysis to ensure the convergence of the proposed MUD. Extensive experimental results show that our approach achieves faster convergence and superior accuracy compared to relevant baseline methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Leopold1423/fedmud-icml25.

paragraphs: Federated learning uses communication between participating models as part of training, so reducing the size of transmitted information can improve efficiency. Low-rank decomposition is one approach to reducing this communication burden. This paper examines how to improve its training performance by separating the design problem into three questions: what to decompose, how to decompose it, and how to aggregate the results.

The authors introduce Model Update Decomposition, Block-wise Kronecker Decomposition, and Aggregation-Aware Decomposition to address those respective questions. These techniques are complementary and can be used together. Their organization matters because the choice of decomposed information, its representation, and its eventual aggregation are all parts of the same communication-efficient training process.

The paper supplies a rigorous convergence analysis specifically for Model Update Decomposition. Extensive experiments show faster convergence and higher accuracy than relevant baseline methods. The results support improving several parts of the decomposition pipeline together, while the stated theoretical guarantee applies to the proposed update-decomposition component.
summary.tldr: Three complementary decomposition techniques improve communication-efficient federated learning, with faster convergence and higher accuracy in experiments.

title: The Panaceas for Improving Low-Rank Decomposition in Communication-Efficient Federated Learning

abstract: Blind face restoration (BFR), which involves converting low-quality (LQ) images into high-quality (HQ) images, remains challenging due to complex and unknown degradations. While previous diffusion-based methods utilize feature extractors from LQ images as guidance, using raw LQ images directly as the starting point for the reverse diffusion process offers a theoretically optimal solution. In this work, we propose Pseudo-Hashing Image-to-image Schrödinger Bridge (P-I2SB), a novel framework inspired by optimal mass transport problems, which enhances the restoration potential of Schrödinger Bridge (SB) by correcting data distributions and effectively learning the optimal transport path between any two data distributions. Notably, we theoretically explore and identify that existing methods are limited by the optimality and reversibility of solutions in SB, leading to suboptimal performance. Our approach involves preprocessing HQ images during training by hashing them into pseudo-samples according to a rule related to LQ images, ensuring structural similarity in distribution. This guarantees optimal and reversible solutions in SB, enabling the inference process to learn effectively and allowing P-I2SB to achieve state-of-the-art results in BFR, with more natural textures and retained inference speed compared to previous methods.

paragraphs: Blind face restoration reconstructs a high-quality face image from an input affected by unknown degradation. Many diffusion methods guide restoration using extracted features of the damaged image. This paper instead develops an approach that starts reverse diffusion from the raw low-quality image, motivated by a theoretical argument for that choice.

The proposed P-I2SB framework uses a Schrödinger bridge to learn transport between image distributions. The authors identify optimality and reversibility issues in existing bridge solutions that lead to suboptimal restoration. Their central modification happens during training: high-quality images are transformed into pseudo-samples using a hashing rule related to the low-quality images, making the distributions structurally similar.

The paper states that this distribution correction guarantees optimal and reversible bridge solutions, enabling the restoration process to learn effectively. Reported results reach state-of-the-art blind face restoration performance, with more natural textures while retaining inference speed relative to previous methods. The approach thus connects how training distributions are prepared with how effectively a model can restore directly from the degraded image.
summary.tldr: P-I2SB reshapes training image distributions to support theoretically optimal, reversible bridge solutions for restoring faces directly from degraded images.

title: Feature out! Let Raw Image as Your Condition for Blind Face Restoration

abstract: Encoding geospatial objects is fundamental for geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) applications, which leverage machine learning (ML) models to analyze spatial information. Common approaches transform each object into known formats, like image and text, for compatibility with ML models. However, this process often discards crucial spatial information, such as the object’s position relative to the entire space, reducing downstream task effectiveness. Alternative encoding methods that preserve some spatial properties are often devised for specific data objects (e.g., point encoders), making them unsuitable for tasks that involve different data types (i.e., points, polylines, and polygons). To this end, we propose Poly2Vec, a polymorphic Fourier-based encoding approach that unifies the representation of geospatial objects, while preserving the essential spatial properties. Poly2Vec incorporates a learned fusion module that adaptively integrates the magnitude and phase of the Fourier transform for different tasks and geometries. We evaluate Poly2Vec on five diverse tasks, organized into two categories. The first empirically demonstrates that Poly2Vec consistently outperforms object-specific baselines in preserving three key spatial relationships: topology, direction, and distance. The second shows that integrating Poly2Vec into a state-of-the-art GeoAI workflow improves the performance in two popular tasks: population prediction and land use inference.

paragraphs: Geospatial learning needs representations that retain where objects are and how they relate to their surroundings. Poly2Vec provides a unified representation for points, polylines, and polygons, aiming to preserve essential spatial properties across these different object types.

The method uses Fourier-based encoding and a learned fusion module that combines the transform's magnitude and phase. That combination adapts to the task and geometry. The shared encoding approach matters for applications involving mixed geospatial objects, because it avoids restricting the representation method to just one type of shape.

Integrating Poly2Vec into an existing state-of-the-art GeoAI workflow also improves population prediction and land-use inference. The findings connect a more general spatial representation to both relationship preservation and improvements in applied prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: Poly2Vec encodes points, lines, and polygons in a shared Fourier-based representation that improves spatial reasoning and GeoAI predictions.

title: Poly2Vec: Polymorphic Fourier-Based Encoding of Geospatial Objects for GeoAI Applications

abstract: We introduce in-context denoising, a task that refines the connection between attention-based architectures and dense associative memory (DAM) networks, also known as modern Hopfield networks. Using a Bayesian framework, we show theoretically and empirically that certain restricted denoising problems can be solved optimally even by a single-layer transformer. We demonstrate that a trained attention layer processes each denoising prompt by performing a single gradient descent update on a context-aware DAM energy landscape, where context tokens serve as associative memories and the query token acts as an initial state. This one-step update yields better solutions than exact retrieval of either a context token or a spurious local minimum, providing a concrete example of DAM networks extending beyond the standard retrieval paradigm. Overall, this work solidifies the link between associative memory and attention mechanisms first identified by Ramsauer et al., and demonstrates the relevance of associative memory models in the study of in-context learning.

paragraphs: The paper introduces in-context denoising as a way to study how attention relates to associative memory. In this task, a query is refined using information provided by context tokens. Through a Bayesian analysis and empirical evidence, the authors show that a single-layer transformer can optimally solve certain restricted versions of the denoising problem.

They interpret a trained attention layer as performing one gradient descent step on the energy landscape of a context-aware dense associative memory, also called a modern Hopfield network. In this interpretation, the context tokens supply the memories, while the query token supplies the initial state from which the update begins.

That single update produces better solutions than exactly retrieving a context token or settling at a spurious local minimum. This gives a concrete example in which associative memory is useful beyond straightforward memory retrieval. The finding strengthens the connection between attention and associative memory while providing a specific account of how contextual information can guide computation in a small transformer.
summary.tldr: For certain restricted denoising problems, one-layer attention achieves Bayesian optimality through an update interpretable as associative-memory gradient descent.

title: In-Context Denoising with One-Layer Transformers: Connections between Attention and Associative Memory Retrieval

abstract: Robust Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) offer a promising framework for computing reliable policies under model uncertainty. While policy gradient methods have gained increasing popularity in robust discounted MDPs, their application to the average-reward criterion remains largely unexplored. This paper proposes a Robust Projected Policy Gradient (RP2G), the first generic policy gradient method for robust average-reward MDPs (RAMDPs) that is applicable beyond the typical rectangularity assumption on transition ambiguity. In contrast to existing robust policy gradient algorithms, RP2G incorporates an adaptive decreasing tolerance mechanism for efficient policy updates at each iteration. We also present a comprehensive convergence analysis of RP2G for solving ergodic tabular RAMDPs. Furthermore, we establish the first study of the inner worst-case transition evaluation problem in RAMDPs, proposing two gradient-based algorithms tailored for rectangular and general ambiguity sets, each with provable convergence guarantees. Numerical experiments confirm the global convergence of our new algorithm and demonstrate its superior performance.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes seek policies that remain reliable when the environment's transition model is uncertain. This paper studies the average-reward objective, which concerns sustained performance over time. It develops a policy gradient method for this setting that can operate beyond the usual rectangularity restriction on how transition uncertainty is organized.

The proposed Robust Projected Policy Gradient algorithm, RP2G, uses an adaptive tolerance that decreases during optimization. This mechanism supports efficient policy updates while progressively tightening their accuracy requirements. The authors provide a convergence analysis for ergodic tabular robust average-reward problems, making that setting an explicit scope of their theoretical treatment.

The method also requires evaluating the worst-case transitions for a policy. The paper studies this inner optimization problem and proposes two gradient-based algorithms: one for rectangular uncertainty sets and another for general sets, each with convergence guarantees. Numerical experiments confirm global convergence and report superior performance. The contribution combines policy improvement with methods for the uncertainty evaluation on which robust decision-making depends.
summary.tldr: RP2G extends provable policy gradient optimization to robust average-reward problems with more general transition uncertainty.

title: Provable Policy Gradient for Robust Average-Reward MDPs Beyond Rectangularity

abstract: Scaling inference compute has become a key driver of advanced reasoning in large language models (LLMs). A proven approach for scaling inference compute is to generate long chains-of-thought (CoTs), enabling models to engage in structured reasoning strategies such as backtracking and error correction. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial method for developing these capabilities, yet the conditions under which long CoTs emerge remain unclear, and RL training requires careful design choices. In this study, we systematically investigate the underlying mechanics of long CoT reasoning—examining the factors that enable models to generate extended reasoning trajectories. Through extensive supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RL experiments, we identify three key findings: 1) while SFT is not strictly necessary, it significantly simplifies training and improves efficiency; 2) reasoning capabilities tend to emerge with increased training compute but are not guaranteed, making reward shaping essential for stabilizing CoT length growth; and 3) scaling verifiable reward signals is critical for RL, and we find that leveraging noisy, web-extracted solutions with filtering mechanisms shows promising potential, particularly in out-of-distribution (OOD) reasoning tasks such as STEM problem-solving. These insights provide practical guidance for optimizing training strategies to enhance long CoT reasoning in LLMs.
