paragraphs: Long chains of thought give language models room to backtrack, correct mistakes, and develop structured solutions. This paper investigates the training conditions that help such extended reasoning emerge. It studies supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to clarify which choices make training more efficient and which help sustain the growth of reasoning trajectories.

The experiments find that supervised fine-tuning is helpful without being strictly required: it simplifies training and improves efficiency. Increasing training compute tends to produce reasoning capabilities, but does not guarantee them. The authors identify reward shaping as essential for stabilizing the growth of chain-of-thought length, showing that additional compute and a suitable training signal play different roles.

A further finding concerns the availability of verifiable rewards. Scaling these signals is critical for reinforcement learning, and filtered solutions extracted from the web show promising potential despite containing noise. This is particularly relevant to reasoning outside the training distribution, including STEM problems. The study offers practical training guidance while preserving an important distinction: longer training can encourage reasoning, but its emergence remains contingent on the training setup.
summary.tldr: Experiments clarify how supervised fine-tuning, reward shaping, and scalable verifiable rewards help develop long reasoning chains without guaranteeing their emergence.

title: Demystifying Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

abstract: In this work we present the BDIA-transformer, which is an exact bit-level reversible transformer that uses an unchanged standard architecture for inference. The basic idea is to first treat each transformer block as the Euler integration approximation for solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE) and then incorporate the technique of bidirectional integration approximation (BDIA) (originally designed for diffusion inversion) into the neural architecture, together with activation quantization to make it exactly bit-level reversible. In the training process, we let a hyper-parameter $\gamma$ in BDIA-transformer randomly take one of the two values $\{0.5, -0.5\}$ per training sample per transformer block for averaging every two consecutive integration approximations. As a result, BDIA-transformer can be viewed as training an ensemble of ODE solvers parameterized by a set of binary random variables, which regularizes the model and results in improved validation accuracy. Lightweight side information is required to be stored in the forward process to account for binary quantization loss to enable exact bit-level reversibility. In the inference procedure, the expectation $\mathbb{E}(\gamma)=0$ is taken to make the resulting architecture identical to transformer up to activation quantization. Our experiments in natural language generation, image classification, and language translation show that BDIA-transformers outperform their conventional counterparts significantly in terms of validation performance while also requiring considerably less training memory. Thanks to the regularizing effect of the ensemble, the BDIA-transformer is particularly suitable for fine-tuning with limited data. Source-code can be found via https://github.com/guoqiang-zhang-x/BDIA-Transformer.

paragraphs: BDIA-transformer aims to reduce training memory by making transformer computation exactly reversible at the bit level. It begins by interpreting each transformer block as an Euler approximation to an ordinary differential equation. Bidirectional integration approximation and activation quantization then provide the basis for reversing the computation exactly.

During training, a parameter independently takes the value 0.5 or -0.5 for each sample and block, controlling how consecutive integration approximations are averaged. The authors interpret this as training an ensemble of differential-equation solvers, which regularizes the model. Exact reconstruction also requires storing lightweight side information to recover information lost through quantization.

At inference, the parameter is replaced by its expectation, zero, giving the standard transformer architecture up to activation quantization. Experiments in language generation, image classification, and translation report significantly better validation performance and considerably lower training memory than conventional counterparts. The authors also identify limited-data fine-tuning as a particularly suitable use case because of the ensemble's regularizing effect. Exact reversibility therefore coexists with a small storage requirement and quantized activations.
summary.tldr: BDIA-transformer combines reversible training and randomized integration with lower memory use, retaining standard transformer inference structure up to activation quantization.

title: On Exact Bit-level Reversible Transformers Without Changing Architecture

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models benefit from Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, but existing approaches incur high inference overhead and rely on discrete reasoning representations that mismatch continuous perception and control. We propose Latent Reasoning VLA (LaRA-VLA), a unified VLA framework that internalizes multi-modal CoT reasoning into continuous latent representations for embodied action. LaRA-VLA performs unified reasoning and prediction in latent space, eliminating explicit CoT generation at inference time and enabling efficient, action-oriented control. To realize latent embodied reasoning, we introduce a curriculum-based training paradigm that progressively transitions from explicit textual and visual CoT supervision to latent reasoning, and finally adapts latent reasoning dynamics to condition action generation. We construct two structured CoT datasets, LIBERO-LaRA and Bridge-LaRA, and evaluate LaRA-VLA across simulation benchmarks and long-horizon real-robot manipulation tasks. Experimental results show that LaRA-VLA outperforms existing state-of-the-art VLA methods while achieving up to a 90% reduction in inference latency compared to explicit CoT-based VLA approaches, highlighting latent reasoning as an effective and efficient paradigm for real-time embodied control.

The paper also identifies a mismatch between discrete reasoning representations and continuous perception and control. LaRA-VLA addresses both issues by moving multimodal reasoning and prediction into continuous internal representations.

Training follows a curriculum. The model begins with explicit textual and visual chain-of-thought supervision, progressively moves toward latent reasoning, and then adapts those latent dynamics to condition action generation. LaRA-VLA outperforms existing state-of-the-art VLA methods in the reported experiments and reduces inference latency by up to 90% compared with explicit chain-of-thought VLA approaches. These findings support latent reasoning as a way to retain useful task reasoning while making action generation more efficient.
summary.tldr: LaRA-VLA trains robots to reason in continuous latent representations, improving action performance while reducing explicit-reasoning latency.

title: Latent Reasoning VLA: Latent Thinking and Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: We study algorithms in the resettable streaming model, where the value of each key can either be increased or reset to zero. This model is suitable for applications such as active resource monitoring with support for deletions and machine unlearning. We show that all existing sketches for this model are vulnerable to adaptive adversarial attacks that apply even when the sketch size is polynomial in the length of the stream. To overcome these vulnerabilities, we present the first adaptively robust sketches for resettable streams that require only polylogarithmic space complexity in the stream length. Our framework supports (sub) linear statistics including $L_p$ moments for $p\in[0,1]$ (in particular, Cardinality and Sum) and Bernstein statistics. We bypass strong impossibility results known for linear and composable sketches by designing dedicated single-stream sketches robustified via Differential Privacy. Unlike standard robustification techniques, which provide limited benefits in this setting and still require polynomial space in the stream length, we leverage the Binary Tree Mechanism for continual observation to protect the sketch’s internal randomness. This enables accurate prefix-max error guarantees with polylogarithmic space.

paragraphs: Resettable streams allow a key’s value to increase or return to zero, supporting settings such as resource monitoring with deletions and machine unlearning. The challenge is to summarize these streams using little memory while remaining accurate when an adversary adapts its updates to previous outputs. The paper shows that existing sketches are vulnerable even with memory polynomial in stream length.

The authors construct adaptively robust sketches whose space usage grows only polylogarithmically with stream length. Their framework covers statistics including cardinality, sum, L_p moments for p between zero and one, and Bernstein statistics. They use dedicated single-stream designs to avoid impossibility results affecting linear and composable sketches.

This is significant because standard privacy-based robustification still requires polynomial space in this setting. The resulting framework obtains prefix-max error guarantees alongside its compact memory requirement, showing that robustness becomes achievable through a different sketch design and a mechanism tailored to repeated observation.
summary.tldr: Dedicated sketches use differential privacy to support compact, adaptively robust summaries of streams whose values can increase or reset.

title: Adaptively Robust Resettable Streaming

abstract: Diffusion-based neural solvers have shown strong promise for combinatorial optimization (CO), but existing methods typically rely on supervised training with large collections of near-optimal solutions. In this work, we extend adjoint-based trajectory optimization methods to discrete combinatorial domains. We formulate diffusion-based CO as a stochastic control problem over Continuous-Time Markov Chains and introduce discrete adjoint dynamics for propagating optimization signals through discrete generative trajectories. Building on this formulation, we propose Combinatorial Adjoint Matching (CAM), an unsupervised training framework for discrete diffusion solvers with structured and low-variance trajectory-level optimization signals. Empirically, CAM consistently outperforms existing unsupervised diffusion baselines and achieves performance competitive with strong supervised diffusion solvers and even traditional solvers across diverse combinatorial optimization problems. This paper develops an unsupervised alternative. It adapts trajectory optimization ideas to discrete problems so that a solver can receive useful learning signals along its generative process.

The authors formulate discrete diffusion as a stochastic control problem over continuous-time Markov chains. They introduce discrete adjoint dynamics to propagate optimization information through generated trajectories. Combinatorial Adjoint Matching, or CAM, uses this formulation to provide structured, low-variance signals for training the diffusion solver at the trajectory level.

Across diverse combinatorial problems, CAM consistently outperforms the evaluated unsupervised diffusion baselines. It also achieves performance competitive with strong supervised diffusion methods and even traditional solvers. The significance is that learning without near-optimal solution labels can still produce competitive solvers when training signals account for the discrete generation trajectory. The reported comparison is competitive performance across the tested problems, rather than a guarantee of optimal solutions or universal superiority over traditional algorithms.
summary.tldr: CAM trains discrete diffusion solvers without solution labels by propagating structured optimization signals through their generative trajectories.

title: Unsupervised Diffusion Solver for Combinatorial Optimization via Combinatorial Adjoint Matching

abstract: Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) models for robotics have highlighted the importance of reliable uncertainty quantification in sequential tasks. However, assessing and improving calibration in such settings remains mostly unexplored, especially when only partial trajectories are observed. In this work, we formulate sequential calibration for episodic tasks, where task-success confidence is produced along an episode, while success is determined at the end of it. We introduce a sequential extension of the Brier score and show that, for binary outcomes, its risk minimizer coincides with the VLA policy’s value function. This connection bridges uncertainty calibration and reinforcement learning, enabling the use of temporal-difference (TD) value estimation as a principled calibration mechanism over time. We empirically show that TD calibration improves performance relative to the state-of-the-art on simulated and real-robot data. Interestingly, we show that when calibrated using TD, the VLA’s single-step action probabilities can yield competitive uncertainty estimates, in contrast to recent findings that employed different calibration techniques.

This paper formalizes calibration for that sequential setting, including the challenge of observing only partial trajectories. The aim is to make confidence along an episode meaningfully reflect eventual task success.

The authors extend the Brier score to sequential tasks and show that, for binary outcomes, the quantity minimizing its risk equals the vision-language-action policy’s value function. This connects uncertainty calibration to reinforcement learning: temporal-difference value estimation becomes a principled way to adjust success confidence as the episode unfolds.

The authors also find that single-step action probabilities can provide competitive uncertainty estimates after temporal-difference calibration. That result differs from findings using other calibration techniques and suggests that the usefulness of these probabilities depends partly on how they are calibrated over time.
summary.tldr: Temporal-difference calibration links a robot’s evolving success confidence to value estimation and improves reported uncertainty performance.

title: Temporal Difference Calibration in Sequential Tasks: Application to Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: Parallel decoding for diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) is difficult because each denoising step provides only token-wise marginal distributions, while unmasking multiple tokens simultaneously requires accounting for inter-token dependencies. We propose Dependency-Aware Parallel Decoding (DAPD), a simple, training-free decoding method that uses self-attention to induce a conditional dependency graph over masked tokens. At each iteration, edges in this graph capture strong token interactions, while non-edges indicate weak dependence. Parallel decoding is then reduced to selecting an independent set on the graph and unmasking the selected tokens in parallel. This avoids co-updating strongly coupled tokens without auxiliary models or retraining. Experiments on LLaDA and Dream show that DAPD improves the accuracy–steps trade-off over existing methods and enables more globally distributed parallel updates that better exploit the any-order generation capability of dLLMs. The project is available at https://ai-isl.github.io/dapd

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can fill multiple token positions at once, but each denoising step supplies probabilities for individual tokens. Those separate probabilities do not directly capture how simultaneous choices depend on one another. Updating strongly connected positions together can therefore overlook information needed to coordinate their predictions.

DAPD uses the model's self-attention to build a dependency graph over currently masked tokens. Strong interactions become edges, while positions without an edge are treated as weakly dependent. At each iteration, the decoder selects an independent set: a group of positions with no connecting edges. It then fills those positions in parallel, avoiding simultaneous updates to pairs identified as strongly coupled.

This procedure needs no retraining or auxiliary model. Experiments on LLaDA and Dream report a better balance between accuracy and decoding steps than existing methods. The selected updates are also more widely distributed across the sequence. The findings suggest that choosing parallel updates according to estimated dependencies can better use diffusion models' freedom to generate in any order.
summary.tldr: DAPD uses attention-derived dependency graphs to choose parallel token updates, improving the accuracy–steps trade-off without retraining.

title: DAPD: Dependency-Aware Parallel Decoding via Attention for Diffusion LLMs

abstract: In many safety-critical settings, probabilistic ML systems have to make predictions subject to algebraic constraints, e.g., predicting the most likely trajectory that does not cross obstacles. These real-world constraints are rarely convex, nor the densities considered are (log-)concave. This makes computing this constrained maximum a posteriori (MAP) prediction in an efficient and reliable way extremely challenging. In this paper, we first investigate under which conditions we can perform constrained MAP inference over continuous variables exactly and efficiently and devise a scalable message-passing algorithm for this tractable fragment. Then, we devise a general constrained MAP strategy that interleaves partitioning the domain into convex feasible regions with numerical constrained optimization. We evaluate both methods on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, showing our structure aware approach outperforms constraint-agnostic baselines.

paragraphs: A probabilistic prediction may need to satisfy hard algebraic constraints, such as a trajectory avoiding obstacles. Constrained maximum a posteriori inference seeks the most likely prediction among those that are allowed. This becomes difficult when the feasible region is nonconvex and the probability density lacks the shape properties that make optimization straightforward.

The paper first investigates conditions under which continuous constrained MAP inference can be performed exactly and efficiently. For the tractable class it identifies, the authors develop a scalable message-passing algorithm. The exactness and efficiency result is tied to those conditions rather than extending automatically to every nonconvex constrained prediction problem.

For more general cases, the authors propose interleaving two operations: dividing the domain into convex feasible regions and applying numerical constrained optimization. This explicitly incorporates the structure of the constraints into the search for a likely prediction. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that both proposed approaches outperform constraint-agnostic baselines, supporting the value of exploiting feasible-region structure.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies an exactly solvable class of constrained MAP problems and develops a structure-aware optimization strategy for broader nonconvex cases.

title: The Theory and Practice of MAP Inference over Non-Convex Constraints

abstract: Standard attention mechanisms in transformers employ static token representations that remain unchanged across all pair-wise computations in each layer. This limits their representational alignment with the potentially diverse dynamics of each token-pair interaction. While they excel in domains with relatively homogeneous relationships, standard attention may be inadequate in capturing heterogeneous inter-channel dependencies of multivariate time series (MTS) data where different channel-pair interactions within a single system may be governed by entirely different physical laws or temporal dynamics. To better align the attention mechanism for such domain phenomena, we propose attention with dynamic relational priming (prime attention). Prime attention modulates token representations for each token-pair, optimizing each pair-wise interaction for that specific relationship. Our results demonstrate that prime attention consistently outperforms standard attention across benchmarks, achieving up to 6.5% improvement in forecasting accuracy. In addition, prime attention achieves comparable performance using up to 40% less sequence length compared to standard attention, demonstrating its superior relational modeling capabilities and potential for data efficiency.

paragraphs: A multivariate time series contains several channels whose relationships can differ substantially. Within one system, different channel pairs may follow different physical laws or temporal patterns. Standard transformer attention uses token representations that stay fixed across the pairwise comparisons within a layer, which may limit how well those representations fit each distinct relationship.

The paper introduces dynamic relational priming, also called prime attention. It modulates a token’s representation separately for each token pair, allowing the comparison to reflect the particular relationship being considered. This makes the attention mechanism more responsive to heterogeneous dependencies, rather than requiring one representation to serve every pairwise interaction equally well.

Across the evaluated benchmarks, prime attention consistently improves on standard attention, with forecasting accuracy gains of up to 6.5%. It also achieves comparable performance using up to 40% shorter input sequences. These results support stronger relational modeling and suggest potential data efficiency: adapting representations to individual relationships can help extract useful predictive information from less temporal context.
summary.tldr: Prime attention adapts token representations to each channel pair, improving time-series forecasting and reducing required sequence length.

title: Dynamic Relational Priming Improves Transformer in Multivariate Time Series

abstract: Partially relevant video retrieval aims to retrieve untrimmed videos using text queries that describe only partial content. However, the inherent asymmetry between brief queries and rich video content inevitably introduces uncertainty into the retrieval process. In this setting, vague queries often induce semantic ambiguity across videos, a challenge that is further exacerbated by the sparse temporal supervision within videos, which fails to provide sufficient matching evidence. To address this, we propose Holmes, a hierarchical evidential learning framework that aggregates multi-granular cross-modal evidence to quantify and model uncertainty explicitly. At the inter-video level, similarity scores are interpreted as evidential support and modeled via a Dirichlet distribution. Based on the proposed three-fold principle, we perform fine-grained query identification, which then guides query-adaptive calibrated learning. At the intra-video level, to accumulate denser evidence, we formulate a soft query-clip alignment via flexible optimal transport with an adaptive dustbin, which alleviates sparse temporal supervision while suppressing spurious local responses. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Holmes outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code is released at https://github.com/lijun2005/ICML26-Holmes.

paragraphs: A short text query may describe only a small portion of an untrimmed video. This creates uncertainty both about which video is relevant and about which moments support the match. Vague queries can fit several videos, while sparse temporal supervision leaves the model with limited evidence for identifying the relevant clips.

Holmes models these uncertainties at two levels. Across videos, it treats similarity scores as evidence and represents that evidence with a Dirichlet distribution. Fine-grained identification of query characteristics then guides adaptive calibration during learning. Within a video, it uses flexible optimal transport to form soft alignments between the query and clips, with an adaptive dustbin helping suppress spurious local responses.

The combination gathers evidence at multiple granularities while reducing the influence of misleading local matches. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art retrieval methods. The approach matters because it explicitly represents uncertainty in matching brief language to rich video content, connecting decisions across candidate videos with denser evidence inside each video.
summary.tldr: Holmes models uncertainty across videos and within their clips to improve retrieval when a text query describes only partial video content.

title: Revisiting Uncertainty: On Evidential Learning for Partially Relevant Video Retrieval

abstract: While MLLMs show promising capacity on general visual understanding, they suffer from geometric fragility: standard visual representations often degrade rapidly under changes in viewpoint and viewing distance. Our analysis identifies that existing paradigms, whether relying on input-level fusion or latent reconstruction, remain entangled with the view-dependent pixel grid, failing to decouple intrinsic 3D structure from extrinsic camera pose. To address this, we introduce AffIn-Space, a framework that enforces strict affine invariance to enable robust spatial understanding. Unlike implicit learning approaches, AffIn-Space introduces a two-stage explicit decoupling mechanism. First, it employs explicit geometric resampling by utilizing decomposed affine quantities (derived from pose features) to spatially align 3D features to a canonical state before fusion. Second, within the MLLM, we implement affine-invariant constraints via an orthogonal projection mechanism, which mathematically strips away pose-dependent noise from the hidden states while retaining recoverable geometric semantics through conditional reconstruction. Extensive experiments on VSI-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, Scan2Cap, and EmbodiedScan demonstrate that AffIn-Space achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code and detailed instructions will be publicly released. Crucially, our approach exhibits superior stability against affine perturbations, validating the effectiveness of explicitly modeling geometric invariance for complex spatial tasks. Code will be made available. Extensive experiments show that AffIn-Space achieves state-of-the-art performance on spatial reasoning tasks (VSI-Bench, SQA3D and Scan2Cap), and on spatial grounding tasks (ScanRefer and EmbodiedScan), demonstrating the effectiveness of affine invariant representations for complex spatial understanding.

The authors attribute this fragility to representations that remain tied to the image’s pixel arrangement. That makes it difficult to separate the underlying three-dimensional scene from the camera pose used to observe it.

summary.tldr: AffIn-Space explicitly removes camera-pose effects from representations to improve multimodal models’ spatial understanding and stability under affine changes.

title: AffIn-Space: Learning Affine-Invariant Representations for 3D Spatial Understanding with MLLMs

abstract: Biological and neuromorphic recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are subject to spatial and temporal locality constraints on the information that can plausibly be used during learning. A common strategy to satisfy these constraints is to modify gradient descent by neglecting non-local terms to varying degrees, as in random feedback local online (RFLO) learning and truncated backpropagation through time (tBPTT). However, the learning dynamics of these algorithms, and how they compare with BPTT, remain poorly understood. We apply dynamical systems theory to data-aligned linear RNNs—whose dynamics can be separated into orthogonal modes—to compare stationary solutions, stability properties, and convergence rates, finding qualitatively distinct behaviour for RFLO versus BPTT and one-step tBPTT. We further observe that the solutions learned by RFLO are restricted to low-rank perturbations of initial parameters, a result which holds beyond the data-aligned setting. Our work provides analytical insight into how locality constraints shape learning dynamics, with implications for neuroscientific models of learning and alternative optimization approaches for RNNs.

paragraphs: Biological and neuromorphic recurrent networks cannot necessarily access all the information used by standard gradient-based learning. Information may be unavailable across distant connections or earlier moments in time. Algorithms such as random feedback local online learning, or RFLO, and truncated backpropagation through time address these constraints by dropping different non-local terms.

The paper studies what these approximations change about learning itself. Its main analysis uses linear recurrent networks aligned with the data, a setting where network dynamics separate into orthogonal modes. Dynamical systems tools then allow comparisons of stationary solutions, their stability, and convergence rates across RFLO, full backpropagation through time, and one-step truncation.

RFLO exhibits qualitatively different behavior from the two backpropagation methods. The authors also find that RFLO’s learned solutions differ from their initial parameters through low-rank changes, with this result extending beyond the data-aligned setting. These findings show how locality constraints can shape the structure of learned representations as well as learning dynamics, providing analytical guidance for models of biological learning and alternative recurrent-network optimizers.
summary.tldr: Analysis of linear recurrent networks shows that local learning approximations can change convergence behavior and restrict the structure of learned parameter updates.

title: Dynamics and Representation Structure of Local Approximations to Gradient-Based Learning in Linear Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) emphasize long chain-of-thought reasoning; yet, we find that their performance on visual tasks is primarily limited by a lack of visual perception as opposed to reasoning itself. In this work, we systematically study the interplay between perception and reasoning in VLM post-training by decomposing their capabilities into three separate training stages: visual perception, visual reasoning, and textual reasoning, incorporating specialized training data. We demonstrate that visual perception (a) requires targeted optimization with specialized data; (b) serves as a fundamental scaffold that should be solidified through staged training before refining visual reasoning; and (c) is more effectively learned via RL than caption-based SFT. Our experiments across multiple VLMs demonstrate that staged training consistently improves both visual perception and reasoning performance over merged training. Notably, models trained with our approach achieve 1.5% higher reasoning accuracy with 20.8% shorter reasoning traces, suggesting that superior perception reduces the need for excessive reasoning. Furthermore, we show that this capability-based staging represents a new curriculum dimension orthogonal to traditional difficulty-based curricula, and combining both yields further additive gains. Our staged-training models achieve superior performance among open-weight VLMs, establishing advanced results on several visual math and perception (e.g., +5.2% on WeMath and +3.7% on RealWorldQA) tasks compared with the base counterpart.

summary.tldr: Staging vision-language post-training around perception and reasoning improves reported accuracy while shortening reasoning traces.

title: From Seeing to Thinking: Decoupling Perception and Reasoning Improves Post-Training of Vision-Language Models

abstract: One-step diffusion models have demonstrated a promising capability and fast inference in video super-resolution (VSR) for real-world applications. Nevertheless, the substantial model size and high computational cost of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) limit downstream applications. While low-bit quantization is a common approach for model compression, the effectiveness of quantized models is challenged by the high dynamic range of input latent and diverse layer behaviors. To address these challenges, we introduce LSGQuant, a layer-sensitivity-guided quantization approach for one-step diffusion-based real-world VSR. Our method incorporates a Dynamic Range Adaptive Quantizer (DRAQ) to fit video token activations. Furthermore, we estimate layer sensitivity and implement a Variance-Oriented Layer Training Strategy (VOLTS) by analyzing layer-wise statistics in calibration. We also introduce Quantization-Aware Optimization (QAO) to jointly refine the quantized branch and a retained high-precision branch. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method has nearly the performance of the original model with full-precision and significantly exceeds existing quantization techniques. All models and code are available at https://github.com/zhengchen1999/LSGQuant.

Reducing numerical precision offers compression, yet video latent inputs span a wide dynamic range and different layers respond differently to quantization. LSGQuant is designed around these two obstacles.

A Dynamic Range Adaptive Quantizer fits the activations of video tokens. The method also estimates layer sensitivity from statistics gathered during calibration and uses a Variance-Oriented Layer Training Strategy to account for layer-specific behavior. Finally, Quantization-Aware Optimization jointly refines the quantized branch and a retained high-precision branch. The method therefore combines adaptation to activation ranges, layer sensitivity, and joint optimization.

The authors report performance close to the original full-precision model and substantially better than existing quantization techniques in extensive experiments. The stated result supports tailoring quantization to one-step diffusion video super-resolution, where the behavior of both inputs and individual layers matters. It also shows that retaining and optimizing a high-precision branch is part of the proposed compression approach.
summary.tldr: LSGQuant adapts quantization to activation ranges and layer sensitivity, retaining near-full-precision performance in reported video super-resolution experiments.

title: LSGQuant: Layer-Sensitivity Guided Quantization for One-Step Diffusion Real-World Video Super-Resolution

abstract: Image editing has achieved impressive results with the development of large-scale generative models. However, existing models mainly focus on the editing effects of intended objects and regions, often leading to unwanted changes in unintended regions. We present a post-training framework for $\textbf{Co}$ntent-$\textbf{Co}$nsistent $\textbf{Edit}$ing ($\textbf{CoCoEdit}$) by using region regularized reinforcement learning. We first augment existing editing datasets with refined instructions and masks, from which 40K diverse and high quality samples are curated as training set. We introduce a pixel-level similarity reward that complements MLLM-based rewards, enabling models to ensure both editing quality and content consistency during the editing process. To overcome the spatial-agnostic nature of the rewards, we propose a region-based regularizer, aiming to preserve non-edited regions for high-reward samples while encouraging editing effects for low-reward samples. For evaluation, we annotate editing masks for GEdit-Bench and ImgEdit-Bench, introducing pixel-level similarity metrics to measure content consistency and editing quality. Applying CoCoEdit to Qwen-Image-Edit and FLUX-Kontext, we achieve not only superior editing scores to state-of-the-art models, but also significantly better content consistency, measured by PSNR/SSIM metrics and human subjective ratings. Codes, data and models of CoCoEdit can be found at https://github.com/langmanbusi/CoCoEdit.

We introduce a pixel-level similarity reward that complements MLLM-based rewards, enabling models to ensure both editing quality and content consistency during the editing process. To overcome the spatial-agnostic nature of the rewards, we propose a region-based regularizer, aiming to preserve non-edited regions for high-reward samples while encouraging editing effects for low-reward samples. For evaluation, we annotate editing masks for GEdit-Bench and ImgEdit-Bench, introducing pixel-level similarity metrics to measure content consistency and editing quality. Applying CoCoEdit to Qwen-Image-Edit and FLUX-Kontext, we achieve not only superior editing scores to state-of-the-art models, but also significantly better content consistency, measured by PSNR/SSIM metrics and human subjective ratings. Codes, data and models of CoCoEdit can be found at https://github.com/langmanbusi/CoCoEdit.

paragraphs: An image editor can successfully change the requested object while also altering parts of the image that should remain untouched. CoCoEdit addresses both responsibilities during post-training: making the intended edit and preserving unrelated content. The authors first refine instructions and region masks in existing editing datasets, curating 40,000 training examples.

The training objective combines rewards from multimodal language models with a pixel-level similarity reward. Because an overall reward does not by itself specify where changes should occur, CoCoEdit adds a region-based regularizer. For high-reward examples, it aims to preserve regions outside the edit; for low-reward examples, it encourages the desired editing effects. This gives spatial structure to the training feedback.

The authors also add editing masks to GEdit-Bench and ImgEdit-Bench so evaluation can measure both successful changes and preservation. Applied to Qwen-Image-Edit and FLUX-Kontext, CoCoEdit achieves better editing scores than state-of-the-art models and significantly better content consistency. Pixel similarity measures and human ratings support the reported gains, indicating that improved editing need not come at the expense of unrelated image content.
summary.tldr: CoCoEdit uses spatially targeted reinforcement learning to improve requested image edits while better preserving untouched regions.

title: CoCoEdit: Content-Consistent Image Editing via Region Regularized Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Estimating the difference of two Stein’s score functions is a fundamental problem in generative modeling. In particular, score differences arise naturally in transfer learning, where the score difference provides the mechanism for adapting a pre-trained model to a new target distribution, and in diffusion model-based post-training methods such as discriminator guidance. Existing estimators for score differences in these settings either lack of statistical consistency or are difficult to scale up in high-dimensions. We propose a statistically consistent and scalable estimator for score differences based on Sobolev regularization, which plays a crucial role in ensuring consistency and stablizing the training in the small-sample regime. Mathematically, we establish a convergence rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-\frac{s-1}{d+2s-2}})$ where $d$ is the dimension and $s$ denotes the smoothness of the underlying densities, and provide a minimax lower bound of $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{-\frac{2(s-1)}{d+2s}})$ (in mean-squared error). Empirically, our estimator exhibits significantly improved stability in small-sample regimes compared to existing methods. We demonstrate its effectiveness on real-world tasks, including transfer learning for ECG signal generation, where it substantially outperforms non-regularized score difference estimators in downstream classification performance.

paragraphs: Adapting a generative model to a new distribution can require estimating the difference between two score functions. That difference also appears in diffusion post-training methods such as discriminator guidance. This paper addresses the difficulty of estimating it reliably while retaining scalability to high-dimensional settings.

The proposed estimator uses Sobolev regularization, which the authors identify as important both for statistical consistency and for stable learning with small samples. Their analysis establishes a convergence rate depending on sample size, dimension, and the smoothness of the underlying densities. It also provides a minimax lower bound in mean-squared error, describing a fundamental statistical constraint on this estimation problem.

Empirically, the regularized estimator is substantially more stable than existing methods in small-sample settings. The paper demonstrates its use in transfer learning for ECG signal generation, where it substantially outperforms non-regularized score-difference estimators on downstream classification. This connects the estimator’s mathematical properties with practical benefits when adapting a generative model from limited target data.
summary.tldr: Sobolev regularization enables a consistent, scalable score-difference estimator with improved small-sample stability and demonstrated benefits for ECG generation transfer.

title: Sobolev Regularized Score Difference Estimation in Diffusion Models

abstract: Relational databases (RDBs) contain vast amounts of heterogeneous tabular information that can be exploited for predictive modeling purposes. But since the space of potential targets is vast across enterprise settings, how can we avoid retraining a new model each time we wish to predict a new quantity of interest? Foundation models based on in-context learning (ICL) offer a convenient option, but so far are largely restricted to single-table operability. In generalizing to multiple interrelated tables, it is essential to compress variably-sized RDB neighborhoods into fixed-length ICL samples for consumption by the decoder. However, the details here are critical: unlike existing supervised learning RDB pipelines, we provide theoretical and empirical evidence that ICL-specific compression should be constrained within high-dimensional RDB columns where all entities share units and roles, not across columns where the relevance of heterogeneous data types cannot be determined without extensive label information. Conditioned on this restriction, we then demonstrate that encoder expressiveness is actually not compromised by excluding trainable parameters. Hence we arrive at a principled family of RDB encoders that can be seamlessly paired with already-existing single-table ICL foundation models, whereby no training or fine-tuning is required. From a practical standpoint, we develop scalable SQL primitives to implement the encoder stage, resulting in the easy-to-use open-source RDBLearn foundation model capable of robust performance on unseen datasets out of the box.

paragraphs: Relational databases spread predictive information across interconnected tables. Existing in-context learning foundation models largely expect single-table inputs, creating a representation problem: database neighborhoods of varying sizes must become fixed-length examples. This paper investigates how to perform that conversion without training a new encoder for each predictive target.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that compression for in-context learning should stay within columns whose entities share units and roles. Compressing across heterogeneous columns requires judgments about relevance that may need extensive labels. Under the within-column restriction, they show that excluding trainable parameters does not compromise encoder expressiveness. This qualification is central to the claim that an untrained encoder can be sufficient.

The resulting encoder family can connect relational data to existing single-table in-context learning models without additional training or fine-tuning. The authors implement the encoding stage with scalable SQL primitives in RDBLearn and report robust performance on unseen datasets. The work makes the organization of database information, rather than newly learned encoder parameters, central to this adaptation.
summary.tldr: RDBLearn uses parameter-free, within-column encoders to connect relational databases to existing in-context learning models without additional training.

title: No Need to Train Your RDB Foundation Model

abstract: Efficiently scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) necessitates exploring alternatives to dominant autoregressive (AR) methods, with Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) emerging as candidates. However, comparing AR (typically decoder-only) and MDM (often encoder-only) paradigms is confounded by differing architectures, obscuring true algorithmic and efficiency trade-offs. This research decouples these factors by evaluating MDMs within a decoder-only framework to: (1) Equitably compare MDM (as Any-Order AR) and standard AR paradigms through discrepancies on orders. (2) Investigate MDM architectural impacts on computational efficiency. We show decoder-only MDMs, despite a larger modeling space, can achieve significant inference speedups ($\sim25\times$) and comparable perplexity with techniques like temperature annealing, offering a path to reduced inference compute. This work provides insights for developing more computationally efficient foundation models by disentangling core modeling choices from architectural influences. Code is available at https://github.com/scxue/AO-GPT-MDM.

paragraphs: Comparisons between autoregressive language models and masked diffusion models often change two things at once: the generation procedure and the network architecture. Autoregressive models typically use decoder-only networks, while masked diffusion models often use encoder-only networks. This makes it difficult to determine whether differences in quality or speed come from the modeling approach or the architecture.

The paper separates these choices by implementing masked diffusion within a decoder-only framework. It treats masked diffusion as an any-order autoregressive formulation, making generation order a central point of comparison with standard autoregressive modeling. Holding the architectural family consistent also allows the researchers to investigate how architectural choices affect the computational efficiency of masked diffusion.

The authors report that decoder-only masked diffusion models can achieve approximately 25-fold inference speedups and comparable perplexity using techniques including temperature annealing. These findings show that the larger modeling space associated with flexible generation order need not prevent efficient inference. The contribution is both a route toward reduced inference compute and a clearer way to compare generation methods without conflating them with different network designs.
summary.tldr: Evaluating masked diffusion in decoder-only networks separates generation choices from architecture and demonstrates roughly 25-fold inference speedups with comparable perplexity.

title: Any-Order GPT as Masked Diffusion Model: Decoupling Formulation and Architecture

abstract: While visually grounded Chain-of-Thought (CoT) has emerged as a promising paradigm to enhance fine-grained perception in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), its efficacy during the inference phase remains underexplored. In this work, we empirically find that mandating explicit object boxes in visually grounded CoT during inference often degrades performance compared to standard textual CoT, which reasons without explicit visual grounding. We hypothesize that the visual localization capability can be internalized into the textual CoT and that the mandatory explicit grounding introduces unnecessary interference with the model’s primary objective of answer prediction. To address this problem, we propose Internalizing Visually Grounded Reasoning (iVGR), a novel reinforcement learning framework that transfers localization capabilities into the textual reasoning process. We employ a dual-stream training strategy, where a textual stream is aligned with a high-quality visually grounded stream via a proposed consistency reward, enabling the model to localize accurately without explicit grounding during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines on fine-grained benchmarks, while maintaining the flexibility to support tool-assisted inference workflows. Project page: https://visual-ai.github.io/ivgr/

paragraphs: Requiring a vision-language model to name explicit object boxes while reasoning might seem helpful for precise perception. This paper finds that doing so at inference often reduces performance compared with ordinary textual reasoning. The authors hypothesize that mandatory localization output can interfere with answering, even though the underlying ability to locate objects remains valuable.

iVGR aims to transfer that localization ability into textual reasoning through reinforcement learning. Training uses two streams: a textual reasoning stream and a high-quality visually grounded stream. A consistency reward aligns the textual stream with the grounded one, teaching the model to use localization capabilities without requiring explicit grounding outputs when answering at inference time.

Experiments report significant improvements over existing baselines on fine-grained benchmarks. The trained model also retains support for workflows that use tools during inference. The contribution is a training strategy that separates learning from explicit visual grounding from the requirement to display it in every answer, with the proposed explanation for interference remaining a hypothesis.
summary.tldr: iVGR transfers visual localization skills into textual reasoning, improving fine-grained performance without requiring explicit object boxes at inference.

title: iVGR: Internalizing Visually Grounded Reasoning for MLLMs with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In the era of transformer models, masked self-supervised learning (SSL) has become a foundational training paradigm. A defining feature of masked SSL is that training aggregates predictions across many masking patterns, giving rise to a joint, matrix-valued predictor rather than a single vector-valued estimator. This object encodes how coordinates condition on one another and poses new analytical challenges. We develop a precise high-dimensional analysis of masked modeling objectives in the proportional regime where the number of samples scales with the ambient dimension. Our results provide explicit expressions for the generalization error and characterize the spectral structure of the learned predictor, revealing how masked modeling extracts structure from data. For spiked covariance models, we show that the joint predictor undergoes a Baik–Ben Arous–Péché (BBP)-type phase transition, identifying when masked SSL begins to recover latent signals. Finally, we identify structured regimes in which masked self-supervised learning provably outperforms PCA, highlighting potential advantages of SSL objectives over classical unsupervised methods.

paragraphs: Masked self-supervised learning trains a model to predict hidden parts of data from the parts it can see. Because training combines many different masking patterns, the learned relationships form a matrix describing how coordinates help predict one another. This paper studies that combined predictor, making it the central object of its mathematical analysis.

The analysis considers a high-dimensional setting in which sample count grows proportionally with data dimension. Within this regime, the authors derive explicit generalization-error expressions and characterize the predictor’s spectral structure. For spiked covariance models, they identify a phase transition: recovery of latent signals begins across a mathematically characterized boundary.

The paper also identifies structured settings where masked learning provably outperforms principal component analysis. This establishes an advantage under those settings, rather than a universal ranking of the methods. Together, the results explain how masking objectives can extract underlying structure and specify circumstances in which their benefits extend beyond classical unsupervised learning.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis identifies when masked self-supervised learning recovers latent signals and structured settings where it provably outperforms PCA.

abstract: Motivated by the interest in relational reinforcement learning, we introduce a novel relational Bellman update operator called ReBel. It employs a constraint logic programming language to compactly represent Markov decision processes over relational domains. Using ReBel, a novel value iteration algorithm is developed in which abstraction (over states and actions) plays a major role. This frameworkprovides new insights into relational reinforcement learning. Convergence results as well as experiments are presented.
originalAbstract: Motivated by the interest in relational reinforcement learning, we introduce a novel relational Bellman update operator called ReBel. It employs a constraint logic programming language to compactly represent Markov decision processes over relational domains. Using ReBel, a novel value iteration algorithm is developed in which abstraction (over states and actions) plays a major role. This frameworkprovides new insights into relational reinforcement learning. Convergence results as well as experiments are presented.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bellman update for reinforcement learning in relational domains. The proposed operator, ReBel, is designed to work with a compact description of a Markov decision process expressed in a constraint logic programming language. The representation makes relational structure part of the machinery used to describe the decision problem.

Using ReBel, the authors construct a value iteration algorithm in which abstraction over both states and actions has a central role. The contribution connects the representation of the problem with the operation used to update values. State and action abstraction are therefore part of how the algorithm performs its reasoning about the relational decision process.

The paper presents convergence results and experiments, alongside the new operator and algorithm. Its significance is a concrete framework for bringing relational representations into Bellman-style computation. The theoretical results address convergence within that framework, while the experiments provide an additional examination of the proposed approach to relational reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: ReBel combines a relational Bellman update with state and action abstraction to support value iteration on compactly represented decision processes.

title: Bellman goes relational

abstract: This paper studies the aggregation of predictions made by tree-based models for several perturbed versions of the attribute vector of a test case. A closed-form approximation of this scheme combined with cross-validation to tune the level of perturbation is proposed. This yields soft-tree models in a parameter free way, and preserves their interpretability. Empirical evaluations, on classification and regression problems, show that accuracy and bias/variance tradeoff are improved significantly at the price of an acceptable computational overhead. The method is further compared and combined with tree bagging.

paragraphs: A tree-based model can be evaluated on several slightly altered versions of a test example, and its predictions can then be combined. This paper studies that approach to prediction. The changes are made to the example's attribute vector, so the aggregation reflects how the tree responds around the input being evaluated.

The authors propose a closed-form approximation to this procedure, together with cross-validation to select the amount of perturbation. This produces soft-tree models while preserving interpretability. The approach is described as parameter free because perturbation strength is selected through the procedure, rather than left as a manually chosen setting.

Empirical evaluations cover both classification and regression. They report significant improvements in accuracy and the bias–variance tradeoff, with computational overhead the authors judge acceptable. The method is also compared and combined with tree bagging. These results support smoothing a tree's predictions through perturbed inputs as a useful approach that can also be considered alongside an ensemble technique.
summary.tldr: A closed-form approximation to averaging tree predictions over perturbed inputs improves accuracy empirically while preserving interpretability.

abstract: Prediction suffix trees (PSTs) are a popular tool for modeling sequences and have been successfully applied in many domains such as compression and language modeling. In this work we adapt the well studied Winnow algorithm to the task of learning PSTs. The proposed algorithm automatically grows the tree, so that it provably remains competitive with any fixed PST determined in hindsight. At the same time we prove that the depth of the tree grows only logarithmically with the number of mistakes made by the algorithm. Finally, we empirically demonstrate its effectiveness in two different tasks.

In this work we adapt the well studied Winnow algorithm to the task of learning PSTs. The proposed algorithm automatically grows the tree, so that it provably remains competitive with any fixed PST determined in hindsight. At the same time we prove that the depth of the tree grows only logarithmically with the number of mistakes made by the algorithm. Finally, we empirically demonstrate its effectiveness in two different tasks.

paragraphs: Prediction suffix trees model sequences using a tree of contexts drawn from preceding symbols. They have applications including compression and language modeling. This paper adapts the Winnow learning algorithm to learn such trees, addressing both predictive performance and how the tree's structure should expand during learning.

The proposed algorithm grows its tree automatically. The authors prove that its performance remains competitive with any fixed prediction suffix tree selected in hindsight. This comparison matters because the reference tree can be chosen after the sequence is known, whereas the learning algorithm must build and use its own representation as it proceeds.

A second guarantee links structural growth to errors: the depth grows only logarithmically with the number of mistakes the algorithm makes. This controls tree depth while allowing the representation to adapt, rather than requiring a fixed depth from the outset. Experiments on two tasks demonstrate effectiveness. Together, the results connect automatic structure growth, a predictive comparison guarantee, and restrained growth in the length of contexts represented.
summary.tldr: A Winnow-based learner automatically grows prediction suffix trees with a competitiveness guarantee and logarithmic depth growth in its mistake count.

title: Learning prediction suffix trees with Winnow

abstract: We show how the SVM can be viewed as a maximum likelihood estimate of a class of probabilistic models. This model class can be viewed as a reparametrization of the SVM in a similar vein to the $\nu$-SVM reparametrizing the original SVM. It is not discriminative, but has a non-uniform marginal. We illustrate the benefits of this new view by re-deriving and re-investigating two established SVM-related algorithms.
originalAbstract: We show how the SVM can be viewed as a maximum likelihood estimate of a class of probabilistic models. This model class can be viewed as a reparametrization of the SVM in a similar vein to the $\nu$-SVM reparametrizing the original SVM. It is not discriminative, but has a non-uniform marginal. We illustrate the benefits of this new view by re-deriving and re-investigating two established SVM-related algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper shows that a support vector machine can be interpreted as a maximum likelihood estimate within a class of probabilistic models. The result connects the SVM learning procedure to probabilistic estimation. Its central contribution is a different mathematical view of the classifier and of the model family that it represents.

The authors describe that family as a reparameterization of the SVM, drawing an analogy with the way the nu-SVM reparameterizes the original formulation. The probabilistic model is not discriminative and has a non-uniform marginal distribution. Those properties are part of the proposed interpretation, so the result should not be reduced to the claim that the SVM simply learns conditional class probabilities.

To illustrate the usefulness of the perspective, the paper re-derives and re-examines two established SVM-related algorithms. This makes the interpretation operational: it supplies a framework for revisiting existing procedures as well as describing the SVM itself. The stated benefit is a new route to understanding those algorithms, with no empirical performance improvement asserted in the abstract.
summary.tldr: The SVM is recast as maximum likelihood estimation in a non-discriminative probabilistic model family with a non-uniform marginal.

title: Support Vector Machines as Probabilistic Models
